news.title: Homeless man faring better due to his Cork Simon Community 'guardian angel', court told
news.text:
Eddie Burke, solicitor, said: “He was recently very badly assaulted and his jaw broken. He is not under the influence of intoxicants now. He is in much better condition in that regard than a recent court appearance.

“He is usually accompanied by his key workers from Simon. He is not drinking as much. He has just been put on a housing list with Simon and he is hoping to get his own accommodation. 

"His key worker is very much his guardian angel.” 

Sergeant Aisling Murphy outlined details of the public order incident which occurred at St. Patrick’s Street, Cork, on August 24.

Gardaí encountered Kamil Raban stumbling around the pavement, slurring his words and there was a smell of intoxicating liquor from his breath. When approached by gardaí, Kamil Raban became highly aggressive calling gardaí c***s and telling them to f*** off several times.

Sgt Murphy said Mr Raban had 40 previous convictions including seven for being abusive and insulting and 16 for being so intoxicated that he was a danger.

Judge Waters said: “While it was verbal, it was unpleasant and it was a nuisance. I am not going to keep giving him fines — he needs to understand that. If this happens again I will be considering a jail sentence.” 

In this case, the judge fined him €350 on the threatening charge and took the drunkenness into consideration.
news.summary: 'He is not under the influence of intoxicants now. He is in much better condition in that regard than a recent court appearance.'
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,Liam Heylin

Tinker Tailor German Spy

Germany reels amid major spy scandal, but sources say Ireland has little to worry about

August Hanning ran Germany’s BND foreign intelligence agency between 1998 and 2005 and is suspected of charges including “attempted treason” and “espionage”.

8.01pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

Niall O'Connor

AS GERMANY REELS from a major spying scandal at the centre of its intelligence services, it is unlikely to worry Irish security services, sources have said. 

August Hanning, who ran Germany’s BND intelligence agency between 1998 and 2005, is suspected of charges including “attempted treason” and “espionage”, according to a statement from federal prosecutors.

Hanning’s former chief of staff, partially named as Manfred D., was also arrested on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage”.

Premises linked to both men were searched in several locations including the capital Berlin.

Prosecutors say that Manfred D. also served as the chief of staff for Hanning’s successors between 2012 and 2026, and used this role to gain access to confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning “in exchange for remuneration”.

The BND is Germany’s foreign intelligence agency similar to that of the French DGSE, the British MI6 or the American CIA.

The scandal has caused major ripples across Europe’s intelligence services. The biggest concern, sources said, is that the sharing of sensitive intelligence may expose collection methods and the identities of agents and spies. 

The Daily Telegraph reports that a review is underway inside MI6 and US agencies to determine if any of their sensitive data shared with Germany may have been included in what was sold on by Hanning. 

BND reputation

It has not come as a major surprise, with many sources stating that the BND has a reputation internationally as a service with a number of previous compromises or leaks. 

This has caused trust in the service’s interactions with other agencies to be limited for safety reasons.

One source who has direct knowledge of the agency said that much of that exposure can be blamed on the previous East German occupation by Russia.

Sources have also said that one key security problem is that lucrative consultancy jobs for ex-high level security forces officials are not just a German issue but also globally. The sector provides generally high level supposed open source information to businesses. 

Advertisement

The more unique and insightful the information is, the more likely businesses will continue to pay large sums of money.

Besides the exponential increase in pay for greater information, the real concern, sources said, is that some of the consultancy work could be a front for espionage. 

August Hanning, the former president of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND).Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Sources here in Ireland believe that it is very unlikely that Ireland has anything to worry about with the German incident. 

It is understood that the Irish involvement with the BND is limited at most, with only minimum engagement. 

It is understood that most Irish intelligence interactions would be between An Garda Síochána and Germany’s Federal Police. 

An example of their interactions, one source said, is around background information for criminals active in Ireland who may have had a connection to Germany. BND generally would not be the agency with that information to share. 

A number of sources said that Ireland has deeper involvement with other countries in regard to sharing intelligence but Ireland’s ability to provide data that would interest foreign powers is limited. 

Ireland’s intelligence operations are handled by two agencies: the Garda National Crime and Security Intelligence Service and the Defence Forces Irish Military Intelligence Service, known formerly as J2. 

One senior source defined the nature of intelligence sharing as a “traded commodity” and said Ireland would have little to offer the German BND. 

Another source said that Ireland has particular expertise in financial intelligence and corporate knowledge but does not have a network of intelligence officers in foreign countries. 

Multiple sources have said that the Irish Defence Forces presence in South Lebanon and its connections with local communities in Hezbollah strongholds has provided some opportunities to share with other intelligence systems. 

Security sources here have raised issue with the consultancy and lobbying sector risk here in Ireland and how former and serving senior officials retire and join the area. 

Niall O'Connor

news.title: Lack of recruitment in autopsy services causing increased funeral wait times, coroners warn
news.text:
“An advanced mortuary technician had retired, and they hadn't replaced her, and all of a sudden, in one particular area, there were suddenly no PMs (post-mortems) being done in that area, and bodies had to be moved around,” he said.

“There are areas all over the country where funerals are being delayed, that classically would be Dublin, then the South East.

“But all over the areas, there are systems that are functioning under great strain, both in relation to post-mortem pathologists, and even in one situation where the known retirement of an advanced mortuary technician was not planned for and caused short-term chaos in an area.

“It only highlights the situation that this is not a system that's appreciated or planned.” 

In response to queries from the Irish Examiner, the HSE said the vacant post had been offered to a successful candidate.

In a March report to the HSE focused on the state of play across the State’s different pathology services, a survey was conducted across different units. 

Cork University Hospital warned that there was “insufficient space for current workload and staff levels". 

“The service is operating under significant and escalating capacity pressures, with infrastructure that is no longer fit for purpose,” the report read.

“We are operating at full capacity and are unable to safely accommodate additional service developments, staff or equipment.”

A lack of technological innovation was also flagged as a major stress point.

The pathology unit in St Vincent’s Hospital in Co Dublin raised alarm over “critical infrastructure constraints, including inadequate laboratory space, insufficient office accommodation for clinical, scientific, and administrative staff, and a lack of appropriate storage capacity for blocks and slides."

Tallaght University Hospital said it had been without a full complement of staff since 2019 amid a "chronic national shortage" of trained staff.

Justice minister Jim O’Callaghan previously wrote to health minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill (who both share joint responsibility for the sector), and articulated fears that traditional societal norms around funerals could be upended if immediate resolutions weren't put in place.

Strain on the sector's inability to replace outgoing staff nearly forced the bodies of children who died in stillbirth to be exported out of Ireland.

In a letter dated January 5, 2026, Dublin’s Chief Coroner Myra Cullinane wrote to Ms Carroll MacNeill, raising alarm bells over the Coombe Hospital's inability to conduct perinatal post-mortems.

“The Chief Clinical Operating Officer of the Coombe Hospital advises that attempts to recruit a perinatal pathologist and to seek assistance from other centres have met with no success,” Ms Cullinane wrote.

“Where a coroner’s postmortem examination is required in relation to any perinatal death occurring at the Coombe Hospital, I will have no option but to seek extra jurisdictional assistance which will necessitate the transfer of infant remains out of State.”

HSE chief executive Bernard Gloster wrote to the health minister three weeks later that a €3m interim solution had been reached.
news.summary: 'There are areas all over the country where funerals are being delayed', says Irish Coroner’s Society president
news.author: Alex Cunningham,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: Cork man denies dragging passenger out of car at service station and beating him unconscious
news.text:
Detective Garda Conor Cronin objected to bail and in reply to a question from defence solicitor Eddie Burke about what was specifically alleged against Mr O’Shea, the detective said: “He was dragged out by a male other than Timmy O’Shea and then he was beaten unconscious by all three men.” 

Det Garda Cronin said the concern of An Garda Síochána was the alleged robbery was carried out to feed a drug addiction and further offences would be committed to support this habit.

Mr Burke said to his client when he was in the witness box at Cork District Court: “You are adamant you have absolutely nothing to do with these charges.” Timmy O’Shea replied: “Yes, that is what I stated to the guards.”

As regards committing offences to feed an addiction, he said: “I am in Arbour House on Suboxone [medication for drug treatment]. My urines are clean. There is nothing to back up that story. I don’t take drugs. I got steady on Suboxone up in Arbour House. 

"It is not going to happen where I put myself in a position where I get years in prison.” 

Det Garda Cronin said in terms of the strength of evidence, a Revolut card taken from the injured person was found on Timmy O’Shea of Cork Simon Community one hour after the robbery.

Mr Burke queried why it had taken until now to charge the defendant on something that dates back to August 16.

Judge David Waters refused bail and remanded the accused in custody until October 12.

Det Garda Cronin said in his evidence that on August 16 at 7.30am at Top Oil South City Link service station, Timmy O'Shea and two other men were back seat passengers in a car after asking the occupants for a spin. 

The car stopped and the driver went into the shop. The three men then dragged the front seat passenger out of the car and beat him unconscious and proceeded to rob items from his person.

The same defendant, 46-year-old Timmy O’Shea, is also charged with burglary on September 30 at The Shelf bookshop on George’s Quay, where €235 was stolen from the till.
news.summary: Revolut card taken from the injured person was found on defendant one hour after the robbery, court heard

'It punishes people who are addicted': Some opposition TDs question €1 hike on cigarettes

Some TDs said the price hike will hit older people who are addicted to cigarettes, while others criticised the government’s health strategy.

7.56pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

THE PRICE OF a packet of 20 cigarettes rose by €1 from midnight on Tuesday night, pushing a box to over €20. 

“Smoking continues to kill so many Irish people every year. It is important that we continue to discourage and dissuade people, particularly younger people, from smoking,” Harris said as he announced the price increases.

However, a number of TDs have questioned the rationale behind the price hike, with some calling out the government for failing to hit its tobacco-free Ireland targets in recent years. 

The government believes increasing the cost by €1 will prevent people from smoking, but some TDs disagree. 

Kerry TD Danny Healy-Rae said he is against the increase, stating that many elderly people are addicted to cigarettes.

“Even though the minister might say that increasing the cost by €1 will prevent them from smoking, I do not think it will. They will have to endure more hardship. The only comfort that many of these people have is their cigarette. If people buy five packets in a week, that would not be an awful lot. That will now cost in excess of €100,” he said. 

He said he did not like cigarettes and has never smoked, but said he was concerned that the increased cost will eat into elderly peoples’ social welfare or pension payment. 

Tobacco-free Ireland targets

Others, such as Labour’s Duncan Smith, questioned the success of the government’s quest for a tobacco-free Ireland, stating that when the strategy was launched by former health minister James Reilly in 2013, smoking rates were at 22%.

The target was to be at 5% by 2025, he said, but pointed out it now stands at 17%.

“It has been an abject failure by the government’s and the HSE’s own target for Ireland becoming a tobacco-free State,” he said, stating that the annual increase on a pack of cigarettes has become a substitute for what should be a robust public health policy.

Advertisement

“There are 100 deaths per week and 1,000 hospitalisations per week due to smoking. After this budget, it will cost €1 per cigarette. The government can make the cost €10 per cigarette,” said Smith, adding:

If it is not backed up, the taxation side, with a robust public health approach, it will continue to fail.

Sinn Féin’s Thomas Gould said there was a time when increasing the price of tobacco was an effective public health measure. However, he questioned if it is working. 

“We all understood and agreed with that. However, we must be honest about where we are now. This strategy now has diminishing returns in relation to people not smoking or giving up smoking. The reality is that it is just pushing the prices up and up again. As a strategy on its own, that is not enough,” he added. 

He said the government is driving people to the black market, stating that the government needs to take a more nuanced approach to solving addiction. 

Independent TD Barry Heneghan said he supported the increase in excise duty on tobacco products, but said a €1 increase is not really acceptable while coloured and flavoured vapes are being pushed on young people in shops and petrol stations. 

He called for the money raised in taxation to be used to jointly tackle smoking and vape addiction. 

Price hike hitting older people 

People Before Profit’s Richard Boyd Barrett said: 

“I was a smoker for many years, and I am glad to say I am off them. It is very important that we discourage young people from smoking, but I have to be honest and say I do not think adding a bill of €350 to people who are addicted over the course of the year is really the answer to that.

“We often hit older people, people on low incomes and people who are being punished for having an addiction. It would be better if they did not have it, but I do not personally believe in punishing them. I know there is some connection between price and consumption, but it is not an absolute law by any means.” 

Aontú’s Paul Lawless said he could not support the price hike on cigarettes as he believes it is punishing people who are addicted to cigarettes.

There may have been a value in increasing this a number of years ago, but it is at a point now where this is just inflicting more pain and more hardship on people.

“In some cases these are people on the lower margins as well. These are people who will sacrifice food, heating and other essentials for their cigarettes because they are so addicted. I urge the Government to reconsider this policy going forward. 

He asked the government to put its energy into tackling the proliferation of vape shops around the country, which he said are destroying young people.

Related Reads

From income tax cuts to another euro on cigarettes: Here are the main points of Budget 2027

Cigarettes to hit €20 a box for the first time from midnight tonight

“Vapes are a gateway into cigarettes, so this is the new issue we need to tackle,” he said. 

The finance minister was asked at a press conference on Tuesday what the taxation plan is for tobacco into the future and whether the strategy is to just increase the price each year.

No taxation plan

Harris said there was no “taxation map on where to get to”, stating that it is a matter that is reviewed annually.

The Department of Health makes a submission each year to the Department of Finance, and it is considered. 

He said in previous years a price hike of 50c has been placed on a pack of cigarettes, stating that this year the government decided to go even higher to “build momentum” towards a tobacco-free Ireland. 

However, from an economic point of view, the minister acknowledged there is a diminishing return in terms of the tax take the more the government puts the price up.

“You do get to a saturation point in terms of additional taxation that is brought in,” said Harris. 

The Royal College of Physicians of Ireland (RCPI) has said the government should introduce tobacco-free generation legislation which would prohibit the sale of tobacco products to people born after a specified year.

It said it is necessary for what it calls “tobacco endgame,” while it has also recommended that the price of a packet of 20 cigarettes should be raised to over €20.

The HSE states that one in two smokers will die from a tobacco-related disease, and that every week, around 100 people die and around 1,000 people are hospitalised in Ireland from smoking-related illness.

Christina Finn

“As a result, Celia will be unavailable for public engagements for a period of time. Her family asks that their privacy be respected during this difficult period so that they can focus on her care and recovery,” the family added.

They also said they are “deeply grateful for the outpouring of love, prayers and good wishes” they have received.

news.title: Christa Pike ‘angry and confused’ after surviving execution, says lawyer
news.text:
Pike, 50, survived after executioners tried to give her two lethal doses of pentobarbital on September 30. She was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer.

“She is angry and confused about everything right now. She is very aware of what they did to her up to a point,” Mr Spivey said during a news conference.

“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning but I do know she has a long road to recovery,” he added.

The Death Penalty Information Centre says Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.

At a hearing on Wednesday in Nashville, Pike’s lawyers asked the court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to save evidence in the case and provide more information about what went wrong.

A judge ordered the state to preserve “anything that was in the actual room”.

“Part of the issue that we are facing is up until yesterday, our client was unconscious, unable to communicate with counsel, unable to communicate with medical providers, and without her consent” a new lawsuit cannot be filed, Luke Ihnen, a federal public defender, told the court.

Her legal team said on Tuesday that Pike’s prognosis remains unclear and, at a minimum, she faces a lengthy recovery. Her arms were burned and blistered after the attempted lethal injection and she is handcuffed to the hospital bed, they said.

The failed execution has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty, in particular the use of lethal injection. On Wednesday, Texas was set to carry out the first execution in the US since Tennessee attempted to put Pike to death.

Pike’s lawyers wanted a court order to require the prison system to preserve information from the attempted execution, including drug lot numbers, needles, execution logs and other information.

Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles indicated that her order to save the evidence would be sweeping, saying the state should maintain recordings, witness accounts and emails, along with drugs, syringes, IV lines and other medical items.

The Tennessee Attorney General’s Office said a court order was unnecessary. John W Ayers, assistant attorney general, said evidence from the death chamber had already been collected and logged.

Republican governor Bill Lee called what happened “deeply disturbing” and ordered a “comprehensive third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”. He postponed the state’s only other execution scheduled for this year.

The state’s prison chief resigned after the failed execution.

Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on the possibility that a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in Pike’s tissue rather than entering her bloodstream.

Her lawyers wrote in their court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown”.

The attempted execution got under way at around 7.30pm on September 30 when Pike was given a chance to make a final statement. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm was hurting.

At some point she appeared to lose consciousness, but she could be heard breathing until media were escorted from the witness room at 8.53pm. An ambulance arrived at the prison at 9.14pm to take her to hospital.

Dr Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said it could be weeks or months before anyone knows what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored so the state can try again to execute her.
news.summary: Christa Pike is “angry and confused” after regaining consciousness almost six days after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her, one of her ...

Mark Zuckerberg paid over €50m for Strancally Castle in Waterford

It’s far in excess of the estimated sale price of between €20 million and €30 million first reported.

7.36pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

META’S CHIEF EXECUTIVE and co-founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, paid out more than €51 million for Strancally Castle in Co Waterford in August, new figures show.

A new entry on the Residential Property Price Register today shows that Strancally Castle at Knockanore, Co Waterford commanded a sales price of €51,171,155 when the sale was completed on 17 August.

The €51.17 million for the gothic-style mansion and its 178-hectare (440-acre) estate is far in excess of the estimated sale price of between €20 million and €30 million when first reported in August.

In the aftermath of the sale, a spokesperson for Mr Zuckerberg said: “Mark and his family are excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time in Ireland, where Meta maintains its international headquarters”.

While the €51.1 million paid out is by some distance a record price paid for a single residential property here this year it will not trouble Mr Zuckerberg with Forbes putting a current estimate of $248.7bn (€222.51 billion) on his wealth.

It is understood that the billionaire social media company owner and his family will use the property in Waterford when carrying out Meta business in Ireland

The castle was built in 1830 for John Keily, a former Conservative MP, and designed on a grand scale by the architects James and George Richard Pain.

The castle was previously owned by Michael Alen Buckley, a co-founder of London-based private investment firm RAB Capital, and his wife Giancarla, whose father was the late hotelier Charles Forte.

Advertisement

The couple acquired Strancally Castle 25 years ago and carried out an extensive restoration of the three-storey property, which extends to 16,000 sq ft.

In the aftermath of the sale last month, Councillor John Pratt (Labour) who lives in Tallow and is Cathaoirleach of Dungarvan and Lismore Municipal Committee, said he hopes Zuckerberg’s arrival will help showcase the area’s attractions.

“I think it’s great news for the area. I’m sure that people will do everything they can to make Mr Zuckerberg and his family feel welcome to our beautiful community,” he said.

Last week it emerged that Zuckerberg and Chan donated €150,000 to the three GAA clubs which are located closest to Strancally Castle in Co Waterford.

The three clubs – Shamrocks GAA in Knockanore, Tallow GAA in Tallow, and Lismore GAA in Lismore – will each receive €50,000.

The donations are to be paid to the clubs over a two-year period, with each club receiving €25,000 per year.

Facebook opened its international headquarters in Dublin in 2009 and Meta currently employs about 1,500 people in Ireland.

In 2004, a then 19-year-old Mark Zuckerberg started Facebook for students to match names with photos of classmates.

Zuckerberg – now aged 42 – took Facebook public in 2012; he now owns about 13% of the company’s stock.

Today Meta, which also owns WhatsApp and Instagram, has a market capitalisation of $1.85trn.

Gordon Deegan

news.title: Christa Pike's lawyers confirm first words she asked after botched execution
news.text: Christa Pike asked “Where am I and who are you?” after waking in hospital following a botched execution attempt, her lawyers have said. The convicted killer remains in a Nashville hospital after surviving two lethal injections and being rushed for emergency treatment last week. Speaking outside a Tennessee courthouse on Tuesday, her lawyer said Pike was “angry and confused” when she regained consciousness and was “very aware that the state tried to execute her”. He also described “extraordinary” swelling to her hands in the aftermath of the failed execution, saying they looked as though “if you tried to blow up a surgical glove", The Mirror reports. Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, was due to become the first woman executed in Tennessee for more than two centuries. But the execution was halted after she reportedly survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital and later regained consciousness, according to her lawyers. The mother of murdered teenager Colleen Slemmer has said she is losing faith that her daughter’s killer, Christa Pike, will ever face the death penalty after her failed execution attempt. May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, said she had never believed Pike would die during the procedure and now doubts the state will make another attempt to carry out the sentence. Pike's lawyer also described how she had woken up with a blood clot and pneumonia, adding that she couldn't swallow or move her arms - both of which were swollen. "I don't know what function she will regain," he said. The death row inmate's legal team told the court that the botched execution was “foreseeable and foreseen” due to her medical condition. “What happened to Christa is exactly what the state was warned would happen, and there are so many questions that need to be answered, not by Christa - but by the state of Tennessee", Randy Spivey said. "Christa was at peace, she helped the execution team find what that they thought was venous access." Want to see more of the stories you love from the Irish Mirror? Pike has not been able to swallow or eat since she regained consciousness, Mr Spivey said, adding "we do know that there is a long road ahead." A second lawyer for Christa Pike speaking outside the courthouse said that it was her legal team's understanding that she was "brain dead" and "life support would be removed the next day. He said that Pike was a "survivor". He added she had survived "child sexual abuse, rapes of multiple men, she survived a suicide attempt when she was 12 and she survived a state's attempt to execute her.

news.title: Christa Pike is ‘angry and confused’ after failed execution, say lawyers
news.text:
A Nashville judge said she would order Tennessee officials to preserve ‌all evidence from the state’s failed attempt to execute Christa Pike last week for a 1995 murder, including the syringes and other tools used in two botched lethal injections.

Pike (50), was taken to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and with severe arm injuries after two injections of the caustic ​barbiturate pentobarbital failed to kill her at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution last Wednesday.

She had regained consciousness and was speaking ​as of Tuesday and remains shackled to her hospital bed, according to her lawyers, as they ⁠seek to pierce the secrecy that normally surrounds execution procedures in Tennessee and other states.

Her lawyer Randy Spivey said: “Our understanding was the first thing she said was ‘Where am I and who are you?’ There’s still a lot of cognitive confusion, and so I will say that she has wanted to know what’s happened, and she’s asked about several people. She’s asked about her team. She’s asked about the victim’s family ... I think she is angry and confused about everything right now. 

“She is very aware that the state tried to execute her,” Spivey continued.

Earlier Spivey said: “Christa has a long road to recovery. She has a blood clot in one of her arms. She has pneumonia. She is not able to swallow yet, so she has not eaten. She cannot move either of her arms. Both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what, if any, function she will regain in her arms. But we do know that there’s a long road ahead, and that is just the physical toll that all of this is taking,”

Pike’s lawyers have said the botched execution, the ​second this year in Tennessee, amounts to torture in violation of the US constitution’s prohibition on cruel or unusual punishments.

Pike, who was ​sentenced to death for her role as a teenager in the torture and murder of her 19-year-old schoolmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, is the first person known to have survived a “completed execution attempt” in the US, her lawyers say.

They asked the judge in Davidson County chancery court, I’Ashea Myles, to ​order Tennessee officials to preserve all evidence from the failed execution, including syringes, drug packaging and lot numbers, catheters, intravenous lines ​and gurney restraints.

Myles largely sided with Pike’s lawyers at the end of Wednesday’s hearing, describing the litigation, which began in January in an effort ‌to ⁠prevent the scheduled execution, as unusual because no one had anticipated Pike surviving.

“This case is unique, to say the least,” Myles said.

She also ordered the state to preserve internal communications about the attempted execution, including incident reports, witness accounts and encrypted messages.

She has yet to rule on a request by Pike’s lawyers that the Tennessee Department of Correction let them take any residual traces of the ​execution drugs for chemical analysis.

The ​Tennessee Department of Correction has ⁠opposed what it says is a “duplicative and unnecessary” preservation order, arguing it is already legally required to preserve all evidence.

Tennessee and other US states have long struggled to acquire execution drugs. They ​cannot be obtained from major pharmaceutical companies because of a European trade ban on companies that ​sell products for ⁠use in torture or executions.

Tennessee, like other states, has turned to small, largely unregulated compounding pharmacies to make small batches of the drugs, promising to hide their identity.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, a Republican who denied Pike’s clemency request to commute her sentence to life in ⁠prison, has ​called the botched execution a tragedy. He has suspended executions for the rest ​of the year and promised an investigation.

Pike’s lawyers had sought an alternative to lethal injections, saying their warnings had been ignored that her small veins and related ​medical conditions would risk something going wrong. – Reuters

news.summary: Judge says she will order Tennessee officials to preserve ‌all evidence from attempt to execute Pike

news.title: 'Head on collision' with RTÉ and government looming as row erupts over €20 million budget cut
news.text: A row has reignited as RTÉ was dealt a blow with €20 million less funding than promised in Budget 2027, with the broadcaster's top boss threatening: "We now have some important decisions to make." Media Minister Patrick O’Donovan defended the allocation, saying he is "unhappy" with the public broadcaster’s reform since the 2023 Ryan Tubridy payment scandal . But RTÉ Director-General Kevin Bakhurst hit back at this claim , saying: "We completely reject the assertion that the pace of reform and transformation within RTÉ has been slow." Mr Bakhurst threatened that without this funding RTÉ’s five-year strategy transformation will be impacted. A governance and financial crisis was triggered at the broadcaster when it was revealed that it had underreported Tubridy’s earnings by €345,000 over four years. To help it rebuild, the government committed to providing a €725 million public funding bailout over three years. For 2027, RTÉ was due to be given €260 million of this. But Minister O’Donovan said a smaller sum of €240 million was allocated in Budget 2027 as it reflects the overall funding available in his department. This will be made up of €66 million in direct Exchequer support, and €174 million in projected licence fee collections. However, the Fine Gael minister hasn’t solely blamed the €20 million reduction on his department’s allocated budget package. He reignited a row with the broadcaster, accusing top bosses of failing to reform the public broadcaster in a timely manner. Speaking today, the Media Minister said: "While progress has been made across a number of issues, I am not happy that we have seen sufficient progress in delivering the smaller, more agile processes that we sought to be delivered under the strategy." RTÉ is now seeking a meeting with the minister over the funding. Mr Bakhurst rejected Minister O'Donovan's claims, saying his team has delivered “extensive reform” since he took on the role of director general in July 2023. In a statement, he added: "The clarity provided through this multi-annual funding agreement enabled RTÉ to plan ahead, to deliver trusted, independent news and analysis. "To commit to producing more public service programmes and content for audiences, including original Irish drama and live sport, to invest in podcasts, apps and the RTÉ Player, to implement a digital commercial strategy, to stabilise our finances, and to make good on our plans." The top boss criticised the government for reducing the public funding agreement three months before it is due to be given. He said: "The government’s decision to reduce this public funding agreement by €20 million at this late stage, when we have already made important commitments to our audiences, to the independent sector, to other important stakeholders and to RTÉ staff, is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact on our ability to deliver our five-year strategy. "If the three-year multi-annual agreement will no longer be honoured – we now have some important decisions to make." Chair of the Oireachtas Media Committee Alan Kelly has demanded that Minister O'Donovan urgently explain the reason for cutting the agreed public funding by €20 million. He said this needs to be resolved "urgently" as a "head-on collision between RTÉ and government is now looming." news.summary: RTÉ has threatened that without this funding RTÉ’s five-year strategy transformation will be impacted

news.title: Israelis gather to remember victims of October 7th attack
news.text:
Israelis gathered on Wednesday at some 400 protests across the country to mark the third anniversary of the October 7th, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel. 

They renewed calls for a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the worst day in the country’s history, when 1,200 people were killed and 250 taken hostage to Gaza. 

Israeli president Yitzhak Herzog launched the commemorations by lighting a memorial candle at the president’s residence at 6.29am, the time the Hamas attack started.

Herzog then travelled to Netiv HaAsara, a farming community on the Gaza border, where militants on hang gliders landed on October 7th at the start of the invasion.

Memorial services took place at kibbutzim and other communities along the Gaza border that bore the brunt of the Hamas onslaught after the border fence was breached at more than 100 separate locations in the first hour of the attack.

At noon on Wednesday, hundreds of thousands of people observed a moment of silence across the country. 

Protesters brought the burnt-out shells of cars belonging to victims of the Nova music festival massacre to the demonstration outside the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, in Jerusalem.

Some 378 people were killed at the Nova site, the vast majority of them young revellers who were still dancing when the first rockets landed in the area. The rockets were followed minutes later by gunmen on motorcycles who opened fire indiscriminately. 

Provocative art installations were also a feature of Wednesday’s events. At Tel Aviv’s Dizengoff Square, protesters dyed the fountain water red. Rows of cut-out human figures were laid along a Tel Aviv beach, alongside a message reading: “October 7th – the price of the failure.”

Nine-month-old Kfir Bibas was the youngest victim of the Hamas attack. He died in captivity in Gaza along with his mother and elder brother, Ariel (4). His father Yarden, who was kidnapped separately and returned to Israel, issued a heartfelt message at the ceremony in kibbutz Nir Oz. “Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here.”

Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu lit a memorial candle honouring the October 7th victims, saying: “We will complete the mission. We came to settle the score with all the murderers, and we will.”

Netanyahu has rejected blame for the security breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation.

A survey released on Wednesday found that most Israelis believe the goals set out by Netanyahu at the beginning of the war, described as “total victory”, have not been achieved. 

Fewer than 20 per cent believe these goals have been achieved to a large extent or in full. Fewer than half of respondents believe Israel is safer today than it was before October 7th, while nearly a third believe the country is not as safe. 

Israel’s bombardment and ground operations in Gaza ​since the October 7th attack have killed more than 74,000 people, including at least 1,400 killed in the past year since a US-brokered ceasefire, which halted major fighting but has failed to stop Israeli attacks or ​secure the disarmament of Hamas.

Financial adviser on Budget 2027 
 Is the Irish government finally growing up?

Yesterday’s budget showed a more mature approach to Ireland’s finances from the government, but it did also leave some of the country’s biggest problems untouched.

7.16pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

Ralph Benson

IS OUR GOVERNMENT adulting? Our lookalike finance ministers (average age: 37) seem to have grown up. They have set out a budget which opens up opportunities for many people.

The government has moved beyond scattering €500 in every direction and hoping for the best, as witnessed in previous budgets. Instead, there is improved focus on some key areas that will build value for many years into the future.

Above all, there is a definite move towards a more mature culture of personal investing, saving, and wealth-building in this budget. As we’ll see, that’s important, because the government does not show much interest in building rainy day savings of its own. What’s also important is that this budget is less about creating winners and losers, and more about how each of us can take up the opportunities it offers, whatever our current financial position.

A budget for building wealth

There are three big positives for people trying to build wealth. First, the much-ballyhooed investment scheme. It turns out to be a touch more generous than many expected. You can add €12,000 a year, and you’re not taxed on the portion above €50,000. Above that, a 1% rate applies.

To be sure, there will be people who get a shock in a year they lose money and still find themselves paying the 1% wealth tax. But that is some time away – and many others will find a way to squirrel away, say, €24,000 over time, and double their money tax-free as investment markets do their work.

For many people, that’s a sizeable house deposit, or will fund children through third-level, or kill off the mortgage a few years early. It will also help spur a wider culture of investing, in a way the fabled SSIAs never did. We all knew they were too good to be repeated.

A positive aspect of this investment scheme is that you can start from low amounts. And it’ll be widely on offer from banks, brokers and online platforms. It seems likely that in five or seven years’ time, it’ll be as normal a part of our personal finances as opening credit union accounts and swapping Dunnes Stores money-off vouchers.

So much for the new. What about adjustments to existing arrangements? Much-despised taxes on investment returns have been cut, if not fully reformed. Capital gains tax falls from 33% to 31%, a move few expected. And exit tax on mutual funds falls from 38% to 35%, though fixing with Ireland’s weird deemed disposal regime is just too hard. Finance Minister Simon Harris has said that this “rule is something that we need to move beyond”. Just not yet, apparently.

Advertisement

Thirdly, there are the rising inheritance bands. Your son or daughter can now inherit €420,000 tax-free, taking €6,600 out of the tax net. Intergenerational wealth is a fairly new concept in Ireland, and this will help families looking to pass assets on – whether on death or as a gift in life.

So if you are serious about getting on in Ireland in 2027, there is quite a lot on offer. Here’s how three groups of grownups can take advantage:

When we were young

For those who are first-time adulting, a 15% increase in rent tax credit is useful, though the €5,000 rise in help-to-buy deposits will probably just filter through to sellers as these measures tend to. The government also seems serious about making childcare more affordable – but as with housing, shies away from measures that increase supply and fix underlying problems.

Personal investment accounts look quite attractive for younger adults. The fact that they reward risk, and pay no interest on cash will make them inappropriate for most house deposit savings.

But unlike pensions, the benefit of which is so far away, these accounts offer the prospect of building some decent money in a timeframe you can visualise.

Longer term, this group will benefit most from enormous investments into Dublin’s MetroLink, as well as the building up of Ireland’s sovereign wealth fund – the Future Ireland Fund – with a total €5.8 billion commitment, available for spending from 2041 onwards.

Card-carrying grown-ups will welcome a rise in the threshold at which top-rate tax is paid, even if it is a bit stingy. It’s moved from €44,000 to €46,500 for a single person – effectively a tax saving of €500 if you earn €46,500 or more. The risk here was a repeat of last year, where it didn’t move at all.

Fully-grown adults will also benefit from cuts to USC, to third-level costs, and a hike in the amount you can feed to the electricity grid from your solar panels, as well as inflation-based uplift in children’s allowance.

Lastly, if you’re trying to make more with less, there is also a certain amount for you. Rent-a-room relief now enables €16,000 of tax-free income a year – an 11% increase. Social welfare benefits have been moved up, and the main tax credits increased by €125.

Of course, there will always be demands for more. But what looks like generosity comes with trade-offs. For example, in accepting the Low Pay Commission’s recommendation to increase the minimum wage by 5.3% to €14.94, we risk hitting limits where businesses will be willing to employ young people entering the workforce for the first time.

What might have been

The trouble with grownups is they sometimes stay out too late enjoying themselves, when they should be attending to the serious stuff. There’s no doubt the budget misses several opportunities. These can be divided into three kinds:

Where's the protest gone? No rows, no riots, and not even a 'hup ya boy ya'

Budget 2027: What changed at midnight - and what we'll have to wait for

Firstly, there’s the addiction to adding to our already complicated tax system, rather than taking things away. For example, here are some of the tax rates that now apply to investments, depending on where you keep your money in Ireland: 1% (personal investment accounts), 25% (companies), 31% (capital gains), 35% (exit tax next year), 38% (exit tax now). This has little logic behind it.

Then there’s the fact that we continue to depend so much on corporation tax receipts and the top end of income taxpayers. Here’s how the government’s own spending watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (IFAC), marked their homework: “Budget 2027 puts the public finances on a worse trajectory by repeatedly breaking established spending limits and increasingly relying on high-risk corporation tax”.

Ouch. In particular, IFAC points out, corporation tax receipts are volatile and dependent on a handful of US companies, yet the government is spending €6 out of every €7 that it gets. What’s the plan if that dries up? The risk is that the government will be forced to borrow more, at a time when the cost of government borrowing is on the rise.

Finally, there’s the lack of appetite for the real reform on the big problems that dog life in Ireland in 2026. Our government has little to say when it comes to the hard work of fixing the planning, supply and cost control issues that would sort causes rather than symptoms, and help deal with the housing backlog, slow infrastructure delivery and missing football pitches people could really do with.

Instead, we continue to throwing subsidies at housing, childcare, transport and other vocal constituencies. There is no real attempt to control costs. We’ve found a whopping €6 billion of additional cash for MetroLink! That’s €6 million extra per working day, yet is barely noticed compared to much less consequential tweaks.

These missed opportunities at government level are exactly why it’s vital for individuals to make the most of what’s available in Budget 2027. Make sure you take the opportunity.

Ralph Benson is a chartered accountant and head of financial advice at online investments and pensions adviser at Moneycube.ie.

news.title: UPDATE: Traffic advice issued as top of Lurgybrack remains closed due to serious road traffic collision
news.text:
The top of Lurgybrack remains closed due to a serious road traffic collision.

Any HGVs and large vehicles travelling to Letterkenny from the Stranorlar direction, please travel via Convoy or Lifford and avoid the N13.

Any HGV’s departing Letterkenny on the Lurgybrack side of town should also avoid the N13 and travel via the Lifford Road.

The diversion routes in use are quite narrow and traffic is heavy on them.

news.title: Jon Rahm to end LIV Golf involvement due to ‘unacceptable terms’ on offer
news.text:
Jon Rahm is to quit LIV Golf due to the “unacceptable” terms offered for the proposed relaunch of the breakaway series.

LIV is currently going through Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the United States after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund withdrew support at the end of the season having spent $5 billion (€4.46 billion) in four years.

While the likes of Sergio Garcia were successful in petitioning the court to lift the automatic stay on their contracts, effectively freeing them up to pursue other opportunities next year, Rahm was not afforded the same escape.

The Spaniard is one of the two big LIV names – Bryson DeChambeau the other – and is reported to be owed up to $150 million (€134 million) for the remainder of the contract he signed almost three years ago.

“Mr Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0 ... and has determined that those terms are unacceptable to him, and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0,” attorney John Beck told a bankruptcy hearing.

The Athletic also reported Beck told the court Rahm and LIV are working to finalise a separation agreement by October 15th.

Rahm withdrew from this week’s Open de Espana in Madrid in order to remain at home as wife Kelley is expecting their fourth child.

In May, the 31-year-old backed down in his dispute with the DP World Tour and paid around €2.6 million in fines for playing in competing events, giving him conditional releases for 2026 and making him eligible for the Ryder Cup.

He previously opted not to take the PGA Tour’s offer of reinstatement via a specially drawn-up Returning Member Program created in January and applicable to only him, Cam Smith, Bryson DeChambeau and Brooks Koepka – the only player who accepted the offer.

As a result, Rahm would have to serve a mandatory one-year suspension, up until late August next year, before he could return to the American circuit.
news.summary: The Spanish golfer is reported to be owed up to $150 million from the remainder of his contract

ColumnDig Your Heels In

Lise Hand: I'm mourning the era of high heels (but I don't think I'd go back all the same)

Gone are the days when heels were an absolute necessity for days in the office and nights on the town.

7.01pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

ABOUT 5PM LAST Friday evening in Dublin city, just as people high-tailed it from workplaces to head for the hills, the bus, tram, train, the M50 (thoughts and prayers) or to the pub, the skies opened with a biblical vengeance. It rained cats, dogs, pitchforks; it came down like stair rods; it bucketed, lashed, hammered down.

Scurrying down a rapidly emptying side street, a sudden loud racket close by caused this writer’s heart to briefly depart her carcass; a few seconds later a cavalcade of half-soaked young women tottered past, swearing and half-drowned.

It wasn’t the fusillade of swearing which induced the jump-scare though – instead it was the noisy blast of fast-moving stilettos clattering along the pavement, a percussive, staccato rat-tat on concrete.

The women were clearly dressed for going out-out. But while they were perfectly en vogue from the ankles up, a parade of slip dresses and cropped faux fur jackets, their unanimous choice of footwear seemed oddly anachronistic, as if they had just stepped (carefully) out of a Tardis after a round trip to the 1990s.

They were sporting proper high heels.

The standing-on-tippy-toe type which basically requires balancing atop a three or four-inch nail – and not just balancing, mind, but also performing other feats of equipoise such as walking, dancing, standing around for hours and running for a bus.

In other words, the type of shoe which was the automatic accessory of choice or of necessity for at least a couple of generations of women.

The disappearance of heels from office life started with wearing flats for the commute, then grew to switching over altogether.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Until, thank God, it wasn’t. The quasi-extinction of the high-heeled shoe has been as swift as it has been welcome. True, there are still various degrees of slightly elevated footwear out and about to be sure, such as block heels, wedges and kitten heels, but even they’re lesser-spotted objects these days, easily spotted among the forest of flatties.

Advertisement

Heels had a hold over us

Why the hell did we do the high heel thing for so long? Because we bought into the canny propaganda, is the short answer. First and foremost, the stiletto has been long touted as a signifier of feminine sexiness. Think of the iconic scene in the 1950s Hollywood classic ‘Some Like it Hot’ when Tony Curtis and Jack Lemon, gussied up like a pair of dames, goggle at how a stiletto-wearing Marilyn Monroe sashays with ease along a train platform. “Look at that! Look how she moves! That’s just like Jell-O on springs… must have some sort of built-in motor or something,” marvels Lemon.

Then in more recent decades, in an effort to recast the high heel as a feminist statement, spiky heels and a shoulder-padded suit came to signify a ball-breaking boardroom badass high-kicking her way through corporate glass ceilings. In 2012, Victoria Beckham, who by now had remarkably transmogrified from the Spice Girl who pointed rather than sang into the designer darling of New York fashion week, explained her adherence to vertiginous heels. “I can’t concentrate in flats,” she told a TV interviewer.

It was pure Carrie Bradshaw-speak.

If any one figure promoted the high heel as simultaneously an implement of enticement, a girl’s best friend and an ambitious woman’s weapon of choice, it was the Manolo Blahnik-obsessed character played by Sarah Jessica Parker in HBO’s massive hit series Sex and the City who regularly uttered empowering nuggets such as: “The fact is, sometimes it’s hard to walk in a single woman’s shoes. That’s why we need really special ones now and then – to make the walk a little more fun.” Or: “Maybe the reason Cinderella was so happy wasn’t because of the Prince…. but because of the shoes.”

Sarah Jessica Parker's iconic character was well known for her love of shoes.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Sex and the City had perfect timing, coinciding with the boomiest of boom times at the tail-end of the 1990s and the early 2000s, when oodles of money was flying around like snuff at a wake and when the phrase “girl power” made it into the Oxford English Dictionary. However, it’s no coincidence that by the time the second full-length spin-off movie was released in 2010, the economic and societal mood had darkened considerably, and the film was universally kicked to flitters by critics for its tone-deaf materialism and naff consumerism.

Coming back down to earth

Heels, like hemlines, rise in optimistic times, and lower when the outlook is less sunny.

The descent of high heels started slowly; women took to wearing tights and trainers on their commute to work, before slipping into a heeled court shoe (nude-coloured being the ‘colour’ of choice) outside the entrance or as soon as they reached their desk. It wouldn’t do at all to be caught literally flat-footed in the workplace.

Thankfully, once a dazed workforce had emerged from the smoking rubble of the global financial crash of the late naughties, this pointless ritual had largely bitten the dust. Trainers, high-tops, Doc Martens, ballet pumps, biker boots, loafers and brogues pounded pavements and adorned the feet of front row fashionistas from Manhattan to Milan.

The Covid pandemic finally did for the office high heel – the notion of clacking about in any sort of shoe, tight skirt or even an underwired bra for that matter while working from home was ludicrous – sales of high heels reportedly dropped by 65% during the second quarter of 2020, according to market research data.

Interestingly, once the pandemic receded, the stiletto failed to make a triumphant comeback, despite the imprecations and predictions of various glossy magazines.

It turns out that unlike many fashion accessories, flats weren’t just a fad – they represented a redrawing of how women move through the world.

Related Reads

Lise Hand: Hilda Moriarty inspired ‘Raglan Road’, so why isn't she remembered?

Lise Hand: Swear to God, I saw U2 play in the Dandelion Market too 

‘Killer heels’ are no longer status symbols among women who want to be able to run unimpeded and in comfort for a bus or from a creepy stalker or for public office. Even the world of haute couture copped on. “The flat shoe makes the woman equal to men. When they have high (shoes) they play a part like a geisha, and they can’t be expected to be taken that seriously,” observed designer Karl Lagerfeld.

Flat shoes and short heels are back in style.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Therefore it’s unsurprising that one place where high-heeled women are most conspicuous is anywhere in the near vicinity of that doughty defender of gender equality, Donald Trump. MAGA’s botoxed, trout-lipped, stilettoed chattels totter around Mar-a-Lago and the White House, mostly pound shop versions of Melania Trump who is usually spotted perched atop spindly Louboutin stilettos during her rare tight-lipped forays into public with her husband. But wherever they all go, any glass ceilings above them remain unbothered and intact.

However, back in rainy Dublin, I watched the tangle of leggy women scurrying for shelter, and felt a pang for my most beloved-ever shoes, a long-departed pair of sleek, pointy-toed caramel-coloured buttery-leather Prada stilettos which looked sexy as hell, yet which felt like wearing fluffy slippers. They were miraculous, and I mourned them when they were consigned to the bin, finally beyond repair. I’ve never felt similar fierce affection for any pair of trainers or Chelsea boots, to be honest. Flatties are, well, grand.

There’s nothing wrong with sallying forth in a pair of towering stilettos when the occasion, the mood or the outfit calls for it. Sometimes, being Jell-O on springs feels damn fine.

But now it’s a choice, not a duty. And that’s the whole pointy-pointe of it.

Lise Hand is a journalist and writer. This column runs every Wednesday.

news.title: Helen McEntee admits end of peacekeeping mission in Lebanon will likely lead to exodus from Defence Forces
news.text:
Public expenditure minister Jack Chambers told the Dáil during Budget 2027 speeches that funding would provide for an intake of 850 new permanent Defence Forces members.

This will provide for 400 brand new personnel members, with 450 other roles filled due to departures of existing staff members.

Ms McEntee conceded that reaching the target of 11,500 troops by the end of 2028 is “not likely”, with the force expected to reach 8,300 by the end of 2028.

The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (Unifil) mission will finish by the end of the year following the failure of the United Nations Security Council to renew its mandate.

Ireland cannot partake in missions without a UN mandate under the current Triple Lock legislation.

Ms McEntee said that once the Unifil mission is wound down by Easter, the number of defence personnel overseas will fall from over 400 to 90, with those members working in office roles.

The minister contended that the number of Defence Forces personnel is likely to fall once the Lebanon mission wraps up.

“When we talk about recruitment and retention, I had the opportunity to meet with those who were the last battalion that went out to Lebanon," she said. 

"When I spoke to many of them, they joined because they wanted to come to Lebanon. They joined because they wanted to serve in overseas peacekeeping missions.

“If we do not have those opportunities for people, I believe that that will impact on those who wish to join but also retaining people who are actually in the permanent Defence Forces.”

She said that she does not believe that there will be a new UN-mandated mission to Lebanon, but talks are underway for an EU Common Security and Defence Policy mission to be deployed to Lebanon once UNIFIL comes to an end.

However, she said Ireland will not be able to join this while the Triple Lock is still in place.

 Louise Burne is Political Correspondent.
news.summary: The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (Unifil) mission will finish by the end of the year following the failure of the United Nations Security Council to renew its mandate

news.title: Call for safer access to Simon’s Cove near Clonakilty
news.text:
Safety concerns over access to Simon’s Cove, a pretty secluded cove near Clonakilty popular with swimmers, have been raised by West Cork councillors.

Independent Ireland councillor Daniel Sexton said the cliff route down to the water needed to be examined as an increasing number of people visit the location. 

He told a meeting of Cork County Council’s Western Division that the cove was a beautiful spot, but access was a concern.

Mr Sexton said swimmers and other visitors were making their way down to the water and that the council needed to consider whether anything could be done to make the approach safer.

He raised the issue following an update on coastal and marine projects across West Cork.

Fine Gael councillor John Michael Foley also raised concerns about coastal access and safety at Broadstrand. 

A council official said the Simon’s Cove matter had been raised at an earlier local meeting and would be examined. 

The official said the council would investigate the position at the site and consider what options, if any, were available. No works programme, cost estimate, or timeline was given.

The discussion took place as the council outlined ongoing work on coastal protection, harbour infrastructure, and public access at sites across West Cork. 

Its coastal projects report includes monitoring work at vulnerable beaches and coastal locations, where sand movement, erosion, and changing conditions can affect access and existing defences. 

The council said it would revert to councillors once it had examined the Simon’s Cove concern.

 Funded by the Local Democracy Reporting Scheme
news.summary: A councillor John Michael Foley also raised concerns at Cork County Council’s Western Division about coastal access and safety at Broadstrand
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,West Cork

news.title: ‘We need the truth’: Calls for public inquiry into Creeslough tragedy on fourth anniversary
news.text:
Hundreds of people, including the families of those who died in the Creeslough explosion of October 7th, 2022, gathered at the site of the tragedy on Wednesday to remember their loved ones four years on.

Ten people, ranging in age from five to 59, died in the blast. Robert Garwe and his daughter Shauna Flanagan-Garwe (5), Catherine O’Donnell and her son James Monaghan (13), Jessica Gallagher, Martin McGill, James O’Flaherty, Martina Martin, Hugh Kelly and Leona Harper (14) were all killed in the explosion.

Heavy rain gave way to bright sunshine at the scene of the tragedy, as prayers were said for lost loved ones.

At the stroke of 3.17pm, at the exact moment of the explosion, an eerie silence fell over the village.

Some family members who lost loved ones in the tragedy spoke after the short service.

Áine Flanagan, who lost her partner Robert and daughter Shauna in the blast, said that the families were now entering a fifth year without their loved ones.

She said it was “heartbreaking”, and all they wanted was the truth of what happened on that Friday afternoon in October 2022.

“We, the families, we deserve answers,” she said.

When asked what life was like without her partner and daughter, she replied, “It’s painful. I’m missing them every day.”

Donna Harper, whose daughter Leona was just 14 when she was killed in the explosion after entering the garage for an ice-cream, said the pain simply never gets any easier.

She said: “We’re standing here four years on, and it never gets any easier. I still miss my wee girl every single day, every moment of every day.”

“I stood here for almost 24 hours, across the road, waiting for my wee girl to be found, hoping and praying for a miracle that she would be brought out. That didn’t happen, and my wee girl never came home.”

She added that unless the families get the truth of what caused the explosion, they will never be able to move on.

“We need answers, we need to know what happened, why it happened, how it happened. We need to know the truth to be able to move on,” she said.

Her husband, Hugh, said he still recalls waiting at “this very spot” for his daughter’s remains to be taken out from the scene of the carnage.

However, he says it’s wrong to say that his only daughter is not with her family still.

Choking back tears, he said: “She is here. She’s with me. She’s there in the morning, she’s there at night ... first and last thoughts.

“But life is not the same. It’s changed.

“It’s just hard to put it into words, it really is, but the loss, it can’t be measured. It just can’t be measured,” he added.

He said he had one simple request for the Government – to never allow something like this to happen again to any other family.

“I just wish that the Government would come on board, that they would establish a public inquiry for the simple reason as to examine every possible avenue of how this was allowed to happen, and not let it happen again.”

Fr John Joe Duffy read out the names of the victims in the order that they were pronounced dead at the time of the tragedy at the service.

The families were joined in solidarity by members of the Stardust Victims’ Committee as well as members of the Bloody Sunday Trust.

Fr Duffy appealed to everyone gathered to support each other on their journey of healing.

He said: “As we gather here today, as we stand here in this place today, grief does not end, and everyone, while on a collective journey, is at a different stage on the road towards healing.

“Some may have started that journey, while others have found that they have not yet been able to even begin on that journey to healing.”

Members of the emergency services who attended the scene on the day were also present, as well as senior gardaí and a number of elected members of Donegal County Council.
news.summary: Áine Flanagan, who lost her partner Robert and daughter Shauna in the blast, said families ‘deserve answers’
news.author: Stephen Maguire

Defence Forces will not reach target of 11,500 personnel by 2028 despite recruitment commitments

Defence Minister Helen McEntee was speaking at a press conference about the Defence and Foreign Affairs allocations in Budget 2027.

6.41pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

Niall O'Connor

THE MINISTER FOR Defence has said the Irish Defence Forces will not reach 11,500 troops by 2028, breaking a key target promised by the organisation and government. 

The Commission on the Defence Forces report set a target of 11,500 as a critical part of its plan to meet what has been defined as Level of Ambition Two in the military regeneration. 

This was committed to by the government and the Defence Forces, but now Helen McEntee has said she accepts that will not be achieved.

McEntee was speaking at a press conference about Budget 2027 and the Defence and Foreign Affairs allocations. 

When asked if she believed recruitment targets would be met, she accepted that they would not be. 

“It’s a very difficult task at this stage,” she said. 

“However, what is very clear, in particular in the last two years, is that the trajectory for recruits is going in the right direction. So we’re recruiting more, we’re retaining more importantly, and there’s more people applying every year.

“So we’ve increased by 790 last year, to 850 I hope this year, and 900 the year after. So if we can continue in that vein,” she added. 

Advertisement

The minister also spoke about her hopes of increased civilianisation in the Defence Forces with 100 civil servants due to be recruited. McEntee explained that such a move has worked in An Garda Síochána, and she believes it will be of benefit to the military also. 

In the budget there was €340 million in National Development Plan funding. The minister said that this will cover the cost of the Primary Radar Project, which was confirmed in recent weeks. 

This would see Ireland’s first air defence systems and radar around the island to monitor the airspace and detect rogue aircraft that civilian services cannot see. 

In February the Department of Defence announced the purchase of armoured personnel carriers to replace the ageing MOWAG fleet after an agreement with the French government.

Sources have said that this could cost more than €600m, with some suggesting it may be as expensive as €900m due to the ever-increasing level of defence inflation in the cost of equipment. 

However, there was no mention of this in the budget. McEntee said that there would be “budgets beyond next year to fund our armoured vehicles”. She explained that she was looking for an increase in 2028 in the NDP provision for Defence.

The minister said she was open to exploring the EU’s SAFE defence loans – this is a money pot developed by Brussels to give long term loans of 30 to 40 years in duration.

“I would like us to be part of SAFE. I’ve made that ambition very clear. It is open again and will be for some time, albeit with a smaller figure than the last time. That’s something that I’m working on at the moment.

“I think it’s not just about accessing the funding, for me, I think it’s also about showing that commitment to European solidarity, showing that commitment to working with our European colleagues and indeed others, [like] Canada is now in it as well, when it comes to our overall security,” she added. 

Niall O'Connor
