news.title: Walls, windows and ceilings of Limerick house destroyed during ‘student party’
news.text:
Gardaí are investigating after a house in a Limerick city suburb was vandalised by youths attending a party.

The house, located at College Court, Castletroy, was designated a crime scene by gardaí, after walls and ceilings, and fixtures and fittings were torn down, in the early hours of Wednesday.

A video shared on social media showed young people throwing a shelving unit through a window of what appears to have been the property in question.

Other homes in the same estate and surrounding areas have been badly damaged in similar incidents over the years.

The video showed a group of suspected students screaming and laughing as more damage was caused to the property.

A male voice is heard shout “Oh my god,” as a wheelie bin is thrown at glass doors.

Walls and ceilings were also torn down in the property.

At one point during the video footage the camera is pointed up at a ceiling on the first floor, revealing no ceiling but a void into the attic and roofing joists.

The first floor of the property was also littered with what appeared to be attic and wall insulation, and fixtures and fittings in an upstairs bathroom were also destroyed.

“This is f*cked,” said another male on the video while a female voice is heard state “no lads, every f*cking room, welcome to our house tour”.

A local person at the scene said: “All the windows have been knocked out of it. A couple of students said there was a party there, they must have all gone berserk.”.

A garda spokeswoman said: “Gardaí received a report of an incident of criminal damage that occurred in College Court, Castletroy, Co Limerick, in the early hours of Wednesday morning 7th October 2026.”

The spokeswoman said gardaí conducted a “technical examination of the scene” and “investigations are ongoing”.

It was unclear if the youths filmed inside the property have any affiliation with University of Limerick (UL) which is located close to College Court.

However, in a statement, UL said it was “aware of an incident that took place off campus and that an investigation by An Garda Siochana is underway”.

“UL strongly promotes responsible behaviour and positive engagement with the community. While the vast majority of students are respectful and valued members of the community, the university recognises that instances of antisocial behaviour, including property damage, public disorder and other actions that negatively impact residents, are a matter of serious concern,” it said.

“There are mechanisms within the university student code of conduct for breaches of the code to be dealt with and complaints made to the University about individuals are taken very seriously.”
news.summary: Gardaí investigate damage caused to property in city in the early hours of Wednesday
news.author: David Raleigh

news.title: Covid-19 PPE fraudster jailed for scamming medical companies out of millions
news.text: A conman who defrauded medical firms of millions through bogus PPE transactions during the Covid-19 crisis has been imprisoned. Craig Morris, 43, along with his employer Jogesh Bhandari, 60, splashed out hundreds of thousands on high-end vehicles, timepieces, getaways and property after falsely claiming they could deliver millions of boxes of nitrile gloves to clients in the United States and Germany . Morris and Bhandari were found guilty of money laundering and conspiracy to commit fraud by false representation following a five-week trial at Leicester Crown Court in July. Bhandari's spouse, ex-pharmacist Meenakshi Bhandari, 58, was convicted of money laundering after the pair used the proceeds to purchase Rolexes and motors including an Audi A5, a Land Rover Discovery and a Porsche valued at £126,000. On Wednesday, Morris received a custodial sentence of three years and nine months at Northampton Crown Court, while Meenakshi Bhandari was given a two-year prison term, suspended for two years, 250 hours of unpaid work and 15 days of rehabilitation activity. The court was told that Jogesh Bhandari failed to appear at the hearing because he informed his legal representative he was taking a "very extreme painkiller" following a pacemaker procedure last week and was unable to make the journey to Northampton. Judge William Harbage KC proceeded to sentence the remaining two defendants in his absence as "the case cannot just be put off and put off at Mr Bhandari's will". The judge stated there is "no medical evidence" to adequately explain Jogesh Bhandari's absence from the sentencing hearing and a bench warrant will be issued for him. Prosecutor Michael Bisgrove told the court Jogesh Bhandari was the "driving force and the instigator" of the offending, while Morris was "very much working for" him. He said: "The offences took place during the Covid-19 pandemic at a time when there was a desperate shortage of personal protective equipment (PPE). "In that shortage, the offenders, particularly Mr Bhandari and Mr Morris, saw the opportunity to make money by fraud." The court was told that Jogesh Bhandari and Morris conducted fraudulent transactions through a company called Banton. He continued: "They pretended to be big players in the PPE market. They pretended to have PPE for sale and to be able to buy vast amounts of it." The court heard they swindled American company Med18 and German business MedTech by issuing contracts for equipment they didn't possess. Mr Bisgrove said: "In the course of the fraud, they took millions of pounds which they used for their own benefit – to buy cars, luxury goods and property." The court was informed the Bhandaris, from Mitchell Drive in Loughborough, Leicestershire, also utilised funds to settle family debts. Morris, from All Saints Road in Lytham St Annes, Lancashire, who has two teenage children, purchased a property, the court heard. The court was told that Jogesh Bhandari fraudulently obtained and retained £1.75 million, while Meenakshi Bhandari laundered funds totalling £960,000. The National Crime Agency (NCA) had previously revealed that Morris had been receiving regular payments of £5,000 from Jogesh Bhandari before the pair had a falling out at the end of 2021. Bhandari had been working alongside Frank Labruzzo, a US assistant attorney general at the Louisiana State Department of Justice, who facilitated a fraudulent escrow service – a bank account designed to hold funds until pre-agreed conditions are fulfilled. The court was also informed that Labruzzo and another individual involved in the scheme have since been convicted and sentenced in the United States . Jogesh Bhandari is due to be sentenced on October 16. When handing down sentences to Morris and Meenakshi Bhandari, Judge Harbage remarked that the pandemic was a period when "all of us had to make sacrifices and pull together for the good of society as a whole". He went on to say: "There were a few people though who sought to exploit that to make money for themselves, motivated by greed. "I'm satisfied Jogesh Bhandari and Craig Morris fall into that category."
news.summary: Craig Morris, 43, and his boss Jogesh Bhandari, 60, splashed hundreds of thousands of pounds on luxury cars, watches, holidays and a new home
news.author: Emma O'neill,Sophie Robinson Press Association

news.title: Watch: Heydon outlines initial details of fertiliser scheme
news.text:
Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine Martin Heydon has outlined some of the initial details of an upcoming fertiliser support scheme.

The scheme was announced as part of Budget 2027 yesterday (Tuesday, October 6).

Although the ins-and-outs of the scheme are yet to be finalised, Minister Heydon has outlined some details on how access to the scheme will operate, and what payments will be based on.

Speaking to Agriland, the minister said: "€77 million will go into farmers' pockets between now and the end of this year in cash injection, both with another run of the Fuel Income Support Scheme and with a newly-designed fertiliser scheme.

"€46.1 million I have for a fertiliser scheme. It will be based off last year's usage in 2025, off the [National] Fertiliser Database," the minister added.

He said: "I'm finalising details on that scheme, once I have the money this week. I had done significant work on it over the summer."

Minister Heydon indicated that farmer participation in the scheme will be based on the National Fertiliser Database, rather than on an application process.

He said: "I envisage that farmers won't have to apply for that, that I'll be able to do it in a way based off the database.

"I'll have to set minimum and maximum criteria and I'll engage with farm organisations on that before finalising the scheme," he added.

On the extended Fuel Income Support Scheme, Minister Heydon said it will be a "rerun of what people got earlier this year, again to be paid out before the end of this year".

Funding for both schemes will come from the underspend from the €100 million that was announced for the Fuel Income Support Scheme earlier this year.

"€38 million was spent of the €100 million I was allocated back in April... Of the €62 million remaining, €31 million will go on the Fuel Income Support Scheme again, paying the same amount out again before year-end," Minister Heydon said.

"Then on the fertiliser scheme, I received €15.4 million from the EU, as part of [Commissioner for Agriculture Christophe Hansen's] exceptional aid because of the impact of high prices on fertiliser," he explained.

"Member states were given the ability to add 200% to that figure that we each received, so that's another €31 million. So I have €62 million left out of the €100 million, €31 million is going on fuel, €31 million is going to the €15.4 million that we've got from the EU, so that's a €46 million fertiliser package," the minister added.

It is understood that memos will be brought to cabinet next week on these two schemes, which will be followed by talks with farm organisations on the fertiliser scheme to work through the final details.

Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine Martin Heydon has outlined some of the initial details of an upcoming fertiliser support scheme. 'Josh Ericson has been impressive... Todd Lawlor is very exciting'

Leinster hooker Dan Sheehan is happy to see young players making an impression.

6.31pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

DAN SHEEHAN IS raring to get his Leinster season going on the pitch, but he has enjoyed being part of the support crew for the past fortnight.

Sheehan was among the Ireland internationals who were part of Leinster’s URC tour of South Africa without playing in either game against the Lions and Sharks.

With those frontliners unavailable for match-day selection after their summer efforts with Ireland, a host of younger players made a positive impression for Leo Cullen’s side as they took three losing bonus points home.

Speaking on The 42 Rugby Weekly Extra podcast today, Sheehan picked out a couple of players who caught his eye in particular, namely 22-year-old number eight Josh Ericson and 20-year-old fullback Todd Lawlor.

“Josh has been very impressive,” said Sheehan.

“He kind of came out of nowhere into the pro circle a little bit last year; he played a lot of AIL for a while with Belvo, and I just thought he stepped up massively.

“You see him or you walk by him a few times and, you know, maybe he’s not the biggest fella, but he’s able to run over people. I thought the way he carried himself over the last two weeks and how physical he was in games was impressive.

“And then Todd Lawlor also making his debut down in South Africa, I thought he was very exciting to watch. A good person to have around the changing room, good craic but also a good running talent.

“We’ve seen it in training over the last few years. He probably had a bad season of injuries last year. But I remember him coming in, I think it was the start of last season when we all came back from the Lions tour, and he was training with us while the rest of the lads were off to South Africa, and you could see the talent in him.

Advertisement

“It’s nice to see him get his break like that and going well over the two weeks.”

Josh Ericson carrying the ball for Leinster.Steve Haag Sports / Christiaan Kotze/INPHO

Steve Haag Sports / Christiaan Kotze/INPHO / Christiaan Kotze/INPHO

Sheehan is fit and ready to go as Leinster get set for their competitive return to Laya Arena in Dublin when they face Cardiff this Saturday evening.

Having captained Ireland on their July tour of Australia and New Zealand in the Nations Championship, he enjoyed a five-week off-season before getting back into pre-season.

The return to training involved a fitness test, with a change-up from the ‘Bronco’ that has been done in recent years.

“It was ‘Double Efforts’ this year, which is a more forward-specific fitness test which involves a bit more down-up, backpedalling, shorter bursts,” said Sheehan. “But it’s also equally as grim as a Bronco.

“Josh van der Flier is always very good at it, as you can imagine, the perfect child.

“Do you know what? Tadhg Furlong is pretty good at that compared to the Bronco. He can bounce off the ground pretty well.”

With plenty of training under their belts now, Sheehan and his fellow Ireland frontliners are excited to get back into the swing of playing with Leinster.

The coming weeks include a big inter-pro against Munster at the Aviva Stadium, as well as the start of the Champions Cup away to Clermont before Ireland’s second Nations Championship window in November.

First up, it’s the homecoming game at Laya Arena.

“The changing room is buzzing to be back,” said Sheehan.

Laya Arena in Dublin.Eoin Burke / INPHO

Eoin Burke / INPHO / INPHO

“We were told that the redevelopment was going to happen, and then all of a sudden it’s two years, it was meant to be one-and-a-half years, and I think people are itching to get back in.

“We all have great memories of the RDS or the Laya Arena, whether it be debuts or big first European games or whatever it might be and going as a child.

“We owe it to the fans to make sure we show up properly and enjoy ourselves out there and put a performance in because it has probably been a different feel at Leinster games over the last two years, and we look forward to hopefully making this a proper home.

“I got to go to the Horse Show and obviously the Zebre pre-season game, and it’s a proper stadium, proper club ground, nice and intimate.

“The new stand is right on the pitch, you get access to players, and hopefully we can create a buzz for the season ahead because everyone in our changing room is excited to be back.”

Dan Sheehan was speaking ahead of Leinster Rugby’s homecoming game against Cardiff at Laya Arena on Saturday 10 October. All Access will be at Leinster home games at Laya Arena all season, so follow @layahealthcare and @layaarena on Instagram for details.

news.title: Gardaí investigate after student house damaged in Limerick
news.text:
Videos widely shared on social media show two young men throwing furniture through a window, shattering the glass, while others are heard laughing.

The footage shows extensive damage inside the house, including holes in walls and damage to part of the ceiling.

A Garda spokesperson told the Irish Examiner: "A technical examination of the scene has been conducted. Investigations are ongoing."

Some of the social media clips have since been taken down. 

One video was filmed by a young woman using Sabrina Carpenter's song House Tour, part of a social media trend in which users showcase their homes.

A University of Limerick spokesperson said it promotes responsible behaviour and takes incidents of anti-social conduct seriously.

While the vast majority of students make a positive contribution to the local community, the university acknowledged that issues such as property damage and public disorder are a source of serious concern.

The spokesperson said complaints involving students are investigated under the university's code of conduct.

"Students have been urged to be mindful of their actions and the impact they have on the community around them," the spokesperson said.
news.summary: A student property near the University of Limerick was extensively damaged in an incident that was filmed and shared on social media
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,Mick Clifford

Under Pressure

'I've been called a lot worse': O'Donovan reacts to criticism and plays down reports of walkout

The Media Minister faced a litany of questions today about the various dramas involving him in the run up to the budget. 

6.21pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

DURING A LENGTHY post-budget press conference this afternoon, Media Minister Patrick O’Donovan played down reports that he stormed out of a budget meeting with Public Expenditure Minister Jack Chambers and brushed off criticism from an Irish language podcaster who said he is a “fucking eejit”.

In the lead-up to this year’s budget, O’Donovan found himself the subject of many news articles, with reports that he was locked in contentious arguments with both his junior minister Charlie McConalogue and the public expenditure minister. 

Last Friday, the Irish Examiner reported that O’Donovan walked out of a meeting with Chambers after just eight minutes because his budget requests were not being met.

O’Donovan made the €100 culture card for 16-year-olds a cornerstone of his budget asks this year, but the initiative, which would have cost between €7 and €8 million, was not greenlit by Chambers. 

Asked about the reports of a walkout today, O’Donovan said:

“When this press conference ends, regardless of however long or short it goes on I presume you will stand up from your seat and leave. I wouldn’t attribute that to being a walkout. 

“When a meeting ends, people naturally go about the rest of their lives.

“That’s what happens when a meeting ends.”

Separately, relations between O’Donovan and his junior minister for sport Charlie McConalogue have also reportedly soured in recent months.

The public row centred around which government party got to claim credit for new sports grants, with Fianna Fáilers unhappy Fine Gael TDs were beating them to the punch.

McConalogue and O'Donovan pictured today.Alamy

During an interview on Today with David McCullough on RTÉ Radio 1 last Friday, McConalogue failed to characterise relations with O’Donovan as “good” when asked. 

Asked today by a reporter if he was a liability to the government, given the number of arguments he has reportedly been involved in since he returned to work in September after a period of illness, O’Donovan said he did not “accept that assertion”.

Advertisement

“The most important group of people that have to like me are the people of County Limerick that gave us nearly 12,000 votes in the last election,” the minister said, adding:

“And after that, I have a job to do for the arts, culture, communications, media, and sports community in Ireland, given the seal of office that the president gave me to carry out my constitutional prerogatives.

“And if that means that I have to step on toes to stand up for the people who I am the minister with responsibility for, I’m sure that there’s other ministers that do that as well, and I’m not so sure that the word liability would attach to them.”

Asked how his relationship with Jack Chambers is, O’Donovan said it is “very good” and that they each have jobs to do and are both doing them.

On the timeline for the introduction of the culture card, O’Donovan said there are “things that we would have loved to have done this year, but we’ll get around to doing next year and the year after”.

“The concept of the culture card is not in any way going to be stopped,” he said. 

He added that he will be bringing a memorandum to government during 2027 on its development. 

It is worth noting, however, that Chambers said yesterday the card was “obviously” something that couldn’t be delivered next year.

Public sentiment

It was also put to O’Donovan that, given all the recent reports of arguments involving him, the public are “slightly exacerbated” by him. 

Specifically, it was put to him that during a recent episode of Irish language podcast How to Gael, during a discussion on comments O’Donovan made about Coimisiún na Meán, host Doireann Ní Ghlacáin said: 

“Can Patrick O’Donovan just take a day off from being a fucking eejit? Seriously?” 

Responding to this, the minister said he has been “called a lot worse than that”. 

“I’ve far more important things to answer than commentary like that. But I would like to say that the budget that I secured for the Department of Cultural, Communications and Sport will speak for itself,” he said, adding that it was “disappointing” that “very few” people raised his decision to continue funding for the basic income for the arts scheme.

Jane Matthews

news.title: 'Simply untenable': 1,200-bed DCU student development scrapped over soaring costs
news.text:
The development was to be delivered through a combination of State capital funding and university investment.

The Irish Examiner previously reported that planning permission was granted in 2019, with the first phase of the project, comprising 405 bed spaces, brought to tender in 2023.

However, Mr Raftery said inflation in construction costs meant accommodation charges would have had to rise to about €16,000 for an academic year in order to make the project viable.

He said DCU was unable to “bridge the viability gap” between construction costs and capital grant supports. It would require €6.7m more in State funding in order to develop the project and bring rents down to €9,500 for an academic year.

“The department took a view that they couldn’t go any further because of availability of funds or value for money at that point in time,” said Mr Raftery.

The project has now been put forward to the Higher Education Institution Student Accommodation Programme, with hopes to be developed in conjunction with private developers.

Private-public partnerships form the cornerstone of a national student accommodation strategy launched by higher education minister James Lawless earlier this year. Under the plan, private developers would build on university-owned land.

People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd Barrett questioned whether collaboration with private sector involvement was necessary in addressing the student bed deficit. The Department of Higher Education aims to unlock 42,000 more beds in the space of a decade as part of the plan.

Sinn Féin TD Donna McGettigan said students would rather see the strategy “ripped up and thrown in the bin".

Mr Raftery suggested that accommodation could be delivered more effectively by universities because they could avoid corporation tax and take loans at low interest levels, positing that straight builds from the private sector would run into similar issues and price out students.

Deirdre Lillis, president of Technological University Dublin, said that in an ideal world, student accommodation would be 100% publicly funded.

Experts before the committee cited a funding gap in the higher education sector, which is estimated to be an accumulated deficit of €780m over four years.

Higher education institutions have long struggled to meet demand for student accommodation, the committee heard.

University of Limerick chief operations officer for Campus Life Services, John O'Rourke, said 5,500 students were unsuccessful in securing on-campus accommodation this year. He warned that shortages disproportionately affect students from lower socio-economic backgrounds.

"Student accommodation is therefore no longer simply a housing issue, it's an issue of higher education, student success and access to higher education," he said.

The rent-a-room scheme has created approximately 250 student beds for UL students over the past four years.

Traffic gridlock in Cork

At the same committee meeting, MTU president Maggie Cusack said a lack of purpose-built student accommodation and transport infrastructure was creating an “appalling” gridlock centred around the college’s Bishopstown campus in Cork.

Ms Cusack said traffic was “creating a really poor student experience, quite appalling actually, thinking about the time our students are spending in cars".

“We’re literally driving all of the measures in the wrong direction, from climate to student experience."

Ms Cusack said housing was now the biggest barrier to student education.

"It saddens me to see large queues of traffic and to think that's the experience our students have day to day... We often think about what things cost, and I would challenge us to think of opportunity costs and what we're losing there."
news.summary: Lack of purpose-built student accommodation and transport infrastructure creating 'appalling' gridlock around MTU campus in Bishopstown
news.author: Alex Cunningham,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: Social welfare Ireland: One major group is excluded from receiving the Christmas Bonus
news.text: In December, over a million people will receive a social welfare bonus ahead of Christmas. The bonus will be paid from the 7th of December, as confirmed in Budget 2027 earlier this week. Here's everything you need to know about it and who will receive the double week. A Christmas Bonus is paid to people getting long-term social welfare payments. You are paid a Christmas Bonus if you are getting: Back to Education Allowance - people coming from jobseeker's payments need to be getting the Allowance for at least 12 months (312 days), but you may be able to use your time on your jobseeker’s payment to help you qualify. Back to Work Enterprise Allowance - people coming from jobseeker's payments need to be getting the Allowance for at least 12 months (312 days), but you may be able to use time on jobseeker’s payment to help you qualify Back to Work Family Dividend Benefit Payment for 65 Year Olds Beneficiary of Temporary Protection Weekly Payment Bereaved Partner's Pension (Contributory) and (Non-Contributory) Blind Pension Carer's Allowance and Carer's Benefit (including half-rate Carer's Allowance) Community Employment Deserted Wife's Allowance and Deserted Wife's Benefit Daily Expenses Allowance for 12 months or more Disability Allowance Disablement Benefit Domiciliary Care Allowance Farm Assist Guardian's Payment (Contributory) and (Non-Contributory) Illness Benefit for 12 months or more Invalidity Pension Job Initiative Scheme Jobseeker's Allowance for 12 months (312 days or more) Jobseeker's Transitional payment Magdalene Commission Scheme Death Benefit Scheme (under the Occupational Injuries Scheme) One-Parent Family Payment Partial Capacity Benefit Rural Social Scheme State Pension (Contributory) and State Pension (Non-Contributory) Supplementary Welfare Allowance for 12 months (364 days or more) Tús Work Placement Experience Programme (if your primary payment is a qualifying social welfare payment) You will get a Christmas Bonus if you are getting a VTOS or Youthreach training allowance for at least 12 months subject to having an underlying DSP entitlement/qualifying payment (see list above). If you were getting a qualifying payment (see list above) immediately before your training allowance, you can combine this time to reach 12 months. If you live in a nursing home under the Fair Deal Scheme, your Christmas Bonus will not be counted as income or assessed under the Nursing Home Support Scheme. Fuel Allowance is not a qualifying payment for the Christmas Bonus. How much is the Christmas bonus? In 2025, the Christmas Bonus was 100% of your normal weekly payment. The minimum Bonus amount that is paid is €20. If an Increase for a Qualified Adult is paid directly to your dependent spouse, civil partner or cohabitant, the Christmas Bonus is also paid directly to them. If you are getting 2 eligible social welfare payments (for example, a One-Parent Family Payment and the Domiciliary Care Allowance or a half-rate Carer’s Allowance as well as your primary payment) you will get the Christmas Bonus for both payments. For Domiciliary Care Allowance (DCA), which is paid monthly, the bonus is 100% of the weekly DCA rate. The DCA portion of the bonus is calculated independently of other payments. news.title: Brian McFadden calls on teen singers as he searches for Ireland's next boy band
news.text: Brian McFadden is on the search for Ireland's next big boy band and is calling on aspiring singers aged between 17 and 19. The singers are being invited to put their voices, personalities and passion for music to the test in the hope of becoming part of a new Irish pop group. Leading the search is former Westlife star Brian McFadden , who brings first-hand experience of life in one of Ireland’s most successful boybands. McFadden rose to fame as a member of Westlife in the late 1990s, with the group achieving a string of chart-topping hits. He went on to pursue a successful solo career, with his debut single ‘Real to Me’ reaching number one, and continues to tour today as part of BoyzLife. Joining McFadden on the search will be Sarah Gallagher, founder of NDA Talent, who has more than 20 years’ experience in music management. Gallagher spent 17 years with Modest Management, the company behind the careers of major acts including One Direction, JLS and Little Mix, while personally managing Olly Murs and working on the comeback of Five. She now manages the careers of Olly Murs and Five through NDA Talent. Also joining the panel is Paul Franklin, a highly regarded senior music agent based in London, currently representing talent at Creative Artists Agency (CAA), one of the world’s leading entertainment agencies. With extensive experience across international touring, artist development and the pop and boyband world, Franklin has worked with major artists including Amy Winehouse, Mariah Carey, Demi Lovato, James Bay, Jessie J, McFly, Busted, Five, The Saturdays, The Vamps and The Wanted. Speaking about the search, Brian McFadden said, “I’m really excited to be putting together a brand-new Irish boyband and discovering the next generation of talent. We’re looking for lads aged 17 to 19 who have great voices, personality, ambition and, most importantly, a passion for music. Ireland has always produced incredible talent, and I believe the next big boyband is out there waiting to be discovered. This could be a life-changing opportunity, so if you think you’ve got what it takes, we want to hear from you!” Aspiring singers aged 17 to 19 who believe they have what it takes to become part of the new group are being encouraged to apply online via https://eu.castitreach.com/a/mmm/irishboyband/audition . Applications will close on Sunday, 25th of October at 5pm. Applicants will be contacted with details of an in-person audition in Dublin, with further information to be provided in due course. 'Small number' of workers at Center Parcs at risk of redundancy

It is unclear the exact number and types of roles at risk.

5.57pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

LAST UPDATE

CENTER PARCS HAS confirmed that a “small number” of roles at its holiday resort in Co Longford “may be at risk of redundancy”.

The Department of Enterprise confirmed this evening to The Journal that it was notified of proposed collective redundancies by the company on Monday.

A company of its size that intends to make 30 or more people redundant within a 30-day period is required to notify the Department.

Center Parcs Longford Forest is a large resort that takes up 400 acres of forest a short drive from Ballymahon. It is a hugely successful holiday destination for both those in Ireland and abroad, and is popular with families.

Last year, its accounts showed it was raking in close to €2 million a week in revenue.

Advertisement

However, the company said it has begun “a review of some of our structures to make sure they remain right for our business today and for the future”.

A spokesperson for Center Parcs Ireland told The Journal: “Sadly, this means a small number of roles may be at risk of redundancy.

“We recognise the significant impact this uncertainty can have on colleagues and their families, and we are committed to supporting everyone affected with care and respect throughout the consultation process.”

The resort employs a large amount of people locally, reporting 1,268 staff members in 2025.

It is unclear the number and types of roles at risk.

The resort this year saw €100 million invested into the site, resulting in an additional 83 lodges, which pushed its occupancy capacity to around 3,500. Facilities were also upgraded and new amenities made available.

Emma Hickey

news.title: Martin King and Jenny McCarthy's key to a happy marriage ahead of anniversary milestone
news.text: Martin King and Jenny McCarthy have shared their secret to a long and happy marriage as they prepare for an anniversary milestone. The Ireland AM presenter and photographer got married in a beautiful winter wedding in November 2011 and are set to mark 15 years since the big day next month. They tied the knot in the stunning Killashee Hotel in Naas and it's such a special day for them. The couple told RSVP Magazine: "It was a fairly traditional wedding with all the people who mattered most to us there. Looking back now, we think what made it so lovely was that it was really about celebrating us and having our family and friends together. "There were nerves, of course, but mostly we remember feeling really happy and excited that this was actually happening. There’s something very surreal about getting ready in the morning knowing that by the end of the day you’re going to be married to the person you love." See inside Martin and Jenny's wedding through the gallery below... The special day was full of sweet moments. "Honestly, it’s the little moments that stand out," Martin and Jenny gushed. "Seeing each other for the first time, being surrounded by our five children, family and friends and just the sheer happiness of the day. As if it was written in the stars, Dublin won their first All-Ireland in 16 years with a last-minute free by Stephen Cluxton and Jenny organised for Sam Maguire to arrive at the wedding as a surprise for GAA mad Martin. That moment was epic for all of Martin’s family, especially his dad." They added: "We also remember the laughter and the craic, because that’s very much us! And now, 15 years on, we think one of the loveliest things is looking back at photographs and remembering people and moments that you might otherwise have forgotten." Now as they prepare to celebrate their anniversary soon, the couple shared their secret to a happy relationship: "Friendship, laughter and not taking each other for granted and also making time for each other, even if it’s just sitting together to watch TV. Being able to laugh together, we think that’s hugely important. After 15 years, you realise marriage isn’t about everything being perfect. It’s about choosing each other, again and again, through all the different stages of life." This interview originally appeared in the September issue of RSVP Magazine. Greyhound Racing

State funding for greyhound racing exceeds €20m for the first time in 25 years

The sector’s funding has gone up by half a million compared with 2026.

6.11pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

THE GREYHOUND RACING industry has received over €20 million in funding for the first time since the Horse and Greyhound Racing Fund was established in 2001. 

The fund, which is overseen by the Department of Agriculture, was allocated €102 million in Budget 2027 – an increase of €2.9 million from last year.

The money is split 80:20 between the two sports, with horse racing to receive €79.3 million of the fund and greyhound racing to receive €20.4 million. 

Announcing the allocation, Minister for Agriculture Martin Heydon said: “The proposed increase in the Fund will be linked to the implementation of the Indecon Review’s recommendations in respect of equine and greyhound welfare and integrity. This will form part of the Department’s overall animal welfare package.”

The government has come under fire for consistently funding the industry despite ethical concerns around the sport. The funding is in the context of analysis which shows dwindling popularity among the public.

Greyhound Racing Ireland has welcomed the allocation and said the industry is “well-regulated” and “ethical”, and that it makes a significant contribution to Ireland’s economy and culture.

A 2021 report on greyhound racing estimated the industry contributed €132.3 million annually to the Irish economy; however, Sinn Féin senator Chris Andrews previously said the figure could be as low as around €49 million.

Speaking to The Journal, Andrews said funding for the industry is down to intense lobbying of Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil and “undue influence over public policy”.

“Since 2001, successive Governments have handed €407 million of public money to the inhumane and unpopular greyhound industry. Next year, greyhound racing will receive over €20 million from the state, up half a million from 2026,” he said.

Andrews compared the funding to that of the League of Ireland, which received just €4 million in funding in Budget 2027, despite a report finding it contributed over €160 million to the economy in 2023. 

Andrews said: “This funding is far and away more than what is being given to the League of Ireland, which has to fight for scraps while Greyhound Racing Ireland is guaranteed a mountain of cash every year in perpetuity.”

“Over 1.1 million people attended League of Ireland matches last year. Greyhound meets attracted only a third of that number, and yet the Government barely has an interest in investing in Irish football.”

😡😡😡😡€102 million 😡😡😡❤️❤️
That’s an extraordinary amount of public money being spent on horse and greyhound racing, while animal rescues across Ireland are struggling to survive.💔💔
Those same rescues are taking in the horses and greyhounds who have been discarded, neglected and traumatised. They are paying for veterinary care, rehabilitation, food, shelter and the chance of a second life, often relying on donations and volunteers just to keep going.💔

And yet, our Government continues to put enormous public funding into an industry built around racing and betting.😡😡😡

How can this be right?

While rescues are fighting every single day to repair the damage done to these animals, where is the same commitment to their welfare?

This isn’t just about money. It’s about priorities. It’s about what kind of country we want Ireland to be.

Animals cannot speak for themselves. We have to speak for them.💔💔😡😡😡😡

Email: taoiseach@taoiseach.gov.ie
Phone: 01 619 4000
Address: Department of the Taoiseach, Government Buildings, Merrion Street Upper, Dublin 2, D02 R583— My Lovely Horse Rescue (@MyLovelyHorseR) October 6, 2026

Advertisement

Meanwhile, People Before Profit’s Paul Murphy described the funding as “outrageous”.

Speaking to The Journal, he said: “Why is the public paying for cruel greyhound racing? Why is the public giving money for horse racing prizes which end up as tax-free money in the pockets of some of the richest people in the country?”

Sinn Féin’s Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh believes horse racing and greyhound racing should be decoupled when it comes to funding. 

“Greyhound racing should be required to demonstrate its viability as a standalone industry before receiving further taxpayer support,” she told The Journal.

“At present, the industry benefits from being tied to the far more lucrative horse racing sector, despite declining attendance and growing public concern about animal welfare.”

Greyhound advocacy group Greyhound Action said the funding of industry in the budget is “unjustifiable from either an economic or animal welfare perspective”.

“The greyhound racing industry is losing money; it has chronically poor attendance at its stadia and its economic case for state support relies on outdated evidence,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

“Most damningly of all, it’s an industry whose animal welfare record raises profound questions about whether it should even be allowed to continue.”

The group called on the government to commission an independent, transparent and up-to-date study of the economic value of greyhound racing to the economy.

Animal rescue charity My Lovely Horse criticised the government for funding the industry while animal rescues struggle financially.

“Those same rescues are taking in the horses and greyhounds who have been discarded, neglected and traumatised,” it said on X.

“They are paying for veterinary care, rehabilitation, food, shelter and the chance of a second life, often relying on donations and volunteers just to keep going.”

Greyhound Racing Ireland, also known as Rásaíocht Con Éireann, said it welcomed the government’s announcement and is “looking forward to continuing to govern and deliver a well-regulated, ethical sport and industry; which through its regularly published performance data demonstrates that it has the greyhound’s welfare as its key strategic priority, and is at the forefront of animal welfare governance in the country”.

“RCÉ as a Commercial Semi-State Body, and the wider greyhound racing industry, also make a significant contribution to the economy and the social, cultural and heritage life of our country.”

Horse Racing Ireland and the Department of Agriculture have been contacted for comment. 

Sophie Finn

news.title: RTÉ says €20m cut in funding will impact on strategy as Minister criticises pace of reforms
news.text:
RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst has rejected Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan’s assertion that the pace of reform at Montrose has been inadequate after the Government cut the national broadcaster’s funding in Budget 2027.

RTÉ reached a landmark multiyear funding deal with the previous government in 2024. Under the agreement, the broadcaster would receive €725 million over three years: €225 million in 2025, €240 million in 2026, and €260 million in 2027.

However, O’Donovan announced on Wednesday RTÉ would receive €240 million next year, saying that he was not happy with the pace of change at the broadcaster and its transition to being a “more agile, smaller” organisation.

The decision appears to have been made at the last minute and, according to Bakhurst, it caught the broadcaster off guard. He told staff in an email on Wednesday that he “completely rejects the assertion that the pace of reform has been too slow.”

Bakhurst said the decision “is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact our ability to deliver our five-year strategy”.

Over the past two years, RTÉ has axed its in-house documentary unit, outsourced its religious affairs programming, and cancelled Upfront with Katie Hannon. It has also set out plans to outsource Fair City and The Late Late Show. 

However, the Government has reportedly been disappointed by the pace of a job-shedding programme, through which RTÉ aimed to cut 400 jobs.

“I think it is well documented that you know that there were issues with regard to the voluntary redundancy that could be achieved in the last round, and obviously we would hope that that would be able to be advanced,” O’Donovan said on Wednesday.

[ RTÉ set to run up four-year €960,000 Dublin hotels bill for contributors and celebrity guestsOpens in new window ]

Speaking at a press conference, the minister also said his department had “very little scope, in relation to what resources we had available”.

Most of the State funding to RTÉ is to come from licence fees. However, RTÉ required a €41.3 million top-up from the exchequer last year. Bakhurst told the Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee in July that the organisation will also need €54.8 million in direct funding this year from the Government, due to an ongoing decline in licence fee revenues.

In a statement earlier, Bakhurst said RTÉ had “some important decisions to make” if the funding agreement it had with the Government “will no longer be honoured”.

On job cuts, he said the broadcaster had “already managed to exit almost 100 people from the organisation, despite the late approval of the voluntary exit programme and a short window to enable people to leave.

“The Government’s decision to reduce this public funding agreement by €20 million at this late stage, when we have already made important commitments to our audiences, to the independent sector, to other important stakeholders and to RTÉ staff, is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact on our ability to deliver our five-year strategy. 

“If the three-year multiannual agreement will no longer be honoured – we now have some important decisions to make.”

[ RTÉ’s new Listen app tells us some things about its future direction but keeps others hiddenOpens in new window ]
news.summary: Patrick O’Donovan said he was not happy with progress to date on broadcaster’s transition ‘more agile, smaller’ organisation

Shingles vaccine rollout to begin in June 2027, says health minister

The vaccine will be offered to people who are immunocompromised in early summer.

6.01pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

THE ROLL-OUT OF the vaccine will not start until June next year.

The jab will initially be offered to people who are immunocompromised, according to Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill. 

Speaking today at her department’s post-budget press conference in Government Buildings, the minister said the vaccine will be offered to people who are immunocompromised in early summer, before moving on to the over-80s. 

Advertisement

On a phased basis, the vaccine will then be offered to those over 65. 

Shingles vaccines are available in Ireland, but the HSE does not currently provide free vaccination and people must pay to be vaccinated.

Shingles is a viral infection caused by the same virus that causes chickenpox, and you can only get shingles if you have already had chickenpox.

Three out of every 10 people who have had chickenpox will go on to have shingles at some point in their life and while you cannot pass shingles to another person, coming in contact with shingles can cause chickenpox in someone who has never had chickenpox before.

Shingles causes a painful, blister-like rash, and while symptoms normally clear up within a month, some people may continue to experience pain for months, or even years after the rash heals.

Where's the protest gone? No rows, no riots, and not even a 'hup ya boy ya'

The minister said the HSE is currently negotiating the price with the pharmaceutical company, with MacNeill stating she wants “to be careful in relation to that”. 

The minister said the vaccine lasts about 10 to 11 years, adding that it is a very significant investment in health, particularly for older people.

Two years ago, the Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA)) deemed that introducing a shingles’ vaccine programme would “not be an efficient use of resources” at the current vaccine price.

news.title: Richard Hogan: What is resilience and how can we boost it in our children?
news.text:
But true resilience is not about being immune to everything life throws at you, it’s not that you won’t feel stress from time to time; it’s about how you learn to adapt and recover when life inevitably becomes a little tricky.

I carried out a study in 2018 when I was writing my first book, Parenting The Screenager. I interviewed more than 500 primary and secondary school students, investigating their use of technology, resilience, and pornography.

The insights I received from that study is why I have been such an advocate for action to stop our children from consuming hardcore, sexual images.

Primary school students were viewing very problematic images. I still can’t believe nothing has changed, to stop that poison reaching the minds of our children.

The study also showed that children who exhibited resilience spoke to themselves more positively than the students that showed low levels of resilience.

For example, a student with high levels of resilience understood that challenges and negative experiences were only temporary. If they missed a penalty in football they would tell themselves, ‘I’ll get it next time’. 

If they had a fight with their mother, ‘we will make up later’. If they didn’t get the result they wanted in an exam, ‘that was a tough exam, I’ll do better next time’. If they don’t feel great emotionally, ‘I don’t feel good today, but I was fine yesterday so more than likely I’ll be grand tomorrow’.

 They had the capacity to talk to themselves in a more positive way. So, a resilient child feels everything any other child feels, but it’s how they interpret those feelings that makes the difference.

In my experience, a child who lacks resilience will selectively abstract one negative experience or feeling and make it a gestalt, the whole, of their experience. 

Miss a penalty, ‘I’m crap at football’. If they have a fight with their mother, ‘no-one loves me’. If the exam doesn’t go their way, ‘I’m stupid’. If they feel emotionally upset, ‘I never feel good’. Their capacity to speak positively to themselves is significantly diminished.

So, we have to get in there early as parents and disrupt that negative voice. The brain leans more towards negativity than positivity because that helps us survive.

 But we can help prime our children’s brains a little more positively, by how we talk about them, and how we help them to challenge their inner talk.

Something I say as a mantra in my house is the following: “We go for things in this house, in the belief we can get it, and in the knowledge we don’t always get everything we go for, and if we don’t get it, we go again.” 

My children have heard me say that a thousand times. I want them to have the message; you can’t get anything if you don’t go for it.

I think today’s children have a terrible fear of not getting something they want, and therefore they don’t go for it. They believe that if they don’t go for something they really want, like the school play or a try-out for the school football team, well, then, they cannot be disappointed when they don’t get selected.

It’s a paradoxical intervention for fear of failure, the paradox is that by avoiding, they create the outcome they so desperately fear.

 I have always believed that the family should model what the real world is like, and parents should be disrupters and push their children when the stakes are low.

We want our children to be able to take healthy risks and believe that they will be able to manage whatever life throws at them.

There is a lot of talk in the media about how soft today’s young adults are and how unprepared they are for the world they are going into.

Normal ups and downs like romantic break-ups or friendships ending seem to have a greater impact on this generation than previous ones.

If this is the case, we can’t blame the young adults. They didn’t grow up in a vacuum, we created environments for them that didn’t challenge them or push them so that they developed the ability to adapt to difficult situations.

 We removed obstacles for them, we resolved moments when they were stressful, and they didn’t learn how to manage those moments.

Whenever my children come to me with an issue, I ask them questions: What do you think you are doing that is helping in the situation? What are you doing that is not helping? And what do you think you could do to change how things are going?

Simple questions empower children so that they learn that they have agency over their feelings and behaviours.

We will all feel low from time to time, life will throw plenty at us, the kitchen sink at times, but how we talk to ourselves in those moments will make the difference between collapsing and moving through.
news.summary: It's vital that adults teach the next generation the power of emphasising positivity when something goes wrong
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,Richard Hogan Family Psychothera

news.title: Sinn Féin says carbon taxes are penalising those who ‘drive tractors’
news.text:
Carbon taxes are penalising people who have "no alternative but to drive tractors and machinery that use green diesel," according to Sinn Féin. 

The Sinn Féin spokesperson on Agriculture and Food, Martin Kenny, today (Wednesday, October 7) also claimed that farmers and contractors "are going to be left behind by government again when it comes to fuel support in 2027".

The Minister for Public Expenditure, Jack Chambers, confirmed yesterday that as part of Budget 2027 the Fuel Income Support Scheme will be extended to cover a further five month period in 2026.

The scheme originally opened this year with a budget of €80 million to provide support to farmers and contractors dealing with large increases in green diesel costs.

However Deputy Kenny said that the measure announced in the budget yesterday "failed to provide any support for farmers or farm contractors in relation to increases in the cost of green diesel for 2027".

“Does the Tánaiste think that farmers are going to stop driving their tractors come the 1st of January," the Sinn Féin TD for Sligo-Leitrim asked.

Deputy Kenny said that currently the government has not provided "any support" on green diesel from January 1.

He is also warning that farmers and contractors could face higher diesel costs next year because the National Oil Reserves Agency Levy (NORA) "will be added back to the price at the pump".

Deputy Kenny said Sinn Féin has called for a reduction in carbon tax on green diesel and for it to be "cut at the pump".

"Farmers and farm contractors have no alternative but to drive tractors and machinery that use green diesel and carbon taxes are penalising them for doing so.“It is effectively a tax on their work and livelihood.“The fuel crisis will not end for farmers or farm contractors on December 31, they need to be supported in 2027 the same as everyone else," Deputy Kenny said.

news.title: ‘Very disturbing behaviour’: Teen jailed for two years for ‘appalling’ abuse of half-sisters
news.text:
A teenager jailed for two years for the “appalling” abuse of his two young half-sisters will also be subject to an eight-year post-release supervision order, a court has ruled.

The Central Criminal Court heard that the abuse came to light in March 2023 after the children’s mother walked into the boy’s room and saw him abusing his five-year-old half-sister while recording it on his phone. His then two-year-old half-sister was also in the room.

The now 18-year-old pleaded guilty to multiple counts, including three of sexually assaulting the older half-sister and one of orally raping her, and two of sexually assaulting the younger half-sister.

The investigation found a video of the boy masturbating on a bus, the court heard. In September 2023, after the abuse of his half-sisters was discovered, he was found viewing child sexual abuse material on a school laptop during a class. 

On Wednesday, the boy was handed a four-year sentence with the final two years suspended on very strict conditions for four years.

He will also be subject to the Sex Offender’s Act for five years and an eight-year post-release supervision order.

The boy was between 14 and 15 when he abused his half-sisters in the family home on various dates between 2022 and 2023. 

He cannot be named as all parties have a legal right to anonymity.

When the boy’s phone was analysed, 408 images and 11 videos were found, including some of him sexually abusing both girls. 

Thousands of videos and images of adult pornography were also found. 

[ Boy (8) settles action over circumstances of birth at Cork hospital for €7.5mOpens in new window ]

The boy was sent to stay with his father the next day, but returned to sit his Junior Certificate. He then went back to his father’s home for the summer before going back to school.

While there was a safety plan, it later became clear that the boy couldn’t remain in the family home. He went into specialised foster care, as he could not live with others under 18. More recently, he has been living in an aftercare placement and completed his Leaving Certificate online. 

After hearing the facts earlier this year, Judge Paul McDermott agreed to a defence application to allow the boy to complete his Leaving Certificate and a therapeutic programme.

However, there had been concerns in recent months that the boy was not fully complying with his strict bail conditions.

The court heard earlier this week that the boy was seen by a case worker with a mobile phone in August. 

[ Woman’s High Court case against adult websites adjourned over $120m US settlementOpens in new window ]

Michael Bowman, defending, said his client is aware he can’t have a phone.

The judge finalised sentence on Wednesday.

The judge noted this case was about “very disturbing behaviour” by a young teenager who had repeatedly abused his “very young” sisters over a protracted period.

He said that the footage was “appalling”. 

The judge said the mother had been placed in the “most difficult position imaginable” and had “done her very best by each of her three children”.

The boy is assessed as being at high risk of reoffending by the Probation Service. 

A multidisciplinary structure is considered necessary by adult services.

Last month, the boy admitted to buying and selling 10 smartphones since his 18th birthday, downloading certain apps, viewing pornography and having a “deviant sexual interest in young girls”.

McDermott indicated that a “different approach is now required” and that a custodial sentence would be imposed.

The judge noted both girls have received counselling and the family decided not to make a victim impact statement. He said the court respected this decision, and considered that “terrible damage” had been done to the girls and to the family unit.

The judge outlined the headline sentences which would apply on each count for an adult, including 12 years for the oral rape.

[ Man charged with murder of Tadhg Farrell (4) and Mary Holt (60) in Edenderry house fireOpens in new window ]

He reduced each headline sentence to reflect that the boy was a child in the eyes of the law at the time of the offending.

The judge also noted the mitigation, including the boy’s early guilty pleas, admissions, his social isolation and exploitation by others.

McDermott suspended the final two years to incentivise his engagement with services and to supervise his return to the community.

The conditions for the part-suspended sentence include that the boy engage with any programmes to address his sexual offending. 

A full Tusla investigation also took place.

The court heard his mother is willing to allow him to remain in her life, so long as he addresses his offending behaviour.
news.summary: The boy was between 14 and 15 when he abused his half-sisters in the family home
news.author: Eimear Dodd

news.title: Petrol bomb attack sent message to criminal who escaped with his life in two recent botched shootings
news.text: Gardai believe an overnight petrol attack was intended to send a message to a criminal who recently survived two shooting attempts on his life. Gardai and Dublin Fire Brigade rushed to the scene of the blaze at a property off the Davitt Road in Drimnagh in the early hours of Wednesday morning. A man in his 20s, who is understood not to have been the intended target of the attack, was taken to hospital for smoke inhalation treatment. Later in the day, the front of the property—which is close to the Drimnagh Luas stop and covered in Halloween decorations—was seen being boarded up. Sources say the attack comes amid a bitter feud that saw a man narrowly escape with his life following two separate shooting incidents in the Bluebell area on September 22 and 23. The 38-year-old criminal, originally from the Drimnagh area, was shot at in two separate incidents in Bluebell and on the Jamestown Road in Inchicore. The target, who was recently spared a jail sentence over a serious weapons-related charge, was lucky to escape with his life in both incidents. It is now feared this latest attack was designed to intimidate the target, or draw him out of hiding. Sources say a bitter dispute between the criminal and a gang has significantly escalated in recent weeks - and there are fears of further violence. Meanwhile local councillor Daithi Doolan condemned the latest attack, saying the community was effectively being "held to ransom." "Last night we witnessed another petrol bomb attack in our community. The latest attack took place in Drimnagh. This comes after several other petrol bomb attacks and gun attacks in the area over the last two weeks," he said. "The situation is clearly out of control. Those involved need to pull back and stop these terrible attacks. This violence is putting lives at serious risk. The attacks are holding the whole community to ransom. We can not let them win." Cllr Doolan said the government needs to take action to prevent further violence. "But we need action at the highest level of government. The silence from the Minister of Justice, Jim O’Callaghan is unacceptable," he said. "I have asked him publicly on three separate occasions to meet with senior Gardaí and local representatives to discuss how he intends to tackle the cause and consequences of this violence. He has clearly lost control. The violence is spiralling and he remains silent. This is simply not good enough. "I will be writing to senior Gardaí and the Minister for Justice demanding an immediate meeting. We need a plan, and we need urgent action to be taken. It is only by working together that we will make our communities safe places for everyone. "I would appeal to anyone with any information about these attacks to please contact the Gardaí." The target of the recent incidents is believed to have been feuding with a gang connected to Josh Itseli, whose death on the Knocknarea Road in Drimnagh is still under investigation. Gardai investigating Itseli’s death subsequently recovered an AR-15 assault rifle believed to have been used in the shooting incident, in a bush nearby. The discovery had been made by local children playing on the street. The target has a number of convictions, including for drug and public order offences. He is known to have addiction issues and was recently spared a jail sentence for a serious conviction. news.summary: Gardai and Dublin Fire Brigade rushed to the scene of the blaze at a property off the Davitt Road in Drimnagh in the early hours of Wednesday morning

news.title: Maura Derrane on 30 years in television and the importance of believing in yourself
news.text: RTE presenter Maura Derrane may be 30 years on our screens this year but she has no intention of slowing down. Starting in the newsroom with TG4 and finding her way to afternoon TV in RTE , the Galway girl has resonated with audiences from day one. With a passion for fashion, wellness, lifestyle and current affairs - presenting the Today Show is the ideal gig for our favourite Gaeilgeoir. “I'm actually 30 years on air now consistently without a break, which is amazing, really, when you think about it.” Maura told RSVP, continuing she said, “I was very lucky that I fell into the career that was to be my whole life and broadcasting will do that, you know, media, broadcasting, journalism. I started as a journalist, then became a presenter, so it's kind of full circle, but I think that it's such a brilliant area because it's so vast. “You can never get bored in an area like this because there's so much involved in it, you can constantly divert to different disciplines. And now there's online, there's podcasts, there's all sorts, there's a whole realm of media that is there now for the next generation and forward generations, which is great.” Maura agreed her chosen career is a precarious one but advises that you cannot get into the industry if you are worried about the next step. Explaining, she said: “It's only in this last year that I've been made staff at RTE , before that I was a contractor. So I worked year to year, not knowing if I had a job every September. And yes, that is very precarious, but it takes a certain mindset to be able to live within that realm. And I'm lucky that I never worried too much about the next year. I always felt, even if one door closed, even if the show I was working on finished, I figured that another door would open.” Speak about confidence and her self belief, Maura said: “I don't think I was brought up to have confidence. My mother was very good at instilling, do what you like best, not what you think you should do. "If you're unhappy in something, don't continue to be unhappy in that field. "She never told us you need to go to school, you need to work really hard, you need to pass all your exams, go to college. It was never that It was always what makes you happy and find out what makes you happy. I really do believe there is a career, job and a place in life for everyone but it shouldn’t be all about career either, that is the difference with the young people today, they have more balance.” Photographer : Kieran Harnett Hair: Roisin Derrane Makeup ;Roisin Derrane Stylist ; Chloe Markham Location : The Intercontinental Hotel, Ballsbridge Simmons Restaurant a new contemporary dining experience has opened at the five star InterContinental Dublin in Ballsbridge, Dublin 4. The Dine at Simmons overnight package is for two people sharing in a Classic King Room, a three course dinner for two in Simmons, complimentary access to the Hotel’s Wellness Area, including the indoor pool, steam room and sauna and a relaxed breakfast the following morning. news.title: Mark Zuckerberg paid more than €50m for Strancally Castle in Co Waterford, register shows
news.text:
Mark Zuckerberg, the billionaire chief executive behind social media giant Meta, and his wife, Priscilla Chan, paid more than €50 million for Strancally Castle in Co Waterford, according to the Property Price Register.

The sale figure of €51,171,155, which was published on Wednesday, is close to double the estimated price tag put on the property at the time of sale by property market sources.

It includes the amount paid for the principal residence and up to an acre of land. Therefore, the couple’s total spend would greatly exceed what appears on the register when the entirety of the 440-acre estate is considered.

The date of sale was recorded as August 17th, 2026.

When the sale was first reported by The Irish Times three days later, on August 20th, it was believed to have achieved in the region of €20 million to €30 million based on the quality of the residence, which has undergone a full restoration over the past 20 years.

Zuckerberg and his wife completed the purchase of the Gothic-revival style house and estate on the banks of the river Blackwater from owners Michael and Giancarla Alen-Buckley.

“Mark and his family are excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time in Ireland, where Meta maintains its international headquarters,” a spokesman for Zuckerberg said. 

Built originally around 1830 for John Keily, a former Tory MP, Strancally Castle was, according to its description in Brian De Breffny and Rosemary Ffolliott’s book The Houses of Ireland, “designed by the Pain brothers on a lavish scale; it took a brisk walk of 4½ minutes to reach the diningroom from the kitchen”.

Architects James and George Richard Pain designed the main house and a nearby folly tower house and an inlet quay on the banks of the river Blackwater.

Alen-Buckley, a cofounder of London-headquartered private investment firm RAB Capital, and his wife, who is a daughter of the late Charles Forte and sister of Rocco Forte of the Rocco Forte Hotels group, acquired Strancally Castle 25 years ago.

[ Original home of Mark Zuckerberg’s Irish castle is immortalised in verse as the site of gruesome deedsOpens in new window ]

The three-storey building extends to 16,000sq ft. In a statement issued to The Irish Times, the Alen-Buckleys said: “We leave our home of 25 years fondly and are grateful for the opportunity we have been given to save and restore Strancally Castle ... We are delighted that Mark and his family intend to build on our stewardship by continuing to invest in maintaining and enhancing the property and grounds as their home in a sustainable manner ... We wish them and their family much happiness in this unique and blessed place.”

It is understood Zuckerberg and his wife will continue to live in the United States and intend to use Strancally Castle when in Ireland, where Meta, owner of social media platforms Facebook and Instagram, has had its European headquarters since 2009. The company employs about 1,500 people in Ireland.

Zuckerberg’s interest in acquiring a home here emerged last summer when Liberty Media billionaire owner John Malone told the Wall Street Journal that the Meta chief had offered to buy his Castlemartin House and Estate in Kildare from him.
news.summary: Sale figure published on Wednesday includes the amount paid for the principal residence and up to an acre of land
news.author: Jessica Doyle,Ronald Quinlan

news.title: Interview: Mayo great Cillian O’Connor retires — 'I'm sorry it took so long but we got there'
news.text:
He couldn’t stand it. He couldn’t sit still. Cillian O’Connor was watching Mayo propel themselves towards the ultimate dream in a game that would have a seismic impact on countless people. It was driving him mad.

When the Ballintubber clubman was playing for Mayo, nerves never crowded his mind. The posts and the white lines and the ball thrown in all provided sufficient outlets to expend that energy. But that seat in the stand that he grudgingly occupied for much of 2026 was nightmare fuel.
news.summary: As he retires from inter-county football, Cillian O'Connor reflects on years of Mayo heartbreak, sacrifices made during his career and the family memories transformed by All-Ireland glory
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,Maurice Brosnan

news.title: High Court to hear Palestinian student visa cases amid urgent Gaza concerns
news.text:
The High Court had been due to hear the students’ judicial review challenges this week against the refusal of visas allowing them to pursue fully funded scholarships at Irish universities.

However, Mr Justice Anthony Barr was told on Wednesday that the cases had been settled following an offer by Mr O’Callaghan to determine the students’ appeals by close of business on Friday.

With the appeal process for student visa refusals normally taking a year or more, and with their courses already underway, the students had sought an order requiring the minister to prioritise their appeals.

Among the reasons cited for refusal of the students’ visas was that they had submitted insufficient documentation of previous education or work qualifications.

Lawyers representing the four students argued that the civilian infrastructure needed to obtain such documents from a bank or post office no longer exists in Gaza.

They argued that the minister’s stance was irrational, unreasonable, disproportionate and discriminatory, and failed to respond to the necessary urgency of the situation.

Mr O’Callaghan had opposed the students’ actions.

Urgent hearing ordered

Following the minister’s agreement to prioritise the four students’ appeals, allowing a decision by Friday, lawyers representing dozens of other students made a separate application to the High Court on Wednesday.

Granting an urgent hearing on the grounds that it was “literally a matter of life and death”, Mr Justice Garret Simons directed that a rolled-up hearing take place on Tuesday, October 13, with the State to file its opposition papers by lunchtime on Monday, October 12.

He said the court recognised the urgent and extreme circumstances in which the other students who had been refused study visas find themselves.

With Israeli authorities requiring 11 days’ notice before evacuations of civilians from Gaza, it is believed that the last possible evacuation this year from the besieged enclave is scheduled for October 26.

This would mean all cases would need to be resolved by Thursday, October 15, at the latest.

The High Court will convene for two days from Tuesday for a rolled-up hearing on the lead cases, while all other filed cases will be mentioned alongside them.

At least eight such cases will be heard, with solicitors likely to continue filing further applications over the coming days.

Palestinian visa refusals rise

More than two million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in Gaza, where an estimated 80% of structures – approximately 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN.

Figures supplied to the Irish Examiner by the Department of Justice show that in 2025, Ireland refused 22 of 164 long-stay study visa applications from Palestine, representing a 13% refusal rate.

This year, 114 of 138 applications were refused, representing an 83% refusal rate.

Year-on-year, Irish refusals of study visas to Palestinian students have increased by 418%.
news.summary: At least eight Palestinian students are challenging visa refusals as lawyers warn of the urgency created by the Gaza evacuation deadline
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,Mr O

news.title: Mary McAleese resigned from integration role over missed deadline, says GAA president
news.text: The former president of Ireland resigned as chairwoman of the body tasked to bring about integration because she was "adamant that we were going to reach every deadline", GAA president Jarlath Burns has said. Mr Burns defended his commitment to integration and said he will "make it happen in a way that our members are comfortable with". Last month, Mary McAleese stepped down as chairwoman of the group overseeing the amalgamation of the Gaelic Athletic Association ( GAA ), Ladies Gaelic Football Association (LGFA) and the Camogie Association. She said she does not believe the integration of the three bodies will happen under the current leadership. Dr McAleese said changes to agreed timelines, issues with the GAA management committee, and her feeling that there were people who were "not entirely happy about the idea of including women in the decision-making" at the top level of Gaelic sports, were holding the integration process back. Mr Burns appeared before an Oireachtas committee on Wednesday when Fianna Fáil Senator Alison Comyn asked him what had happened to cause Dr McAleese to come to "such a stark conclusion that girls were being let down". He explained that the organisations were not ready to have a Special Congress scheduled for September following roadshows where members expressed "differing perspectives" with the proposed structures. "We were all very disappointed and we were all devastated that we lost Dr McAleese, but we’re all back on this wagon, we really want it to happen," he said. Ms Comyn raised concerns about "resistance to women having a meaningful role in decision making" within the GAA. Mr Burns said: "I think that was the thing that we found most regrettable, because this is not a gender issue. "It might be at the level of playing, but at the level of administration it is anything but. "Some of the best females are working in the GAA, and some of the best males are working in the other two organisations, and one of the biggest fears that we would have had at the GAA was that all of the wonderful people working currently in LGFA and camogie might leave this new organisation, and feel that there wasn’t a role for them in it." Cian Ó Lionáin, assistant secretary-general at the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport, said ministers "are happy with the role of women in all three organisations". Fine Gael TD Brian Brennan also asked why the former Irish president stepped back, describing her statement as "very, very strong" and that she claimed "the GAA had no vision for the future". Mr Burns said the "top level" of the GAA is "already fully integrated". He added: "For those people who think that integration has stopped or has gone back, that couldn’t be further from the truth. "What Dr McAleese said is not characterised by the reality, either at the top level or on the ground." Pressed again on why she resigned, Mr Burns said: "I think she resigned because she was very adamant that we were going to reach every deadline that we had and that once she realised we were going to miss the first deadline, I think she decided then that she wanted to walk away from the process. "Which was very disappointing for us, and we regret that deeply, but we are still very much committed to integration. "We really do want it to happen and it is up to us, and we will make it happen. "We’ll make it happen in a way that our members are comfortable with, and will vote for it." The president of the GAA was also asked about the cost of integration, and said: "I don’t want to be throwing out costs as something which is prohibitive. "The GAA will move from a discretionary to an obligatory provision for ladies football, and camogie – it’s going to cost a lot of money for infrastructure. "But this is a change programme, it’s not a project and that’s not going to stop us from achieving it, because a lot of those costs are going to be absorbed in the years after it happens." He said he would not give a "specific cost", because "if I do, it will come across as the GAA throwing out costs to be prohibitive and not supportive of the process". Later in the session, Mr Burns again stressed his commitment to women’s participation in Gaelic games, saying his daughter and granddaughters are involved in football and camogie. "I want the very best equality of opportunity for those four girls, and all of the girls in the school that I’m going to be back in to be principal – exactly the same," he said. "Even more so to ensure that ladies football and camogie can get the rightful place in the new GAA. "I wouldn’t be the proper president of the GAA if I didn’t really mean that from the bottom of my heart, but we have to do it in the way that it’s right and fair to everybody."
