news.summary: Last month, Mary McAleese stepped down as chairwoman of the group overseeing the amalgamation of the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA), Ladies Gaelic Football Association (LGFA) and the Camogie Association
news.author: Claudia Savage

news.title: GAA's delayed integration with ladies associations 'not a gender issue', says Jarlath Burns
news.text:
The former President of Ireland had been tasked by ex-GAA president Larry McCarthy in September 2022 with leading the group to oversee the amalgamation of the GAA, Ladies Gaelic Football Association (LGFA) and The Camogie Association (CA).

Ms McAleese said on her departure that there were some in the GAA "who are not entirely happy about the idea of including women in decision-making at the top level of Gaelic sports", a charge that Jarlath Burns rejected on Wednesday.

He said that while the issue of integration is a "gender issue" on the field, off it he is confident women will have decision-making standing in the integrated organisation.

“I think that was the thing that we found most regrettable, because this is not a gender issue,” said Burns. “It might be at the level of playing, but at the level of administration, it is anything but.

“Some of the best females are working in the GAA, and in the other organisations. And one of the biggest fears that we would have had was that all of the wonderful people working currently in the GAA might leave this new organisation and feel that there wasn’t a role for them.”

Mr Burns said he believes Ms McAleese stepped down because the 2027 deadline for integration was going to be missed.

“I think she resigned because she was very adamant that we were going to reach every deadline that we had,” Mr Burns said.

“And that, once she realised that we were going to miss the first deadline, I think she decided then that she wanted to walk away from the process, which was very disappointing for us, and we regret that deeply. But we are still very much committed to integration.

“And it is up to us to make it happen, but we will make it happen in a way that our members are comfortable with and we’re going for it.”

Cian Ó Lionáin from the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport said the two ministers in his department — senior minister Patrick O'Donovan and junior sports minister Charlie McConalogue — are satisfied women would have decision-making powers in the integration process and after. 

He said that question had been "interrogated" by the department.

Mr Burns said the GAA membership was not angered by missing the 2027 deadline but was keen to get the process right.

"Let's be cool and calm about what has happened. We have missed one deadline. We haven't abandoned integration — we have missed one deadline."

Camogie Association president Brian Molloy said "we can get to a point where we have a single national governing body reasonably quickly", but that it may not be 2028. 

However, Fine Gael TD Brian Brennan said he was "leaving this room confused and a little bit frustrated in relation to timeline".

 Paul Hosford, deputy political editor
news.summary: The GAA president said he believes Ms McAleese stepped down because the 2027 deadline for integration was going to be missed
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,Paul Hosford

Two teenagers sent for trial accused of attacking concertgoer near Dublin's 3Arena

A man in his 20s was left fighting for his life in hospital after the incident in January. 

5.38pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

TWO TEENAGERS HAVE been sent forward for trial, accused of attacking a concertgoer who was filmed on a phone as he was severely injured near the 3Arena in January.

The victim, a Co Laois man in his early 20s, was left fighting for his life in hospital after what was described as a sustained attack.

It occurred outside the venue in Dublin’s city centre after a concert by Scottish DJ Ewan McVicar.

The injured party was taken to Beaumont Hospital with two bleeds on the brain and was placed in an induced coma afterwards.

The pair, aged 17 and 16, had been charged earlier under Section 4 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act for recklessly or intentionally causing serious harm to the man, which carries a possible life sentence.

Advertisement

It was held that the case was too serious to remain in the Children’s Court and that they and a third youth, aged 17, should face trial on indictment.

The prosecution’s books of evidence were served on the two teenagers before Judge Paul Kelly granted orders sending them forward for trial in the Dublin Circuit Criminal Court.

The case will be listed for mention in November.

They were remanded on continuing bail subject to various conditions, including an order to have no contact with each other or the complainant, either directly or indirectly.

A bench warrant was issued for the third youth who failed to appear.

At a previous bail hearing, the court was told the incident was allegedly planned and premeditated and was filmed on a phone. A fourth defendant, an adult male, is also before the courts on related charges.

Planning officials issue enforcement order against IPAS centre at former Tipperary hotel

Dundrum House Hotel in rural west Tipperary had been at the centre of protests when it was transformed into an IPAS centre.

5.36pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

A PLANNING ENFORCEMENT order has been issued against the operators of a former hotel in Tipperary currently used to house asylum seekers. 

Tipperary County Council, in the enforcement note, ordered it to cease operating as an International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centre by early next year. 

A contract for Dundrum House Hotel in rural west Tipperary to be used for asylum seeker accommodation was first agreed in November 2024. (It had been hosting Ukrainian refugees since 2022.) 

The enforcement order, first reported by Tipperary Live, told the operator to stop using parts of the complex in this way by 29 January 2027. 

The order states that use of a number of locations, listed as Holm Oaks, The Square Block, The Coach House and the Old Wing or C Block, is defined as unauthorised development. 

The direction also states that use of an unauthorised wastewater treatment system is a breach of planning. 

It emerged recently that the Department of Justice was not going to renew the contract for the facility, ending its use in March 2027. 

Local TD Michael Murphy said that he was glad that the enforcement order had given further “clarity” to the situation with Dundrum House. 

“I welcome this decision by Tipperary County Council to take enforcement action in relation to Dundrum House.

I’ve consistently maintained that planning law must be respected, must be enforced, irrespective of the nature or development or who’s operating it.

“The planning permission with regard to Dundrum has been the subject of considerable concern within the local community for some time,” he said. 

Advertisement

There was significant media and public interest in protests which began in 2024 when a contract was signed between the Department of Integration and the then newly established company Utmasta to rent a section of the property for three years to house people seeking international protection. 

By that point, the operator of the site’s golf course and leisure facilities – Brogan Capital Ventures – had announced it was closing with immediate effect.

Last month, the Department of Justice said it noted the decision of An Coimisiún Pleanála which was published on 30 July in relation to planning matters at Dundrum House, Tipperary.

“While matters related to planning are between the Local Authority and the accommodation service provider, the Department requires valid confirmation of compliance with planning regulations for all IPAS properties that are newly contracted or renewed.

“In light of these circumstances, the Department has decided not to renew the accommodation contract at this location. This contract is due to expire in March 2027,” it said.

The department said that Dundrum House is currently contracted to accommodate 270 people in families seeking international protection.

“IPAS teams will commence planning for the relocation of the families living at Dundrum House over the coming months.

“The Department recognises that this news may cause uncertainty for residents, many of whom have established connections within the local community. We are particularly mindful of the impact this may have on families with children attending school, and in planning for this transition, aim to provide sufficient notice for families to plan for a change in location.

“IPAS will engage directly with residents to explain the next steps and provide assistance and information,” it said. 

Statements have been requested from Tipperary County Council and Utmasta. Efforts to contact Brogan Capital Ventures, which is now in liquidation, have not been successful. 

With reporting from Eoghan Dalton.

Niall O'Connor

news.title: Greyhound funding tops €20m for first time under Budget 2027
news.text:
The fund is allocated on a 4:1 basis, meaning horse racing will receive €81.6m while greyhound racing will receive €20.4m, up €580,000 on funding for 2026.

The horse and greyhound fund was established in 2001 to support both industries, and has grown steadily in recent years. The €102m allocation for 2027 represents an increase of more than 21% on the €84m provided in 2020.

 "I have allocated a further €2.9m for the horse and greyhound fund,” said Mr Heydon. 

 "The proposed increase in the fund will be linked to the implementation of the Indecon review’s recommendations in respect of equine and greyhound welfare and integrity,” he said, referring to a review carried out by an independent consultancy and presented to the Oireachtas last November.

 That review concluded that the welfare of racing greyhounds is an “existential issue” for the industry in Ireland. 

 Mr Heydon said that the increase in the fund would form part of his department's "overall animal welfare package" within the budget.

 Asked how its additional funding will be utilised, a spokesperson for industry body Greyhound Racing Ireland said it was still "awaiting formal confirmation of our allocation for 2027 and when received it will be considered by the executive and board".

 Nuala Donlon, a spokesperson for Greyhound Action Ireland, called for the Government to "immediately commission an independent, transparent, and up-to-date study of the economic value of greyhound racing" in Ireland.

 She said it should be carried out "without industry involvement in either its methodology or conclusions" and seek to establish "the economic activity that would genuinely be lost if public funding were withdrawn".

The most recent financial appraisal of greyhound racing was carried out by economist Jim Power in 2021 using 2019 data. It concluded that greyhound racing supported more than 4,000 jobs and contributed €132m annually to the Irish economy.

Critics have repeatedly challenged those findings, noting that the report relied heavily on figures supplied by Greyhound Racing Ireland.
news.summary: Horse and greyhound fund will rise by €2.9m next year to €102m
news.author: Cianan Brennan,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: Boy (8) settles action over circumstances of birth at Cork hospital for €7.5m
news.text:
An eight-year-old boy who sued over the circumstances of his birth at Cork University Maternity Hospital (CUMH) has settled a High Court action for €7.5 million.

The settlement to Alex Marcio Hunka Riberio, who now lives in the Czech Republic, is against the HSE. The settlement is without an admission of liability.

Liam Reidy, senior counsel for the boy instructed by Cantillons Solicitors, told the court it was their case that from the very moment Alex’s mother went into the Cork hospital to the moment she left, she did not meet a consultant obstetrician. The boy was born in August 2018.

Counsel said at a very early stage it was realised the baby’s mother had gestational diabetes, and her pregnancy was regarded as high risk due to a high BMI and other matters. 

The CUMH protocol in a high-risk case lays out certain things that should be put in place, including a clear delivery plan, counsel said. Counsel said it was their case that “all were broken in this case”. 

Counsel said there was no consultant obstetrician and no birth plan. Alex was a large baby, he said.

He said during the birth, the baby’s shoulder became lodged and it was claimed that the baby suffered a fracture to the right shoulder area during a forceps delivery.

It is claimed the baby suffered an acute hypoxic ischemic episode during the delivery and was in a very poor condition when born and he required urgent resuscitation.

Reidy said that the boy’s first breath was four minutes after his birth.

Counsel said experts on the boy’s side would say the boy’s neurodevelopmental issues were caused by an alleged brain injury.

Alex had, through his mother Magdalena Hunkova, sued the HSE.

It was claimed that the baby was caused to have an allegedly extremely traumatic labour lasting almost eight hours before instrumental delivery, where he suffered a shoulder dystocia.

It was claimed the baby suffered neonatal encephalopathy, which his side contended occurred over a short period of time immediately before delivery.

His side also contended that the boy’s neurodevelopmental, neurobehavioral and neurocognitive difficulties were allegedly as a result of perinatal hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy.

In the proceedings, it was claimed there was an alleged failure to put in place an agreed management plan for delivery of the baby, which should and would have included the option of delivery by Caesarean section.

It was also claimed there was an alleged failure to consider or recommend delivery by Caesarean section to the mother who had poorly controlled diabetes, an increased BMI and a recognised large baby.

It was also contended there was an alleged failure to provide the mother with adequate informed advice to enable informed maternal choice in the method of delivery of her baby.

All claims were denied, and the HSE contended that the care provided to the mother during the antenatal period was of a reasonable standard.

Judge Denise Brett said she had no hesitation in approving the settlement. The judge noted it as quite a complex case, and she now hoped the settlement would bring Alex a better quality of life.
news.summary: Senior counsel for the boy said his first breath was four minutes after his birth

news.title: Dean Ryan Cup: St Colman's survive late scare to overcome Castletroy
news.text:
St Colman’s 1-20 

 Castletroy 0-17

St Colman’s survived a late scare against Castletroy in the Dean Ryan Cup in Rathcormac on Wednesday.

The Fermoy school started strongly and looked to have a stranglehold on their opponents at half-time, retiring 10 points to the good. However, the second period was a different story.

Castletroy came out all guns blazing in a second stanza that saw St Colman’s hurleys go cold, at one point going 17 minutes without a score. Within that frigid period, Castletroy clawed their way back into the fight, stringing together nine scores with no response.

Now the Limerick contingent were only five behind with a nervy eight minutes to play.

Luckily for St Colman’s, they held strong down the stretch, two late frees from Oran Hegarty settling the Fermoy lads nerves before running out eventual winners by six.

The game’s only green flag was raised after five minutes, courtesy of Colman's Ned Condon.

Tadhg Walsh found his man with a brilliant kick pass off his left leg after losing his hurley before Condon drilled it past keeper Brian Halley in the Castletroy net.

Clocking up a significant 14 first-half wides, Colman’s could and should have been out of sight before the half ended.

Evidently, it didn’t dishearten them. The Fermoy lads moved up a gear after the goal, scoring 11 points on the way in and holding their opponents to three scores.

Hegarty and Condon were running the show, with Fionn Lynch and Bailey Browne chipping in with scores to increase the Colman’s advantage before the break.

Seven minutes into the second half and it looked like a steam-rolling was in store for Castletroy. Tadhg Walsh, Conor Holland, Hegarty and Condon (2) contributed for Colman’s and all of a sudden the lead was extended to 14.

Testament to their fighting spirit, Castletroy never backed down and soon they were the only team playing hurling.

The Limerick school’s star man Conor Langan scored his fourth point of the game to begin the comeback effort. Thus began 12 minutes of utter domination as the rain begun to fall in Rathcormac.

With each Castletroy white flag, the nerves began to build, and it showed as effort after effort slipped wide of the target for Colman’s.

Two magnificent saves, both from Langan efforts, by St Colman’s keeper Cathal Higgins kept it from becoming a real tussle down the stretch.

Seán Sheehan placed his third score over to narrow the gap to five with five to play. Thankfully, St Colman’s, Hegarty rediscovered his mojo and two accurate frees sealed the win late on.

 Scorers for St Colmans: O Hegarty 0-8 (0-6 f), N Condon 1-3, S O’Leary 0-3, B Browne, F Lynch 0-2 each, T Walsh, C Holland 0-1 each.

 Castletroy: O Langan 0-5 (0-1 f), S Sheehan 0-3 (0-1 f), P Quilty 0-3, K Maher 0-2, A Ryan 0-1, B Fitzgerald, J Webster, M O’Grady 0-1 each.

 ST COLMANS: C Higgins (St Catherine’s); J Fitzgerald (Bride Rovers), M Quirke (Kilworth), R Lehane (Watergrasshill); C Holland (Ballycastle Gaels), C Scanlan (Bride Rovers, jc), JJ Cahill (Kilworth); O Hegarty (Kilworth, jc), H O’Brien (Kilworth); B Browne (Kilworth), R Molumphy (Ballyduff Upper), T Walsh (St Catherine’s); S O’Leary (Watergrasshill), F Lynch (Bride Rovers), N Condon (Castlelyons).

 Subs: B O’Connor (St Catherine’s) for B Browne (HT), A Keane (St Catherine’s) for R Molumphy (HT), T Ahern (Kilworth) for F Lynch (51), R McCallum (Kilworth) for JJ Cahill (57).

 CASTLETROY (all Monaleen except where stated): B Halley; A O’Connell (Ahane), D Ryan, J Flannery; R Guinan, D Scully, J Webster; M O’Grady, A Ryan; P Quilty, S Sheehan, S Hendrick (St Pats); B Fitzgerald, O Langan, B Hurley.

 Subs: K Maher (Ahane) for A Ryan (HT), H O’Connell for Hendrick (HT).

 Referee: Michael Carey (Bride Rovers).
news.summary: Fermoy school started strongly, ahead by 10 points, but were pushed hard coming down the stretch at Rathcormac

news.title: Taoiseach says crime data by nationality could help counter claims about ethnicity
news.text:
However, in that interview, he immediately added: “I’m not too sure that murder or crime is specific to any nationality. In fact, a lot of crime is committed by Irish people as well as other nationalities.

“I don’t think crime is specific to any nationality. But there are issues there, and in some cases, yes, there’s been horrific crimes committed, but not all by illegal migrants either.”

Asked about those remarks, Mr Martin clarified to reporters in Cork that he believed publishing such statistics might have a positive benefit.

“What I said in that interview was I was open to it,” he said.

“I’m conscious those putting that question are suggesting that one ethnicity or a couple of ethnicities are more responsible than others.

“I don’t believe that. I believe that crime is not specific to any ethnicity, and I made that point in the interview.

“But sometimes, to deal with presentations and arguments of that kind, the production of the data could deal with it more eloquently than we articulating a position or a perspective.

"But obviously, that’s something we would have to consider very, very carefully.” 

Warning against ‘bait’

However, Edel McGinley, executive director of the Hope and Courage Collective, an NGO which works to counter far-right hatred and disinformation, urged the Taoiseach not to “take the bait” on the issue.

“A handful of haters have been trying to whip up division and create traps for our politicians to walk into, by focusing on nationality and crime,” she said.

“This is a classic part of the playbook of hate and division. We have seen this time and time again, particularly in the USA and the UK.” Ireland, she said, should not allow “Fox News or the USA” to set the political agenda in this country.

“Safer communities mean access to decent affordable homes, good schools and childcare, local support and services and a feeling of belonging,” Ms McGinley added.

“Alongside this, we need effective policing, with a focus on community relations, support for victims, and neighbourhoods where people know and look out for one another.

“To suggest otherwise is just a distraction”.

Social Democrats call for wider data

Dublin South Central TD Gary Gannon, who is the Social Democrats justice spokesperson, said his party was not opposed in principle to collecting demographic data for the prison population.

“We advocate collecting it in areas like stop and search precisely because it can help identify discrimination or disproportionate policing,” he said.

“But we need to distinguish between examining how the justice system treats different communities and just inviting people - some of whom have an obvious agenda - to draw conclusions about entire communities from conviction figures.

“If the Taoiseach wants an evidence-based discussion, it needs to examine the full picture, including poverty, access to appropriate representation while in the courts system, and failures in education, care and disability supports.

“Publishing ethnicity or nationality figures alone would not explain why people end up in the criminal justice system.”
news.summary: Micheál Martin said crime is not specific to any nationality as campaigners warned against allowing nationality and crime to become linked
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,Mick Clifford

news.title: Andy Burnham’s first ballot box test: Labour and Greens clash in Starmer’s old seat
news.text:
The nascent leadership of Britain’s prime minister and Labour leader Andy Burnham faces its first electoral test on Thursday in a byelection in the Holborn and St Pancras seat vacated by the man he ousted from Downing Street, Keir Starmer.

Labour’s candidate, Camden council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali, is seen as being in a two-horse race for the inner north London seat with the high-profile leader of the Green Party, Zack Polanski.

Labour sources are cautiously optimistic about winning the seat but a shock victory for Polanski, whose political base is seen as stronger further east in London towards Hackney, is not being ruled out.

The slate of 15 candidates also includes veteran byelection candidate, George Galloway, of the Workers Party of Britain, although he is not expected to figure in the shake-up for the constituency, which includes well-known London landmarks such as King’s Cross and Euston stations and the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

The southern end of the constituency, closer to the centre of London, includes large numbers of students and young professional flat-sharers, as well as a larger-than-average contingent of foreign-born residents.

Further to the north, the constituency profile changes to include more settled communities around areas such as Kentish Town, where Starmer lives, and also Camden Town, which was traditionally an area with high numbers of Irish and Caribbean immigrants.

Polanski has energised the Green Party since he became its leader in September 2025, although it has also fallen sharply in the polls over the past five months and has been leaking support back to Labour since Burnham ousted Starmer in July.

A YouGov poll this week gave Labour a 16 point national lead over the Greens, although its lead in Holborn and St Pancras would be seen as far tighter.

The Green leader’s byelection bid is taking place against the backdrop of a tumultuous period for his party, which held its annual conference in Brighton last weekend; Polanski missed most of the gathering to campaign in London.

The Greens were roiled by an anti-Israel motion passed by members at its conference stating that “Zionism is racism”. Yet four of the party’s five sitting MPs were opposed to the motion, while Polanski, who was banned from Israel after it was passed, also did not back it. He has since suggested the party needs to “move on” from the divisive debate.

Labour, meanwhile, is on a high after Burnham’s successful first conference as leader. Abdi-Wali, a Muslim woman who arrived in Britain with her family aged six as a refugee from Somalia, has largely avoided wading too deeply into the Israel-Gaza debate during the campaign. 

Instead, her campaign has focused more on local issues in the constituency. Polanski has also tilted his campaign more towards water services and rent controls in the latter stages of the campaign.

Labour’s campaign is being run by an MP based in south London, Liam Conlon, whose father is from Fermanagh and whose mother is Sue Gray, Starmer’s former chief of staff.

[ Why Andy Burnham says ‘Brexit has done more harm than good’Opens in new window ]
news.summary: Today’s byelection will offer the first indication of whether Labour can retain disillusioned progressive voters under its new leader
news.author: Mark Paul

The assault took place during an aggravated burglary at a South Dublin home in 2003. 

5.22pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

A MAN IN his 60s has been arrested in connection with an alleged assault on a woman 23 years ago.

The serious assault took place during an aggravated burglary at a residence in Kilmacud, South Dublin, on the morning of 31 March 2003.

An extensive garda investigation took place at the time with hundreds of investigative jobs undertaken and over 100 statements taken.

Advertisement

An Garda Síochána has continued to maintain an open investigation into the assault.

In 2023, a review of the investigation was commenced by a new investigation team attached to the Serious Crime Unit. 

A man in his 60s was subsequently arrested in connection with the investigation this morning.

He is currently detained under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 at a garda station in the Dublin Metropolitan Region.

Investigations are ongoing.

Hannah Power

Jorge Jesus: I’ve read Cristiano Ronaldo’s statement, now I think about the team

The former Man United star said there had been a ‘breach of trust’ between him and the Portugal boss.

5.20pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

PORTUGAL BOSS JORGE Jesus has read Cristiano Ronaldo’s lengthy explanation for walking out on the national team but opted not to comment further on the matter.

Ronaldo left Portugal’s training camp last week after he was an unused substitute in their 2-1 Nations League win against Norway on 27 September.

The 41-year-old, who has scored a record-breaking 146 goals in 234 appearances for his country, has since issued a near 2,000-word statement saying he withdrew from the squad after a “breach of trust” between him and the head coach.

Advertisement

Jesus told reporters when leaving his home on Wednesday: “I read the statement and now I do (like I do) every day. I’m going to the federation to work, think about the team.”

Ronaldo missed Portugal’s following two fixtures, wins over Denmark and Norway, which left them top of Group A4 with four straight wins, fuelling speculation his international career could be over.

Jesus left the door open to Al Nassr forward Ronaldo in a press conference after Sunday’s win against Norway, saying: “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team.”

Ronaldo said in his statement that he had agreed a game-management plan with Jesus for the latest round of Nations League fixtures, but it changed in the opening game against Norway.

The former Manchester United and Real Madrid star said he was told he would play for 30 minutes and, although asked to warm up in the second half, he was not used.

He also accused Jesus of reneging on an agreement to help explain the player’s frustrations in a press conference before the Denmark game, following a meeting between the pair and Al Nassr sporting director Simao Coutinho.

Ronaldo apologised in his statement to his Portugal teammates and to the Portuguese people and said he would be available to play for his country in future.

“The consequence of this act of mine must be assessed and punished by the Portuguese Football Federation,” Ronaldo said on Instagram.

“I believe the punishment should have no mitigating factors. I am not just any player. I am a team captain, and that is an aggravating factor.

“I have already apologised, but I know that actions must have consequences.”

news.title: Limerick man thought female friend was going to shoot him when she jumped out of her car, murder trial told
news.text:
The prosecution claims he was shot dead in the early hours of the following morning.

32-year-old Kurt Ryan, of Moylish Crescent, Limerick, denies the single charge of murdering 25-year-old Lee Slattery on the grounds of Delmege House, known locally as the Dallies.

Coleen Neill described how she was stopped on Shanabooley Road in Limerick at 7.25pm that evening when she stopped and jumped out of her car. She described the reaction of Lee Slattery, whom she knew, when she swung open the door of the car.

“I saw Lee. He was holding his chest and covering his head. I said, ‘Lee, what’s wrong with you’. He said, ‘Jesus, I thought you were getting out of the car to shoot me’. His fear was very real. We giggled it off — a bit of a nervous laugh. But he was really fearful, cowering low to the ground and holding his hand over his head like he was protecting himself,” Ms Neill said.

Her sister, Ciara Neill was a passenger in the car that evening and she gave a similar description of Lee Slattery’s reaction and him saying: “My heart. I thought you were someone going to shoot me”, and that he appeared to be frightened, but that they laughed it off. She said he was wearing a blue tracksuit top.

Lee Slattery’s mother said they were getting more and more worried as days passed and her son had not returned home. She said Kurt Ryan, who had never called to her house before, called and said he had not seen Lee for a couple of days and he thought Lee was avoiding him because he [Lee] owed him €80.

Lee’s brother, Ray Slattery, testified he and some relatives and friends searched the grounds of Delmege House in the days afterwards when he had not returned home. 

He said they searched for a few hours and as they entered a field near the soccer pitch they saw a fresh, mucky patch covered with branches and he started digging into the ground with a branch, overturning soft sods. 

Ray’s uncle, John, joined this search and overturned some of the spongey ground to reveal a patch of blue tracksuit. They immediately phoned gardaí and did not touch the ground again. Five minutes later, gardaí arrived and cordoned off the scene.

The trial continues.
news.summary: Witness, who knew the deceased man, said he cowered and put his hands over his head when she stopped her car and swung open the door

excise duty

Will consumers feel the bite of the new tax hike on vapes?

Vapes have been hit with a tax hike, adding an extra 20 cent per ml.

5.16pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

EVERYONE IS WELL used to the annual hike in the price of a packet of cigarettes, but a recent vape tax is less familiar. 

The rise in excise duty on cigarettes has seen the price of a pack of 20 finally hit the mark of €20 – meaning cigarettes now come in at an eye-watering €1 a piece. It’s a doubling in the cost over the past decade.

Vapes have also been hit with a tax hike, adding an extra 20 cent per ml. The average disposable vape many people are familiar with contains 2ml of liquid, meaning an increase of 40c per vape. 

This tax hike will come into effect from January 2027.

Unlike how the price increase on cigarettes is passed directly to the consumer, the supplier is liable for E-Liquid Product Tax (EPT). As with tax increases, this is eventually passed to the consumer by way of price hikes at shops.

In theory, with the additional 20 cent per ml tax on top of the inaugural 50 cent per ml tax brought in last year, there should be 70 cent per ml on top of the retail price – meaning an additional €7 for a 10ml bottle of e-liquid that previously retailed for €5.

A 2ml Lost Mary disposable vape now comes in at €9.50 at licensed retailer Hale Vaping online. With the additional tax, this would come in at €9.90.

The brand’s popular BM6000 vape, which contains 12ml between a pre-filled built-in pod and a plug-in container, retails for €26. This would increase by €2.40 to €28.40.

Another popular brand, IVG (I Vape Great), has a similar 12ml product available for €24, which would increase to €26.40.

Hale Vaping also has a clearance section, where an 8ml vape can be picked up for €10, reduced from €22. Bottles of 10ml of e-liquid can be bought for €8.

These excise hikes are intended both to quell smoking and raise more money for the Exchequer, and it is now widely accepted that while ardent smokers may be more out of pocket, the rapidly rising cost has forced less committed smokers from the habit.

Cigarettes have been around for hundreds of years. What has only exploded onto the scene and changed the way nicotine is consumed globally in the past 20 years are vapes.

Advertisement

Initially billed as a way for smokers to move away from tobacco, vapes are now used by many people who don’t or have never smoked. Research published in 2025 said most teenagers who vape have never smoked a cigarette before.

Will the vape tax make a difference?

KerrysWorld / Shutterstock

KerrysWorld / Shutterstock / Shutterstock

Vapes and cigarettes may be more expensive, but that doesn’t stop people from getting around it. 

It is common for smokers to pick up cigarettes in duty-free, or to buy in bulk when abroad. Some people opt to roll their own cigarettes, which works out cheaper per piece. While these are cost-saving measures, they’re 100% legitimate. 

Vapes are dramatically less regulated. Vaping360‘s brand database contains close to 900 vape brands and over 3,700 products. With vape shops popping up in every town and on close to every street in cities, there are hundreds of options for consumers to choose from when buying a device.

Up until January 2025, there was no requirement for retailers to have a licence to sell nicotine-inhaling products, as there is for cigarettes, and many phone shops added them to their offerings.

In reply to a parliamentary question in September, finance minister Simon Harris said that Revenue has advised him that the provisional tax yield of EPT since its start in November 2025 is over €30 million. A total of 91 suppliers had registered with Revenue at that time.

Over €1 billion was raised by Tobacco Product Tax in 2025, the Tánaiste said in reply to a separate parliamentary question. 

The tax yield is way above projections, but it is also true that a lot of retailers don’t pay duties. That same €24, 12ml vape from Hale Vaping is available in some small vape shops for €15, and the 10ml refills can be purchased for €9.50.

Some shops offer even lower prices, and run deals on vapes bought in multiples.

EPT may result in a rise in tax revenue and increased cost at some licensed shops, but with a plethora of shops operating under the radar, many consumers won’t feel the increase in tax on vapes the way they do on cigarettes.

Benny Gilsenan of Retailers Against Smuggling (RAS) told The Journal that smuggling has “taken over the market” for cigarettes and vapes.

Gilsenan said a large volume of vape shops opening up across Dublin city are selling vapes at a price of three for €10 – something legitimate retailers who pay duties and tax on their own offerings can’t compete with.

“Dublin Central, in particular, is rampant with illegal selling of cigarette products and vapes,” he said.

Emma Hickey

news.title: ‘We were chasing inflation’: DCU grilled over almost €4.4m loss on student accommodation plan
news.text:
Dublin City University (DCU) has planning permission until March 2029 to build accommodation housing 1,235 beds, but a “viability gap” is preventing the construction from proceeding, an Oireachtas committee has heard.

The university faced questions on Wednesday on its writing off expenditure amounting to €4.38 million (including VAT) incurred on professional fees for the proposed project, as reported in its financial statement for 2024/2025.

Dr Declan Raftery, DCU’s chief operations officer, said in 2017, the university commenced a capital project to construct 1,235 new student beds on its Glasnevin campus. The project was due to go to tender in September 2020 but “the Covid-19 pandemic changed everything for all of us”.

He noted that by March 2020, the DCU student accommodation project had incurred 69 per cent of the €4.38 million, as the project was “proceeding according to plan”.

He said another €700,000 was spent in 2020.

“We re-scoped the original project from 1,235 beds into a first phase consisting of 405 beds and completed two procurement competitions to try and seek best value for money. 

“However, we have not been able to bridge the viability gap between the cost of construction, capital grant support from Government and the resulting rental levels that we believe by any reasonable measure students could afford to pay.”

[ Units for thousands of campus student beds unbuilt despite having planning permissionOpens in new window ]

He told the committee that DCU is “disappointed and frustrated”.

After coming out of Covid, “we hit unprecedented inflation and supply chain issues that none of us expected or could understand”, he said. “We were chasing inflation.”

Raftery was addressing the Joint Committee on Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science. On Wednesday, it heard from representatives from DCU, University of Limerick, University of Galway, Munster Technological University and Technological University Dublin on the National Student Accommodation Strategy.

People Before Profit-Solidarity TD Richard Boyd Barrett asked Raftery if there was a viable financial model that would allow DCU to progress the 1,235 beds, but it could not be done unless the Government stepped in to help the university bridge the viability gap and deliver genuinely affordable accommodation. 

Raftery responded: “Exactly ... can’t put it any better myself.”

When asked if the €4.38 million that DCU had written off could be salvaged to deliver the student accommodation, Raftery said “a large portion of it” could be.

He said the €4.38 million included costs such as integrated design team fees, a project manager, some surveys and “a tiny amount” of legal fees.

[ Most third-level colleges increase on-campus accommodation costs for coming yearOpens in new window ]

“The capital grant aid available from the department, as far as they thought they could go at that time and the gap between what we thought we needed was €6.7 million. That was the gap we couldn’t bridge.

“What can students afford to pay versus the cost? The gap then is either tax incentives, capital grants ... there is still a viability gap.”

He added that the “pressures are everywhere in terms of cost of living”, citing students who choose to commute as they can’t get accommodation and have part-time jobs “to try and make ends meet”.
news.summary: Oireachtas committee hears about university’s ‘viability gap’ in plan to house more than 1,200 beds

Budget 2027

Tánaiste says he wants to build on inheritance tax changes in future budgets 

A number of TDs were disappointed there were no reforms for those without children. 

5.12pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

THE INHERITANCE TAX changes in this year’s budget are “a step” in the right direction with Tánaiste and finance minister Simon Harris telling The Journal that the government plans to build on it in future budgets. 

Since new budget measures were voted in on Tuesday night, the threshold at which capital acquisitions tax kicks in has increased.

A child can now inherit €420,000 from their parents in their lifetime before capital acquisitions tax of 33% kicks in – up from €400,000 previously. 

The threshold for siblings, nieces, nephews and some other relatives has also increased from €40,000 to €44,000.

For non-relatives, the threshold has increased from €20,000 to €22,000.

Asked about the changes after the budget announcement on Tuesday, Harris said the government could not go further as the fiscal space available in the budget would not allow it this year.

Additional movement on the thresholds “would have cost a lot more than we had available,” said Harris.

Once it was decided by the government that the budget must include a personal tax package, there was limited scope for other measures, with Harris stating that he was pleased he managed to get increases in all three inheritance categories.

Advertisement

Speaking about the changes made, Harris added: 

It is a step and I hope it is something we can build on in the years ahead.

Inheritance tax has seen significant changes in Ireland following the 2008 financial crisis.

In 2008, people in Group A could inherit over €521,000 tax-free, before a tax of 20% was charged.

Between 2008 and 2012, tax-free thresholds on inheritances were steadily decreased while the rate of CAT was increased. 

Harris acknowledged that the changes made on budget day will not satisfy those who want equalisation of the inheritance tax system, particularly those who do not have children and want reforms so they can leave assets to a chosen beneficiary. 

TDs advocate for people who do not have children

During the vote on Tuesday evening on the inheritance tax changes, a number of TDs criticised the government for not taking the opportunity for wider reforms to the system. 

Independent Ireland TD Michael Collins said there were a lot of promises and soundings made that have not been delivered on.

“The bottom line is that this needs to be looked at again. I am pleading with the minister to look at it again and to give everybody a chance,” he said. 

Kerry TD Michael Healy-Rae said he warmly welcomed the changes.

However, he added:

Related Reads

Budget 2027: What changed at midnight - and what we'll have to wait for

Budget 2027 includes income tax band change, carbon tax freeze, and price hike on cigarettes

Rate of deemed disposal tax on investment funds to reduce to 35% from January 

“People who get married, or not, and who do not produce children of their own and do not have what we call direct heirs, those people work very hard. It might be their own house or a second house, or it might be a farm of land and when they eventually pass on, they see their asset being devalued so much because whoever they give it to will have to pay so much inheritance tax on it.

“I know that everything cannot be done all together at the same time but I would be very much hoping that in the future, we will be able to look at those categories of people and do something more to help them.”

However, Sinn Féin’s David Cullinane said he was not in favour of the inheritance tax changes, stating that “Fine Gael represents a cosseted, privileged class”.

“I do not know of many people who are looking for changes to inheritance tax… 

“The scandalous part about this resolution is that if a house is sold for €800,000 and two children benefit from it, they will not pay a single cent in inheritance tax,” he said.

People Before Profit TD Paul Murphy said only a small number of people are impacted by inheritance tax.

“Most people do not get that. Only a third of people get any substantial inheritance whatsoever in the course of their entire lifetime. The average inheritance that people get is about €100,000,” he said.

“It is the most well-off, most comfortable people who will benefit from this tax change at a time when the majority of people are struggling with the cost of living crisis,” added Murphy.

news.title: Teen who abused very young half-sisters caught when mother walked in - and he was recording on phone
news.text: A teenager jailed for two years for the “appalling” abuse of his two very young half-sisters will also be subject to an eight-year post release supervision order, a court has ruled. The Central Criminal Court heard that the abuse came to light in March 2023 after the children’s mother walked into the boy’s room and saw him abusing his five-year-old half-sister while recording it on his phone. His then two-year-old half-sister was also in the room. The now 18-year-old pleaded guilty to multiple counts including three of sexually assaulting the older half-sister and one of orally raping her, and two of sexually assaulting the younger half-sister. He further pleaded guilty to charges of sexually exploiting his half-sisters, of engaging in sexual activity in the presence of a child and the production, possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), known in law as child pornography. The investigation found a video of the boy masturbating on a bus, the court heard. In September 2023, after the abuse of his half-sisters was discovered, he was found viewing CSAM on a school laptop during a class. The court was told this was material obtained from the internet. In total, seven videos were identified, including six assessed as in the most serious category. The boy was today handed a four-year sentence with the final two years suspended on very strict conditions for four years. He will also be subject to the Sex Offender’s Act for five years and an eight-year post release supervision order. The boy was between 14 and 15 when he abused his half-sisters in the family home, on various dates between 2022 and 2023. He cannot be named as all parties have a legal right to anonymity Their mother sent files to her phone after discovering the abuse before deleting them from the boy’s phone. Gardai are satisfied the woman’s sole concern was to preserve any evidence for future investigations, the court was told. When the boy’s phone was analysed, 408 images and 11 videos of CSAM were found, including some of him sexually abusing both girls. One video also showed the boy masturbating on a school bus. Thousands of videos and images of adult pornography were also found. The boy was sent the next day to stay with his father, but returned to sit his Junior Certificate. He then went back to his father’s home for the summer before going back to school. While there was a safety plan, it later became clear that the boy couldn’t remain in the family home. He went into specialised foster care, as he could not live with others under 18. More recently, he has been living in an aftercare placement and completed his Leaving Certificate online. The court was told that the boy also distributed images of the abuse of the older girl on a particular social media app. He also shared material of himself with a Snapchat user. Gardai consider this to be a ‘catfish’ account, pretending to be the boy’s peer. The boy told gardai he stored images in case this Snapchat user got back in touch. The court heard there was no evidence of blackmail or threats and the boy was himself exploited. However, it was noted he continued the abuse after contact from this account had stopped. After hearing the facts earlier this year, Mr Justice Paul McDermott agreed to a defence application to allow the boy complete his Leaving Certificate and a therapeutic programme. However, there had been concerns in recent months that the boy was not fully complying with his strict bail conditions. The court heard earlier this week that the boy was seen by a case worker with a mobile phone in August. Michael Bowman SC, defending, said his client is aware he can’t have a phone. “It’s an easy thing for everyone to say but for an 18-year-old boy in that world, it’s an exceeding difficult place to find himself. It doesn’t excuse it but that is the reality”. Mr Justice McDermott remanded the boy into custody earlier this week and finalised sentence. The judge noted this case was about “very disturbing behaviour” by a young teenager who had repeatedly abused his “very young” sisters over a protracted period. He said the court had viewed the recording made on the day the abuse was discovered, describing the footage as “appalling” and noting its serious nature. The judge said the mother had been placed in the “most difficult position imaginable” and had “done her very best by each of her three children”. He said the recording of the abuse was aggravating and that the boy had breached parental and sibling trust. Reports from a forensic psychologist, the Probation Service and the National Interagency Prevention Programme (NIAPP) were reviewed by the court. The boy is assessed at high risk of re-offending with the Probation Service stating his risk factors include a preoccupation with this kind of abuse, an attraction to children, difficulties repressing urges, and viewing pornography, which the court considered a factor in his offending. A multidisciplinary structure is considered necessary by adult services due to the level of risk the boy presents. The judge noted that the boy’s bail conditions included that he hand over his laptop for school online to care workers at night, with the aim of limiting his online access. Last month, the boy admitted to buying and selling ten smart phones since his 18 th birthday, downloading certain apps, viewing pornography and having a “deviant sexual interest in young girls”. The judge noted one recent report states the boy views his use of pornography as appropriate. Services concluded that his engagement wasn’t meaningful and fully honest. Mr Justice McDermott said that the boy had deceived gardai and support services and that an “enormous effort” had been made to assist his rehabilitation. It had been believed this a community-based approach was working, but this has been undermined by the boy’s failure to fully comply with his bail conditions. The boy also led others to believe he was dealing with issues honestly when he wasn’t, the judge said. Mr Justice McDermott indicated that a “different approach is now required” and that a custodial sentence would be imposed. The judge noted both girls have received counselling and the family decided not to make a victim impact statement. He said the court respected this decision, and considered that “terrible damage” had been done to the girls and to the family unit. The judge outlined the headline sentences which would apply on each count for an adult, including 12 years for the oral rape. He reduced each headline sentence to reflect that the boy was a child in the eyes of the law at the time of the offending, reducing the headline sentence for oral rape to six years. The judge also noted the mitigation including the boy’s early guilty pleas, admissions, his social isolation and exploitation by others. Mr Justice McDermott suspended the final two years of the global four-year sentence to incentivise his engagement with services and to supervise his return to the community. The conditions for the part-suspended sentence include that the boy engage with any programmes to address his sexual offending. He must also have no contact with the victims, stay away from playgrounds and school grounds and have no contact or be in the company of any child under 18 unless another adult is present. The judge directed these conditions apply to the eight-year post release supervision order. The court previously heard that the family home was searched in May 2023, and a letter written by the boy to his parents, which contained some admissions, was handed over. In the letter, he acknowledged sexually abusing his younger sisters and said his behaviour changed due to watching pornography. No disclosure was initially made by the five-year-old girl, but she later spoke to social workers. She disclosed abuse by her older brother to specialist gardai in October 2023. She said she was scared of the boy and that he made her watch scary things. She said he touched her inappropriately on several occasions. Maurice Coffey SC, prosecuting, noted that gardai obtained limited evidence from talking to the girl, given her limited vocabulary and age-appropriate understanding of the situation. The two-year-old girl was not interviewed by gardai. A full Tusla investigation also took place. The boy made admissions when he was separately interviewed by Tulsa and gardai. He admitted ownership of 60 Google accounts, three X (formerly Twitter) accounts and other social media accounts. The court heard his mother is willing to allow him to remain in her life, so long as he addresses his offending behaviour. news.title: Two Cork men appear in court following €500k cannabis seizure
news.text:
Cannabis weighing 25 kilos with a street value of €500,000 was seized in Togher and two men were arrested and brought before Cork District Court today

Lee Crinnion (21) from Blackwater Grove, Togher, Cork, and 25-year-old Aaron Austin of Araglen Court, Togher, Cork, were arrested by Detective Garda Darren Twomey and Det Garda Ruairi McGovern, respectively, from the Cork City Divisional Drugs Unit.

Both of them were charged with possession of cannabis and having the cannabis for sale or supply at Togher Road, Cork on Monday, October 5.

Neither of them made any reply to the charges when they were put to them after caution.

Judge David Waters asked Det Garda Twomey if the value of drugs in the case was significant and if it was likely to stay in the district court. The detective said that the value was substantial at €500,000 and would eventually be dealt with at a higher court.

Sergeant David Fleming said that gardaí were not objecting to bail with conditions. 

Defence solicitors Joseph Cuddigan and Eddie Burke confirmed that their clients were consenting to the bail terms after discussing them with the investigating gardaí.

Conditions included an 11pm to 7am curfew, signing on three times a week at Togher Garda Station, surrendering their passports and not apply for any other travel documents, providing gardaí with mobile phone numbers on which they could be contacted at all times, and that they would have no contact with each other directly or indirectly.

Judge Waters remanded both men on bail to appear again at Cork District Court on November 3 for the DPP’s directions.
news.summary: Lee Crinnion and Aaron Austen were charged with possession of cannabis and having the cannabis for sale or supply at Togher Road, Cork on Monday, October 5

news.title: Cork bathing locations see 'excellent' results after summer monitoring
news.text:
Cork’s bathing waters have enjoyed an exceptionally strong season, with all monitored waters returning “excellent” results to date and 10 beaches holding Blue Flag status. The county also has 12 Green Coast awards, according to Cork County Council’s latest bathing water report.

Brendan Meagher, the council’s acting county engineer, said the sunny weather had helped conditions during the season. The data covers 30 beaches across the county, including 13 designated bathing waters monitored under the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) programme.

One beach holds both a Blue Flag and a Green Coast award, while nine hold Blue Flags only and 12 have Green Coast awards. The council said all designated bathing waters had achieved excellent results so far this year.

Two new locations were added to the monitoring programme for 2026: White Bay in Cork Harbour and the Blue Pool in Glengarriff. Monitoring on Cape Clear has also moved to North Harbour, which the council said offers a safer and more accessible bathing location.

Social Democrats’ Isobel Towse welcomed the move, saying it made sense to monitor the more sheltered North Harbour as it is the part of Cape Clear most frequented by swimmers. She said it was important that water quality there continued to be monitored.

There was one significant incident during the season, when Cadogan’s Strand in Schull was closed as a precaution after reports of discoloured water. Investigations found no evidence of contamination and the bathing area reopened within three days.

The council is continuing investigative work at The Warren, or Cregane Strand, in Rosscarbery and at Fountainstown. DNA source tracking is being used to identify the origin of any contamination and support corrective action.

Strong results this season could support the return of Blue Flag status for Fountainstown and Garryvoe, although the council said this depended on continued performance for the remainder of the season.

It is also too early to determine whether Fountainstown or The Warren will regain their flags for 2027.

Funded by the Local Democracy Reporting Scheme.
news.summary: The data covers 30 beaches across the county, including 13 designated bathing waters monitored under the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) programme.

news.title: Eirgrid hosts event on windfarm locations in Aghada until 8pm tonight
news.text:
EirGrid is continuing its public information events across Cork to discuss the development of onshore and offshore electricity grid infrastructure for the south coast of Ireland.

The events will provide an opportunity for the public, communities and stakeholders to share their feedback on proposed onshore and offshore station locations, landfall sites and grid connection points.

A public consultation open day, from 12 noon – 8pm, is taking place today at Aghada Community Centre and there will be another open day in Garryvoe Hotel on Wednesday November 4.

There will also be mobile unit information stands available on October 27 at Garryvoe beach carpark from 10am – 1pm and in Cloyne GAA carpark from 2pm – 5pm.

The public information events are part of EirGrid's Powering Up Offshore – South Coast programme, which aims to build the transmission grid infrastructure required to connect offshore wind generation to the national grid.

Sinéad Dooley, head of public engagement at EirGrid, said she is encouraging people to attend our consultation events in Cork where they can meet the project team, learn more about the proposals and have their say.

“Local knowledge and stakeholder feedback are critical to helping shape the next stage of the project, and we want as many people as possible to get involved in the consultation process."

“This consultation is an important milestone in the development of the programme. The emerging best performing options we are presenting have been informed by extensive technical and environmental studies, as well as engagement with stakeholders, and we now want to hear directly from communities and interested parties on these proposals.”
news.summary: The next public consultation open day, from 12 noon – 8pm, takes place tonight at Aghada Community Centre and there will be another open day in Garryvoe Hotel on Wednesday November 4.

news.title: Cork man accused of recording 'partially undressed' women in Dublin Airport toilets
news.text:
A book of evidence has been served today on a 31-year-old Cork man accused of recording partially undressed females in a toilet area of Dublin Airport last year.

Garda Denis Callanan charged Eric O’Neill of Delford Drive, Rochestown Road, with a single count in relation to the alleged offence and this week in court he was served with a book of evidence.

On the application of Sergeant Gearóid Davis at Cork District Court, Judge David Waters sent the case forward to the next sessions of Cork Circuit Criminal Court commencing on October 27. The defendant was represented by solicitor Shane Collins-Daly.

The charge against him states that on April 19 2025 at Dublin Airport, he did engage in offensive conduct of a sexual nature, namely the recording of females in a partially undressed state within the confines of the ladies bathroom/toilets within Dublin Airport, contrary to the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 2017.
news.summary: Garda Denis Callanan charged Eric O’Neill of Delford Drive, Rochestown Road, with a single count in relation to the alleged offence.

news.title: New papal nuncio likely to continue radical downsizing of Catholic dioceses in Ireland
news.text:
A new papal nuncio to Ireland has been appointed by the Vatican from Poland. Archbishop Jan Romeo Pawlowski (65) is currently papal nuncio in Greece. 

He was born in 1960 in Biskupiec, northern Poland, and was ordained in 1985 before studying for a doctorate in canon law at the Gregorian University in Rome.

Pawlowski then entered the Vatican’s diplomatic service and was made archbishop in 2009 when appointed papal nuncio to the Republic of the Congo and Gabon. 

In 2015 he returned to the Vatican, serving as its secretariat of state becoming head of its section for diplomatic staff in 2017. In 2022 he was appointed papal nuncio to Greece.

He speaks Italian, French, Russian, English, German and Portuguese.

A papal nuncio is effectively the Vatican’s ambassador to Ireland. He will also automatically become dean of the diplomatic corps in the State.

In church terms his primary role is in the appointment of bishops, making recommendations to Rome. More recently in Ireland the nuncio has also played a key role in the reduction of Irish Catholic dioceses.

[ Called to the church: ‘I broke her heart but I felt I could do more for people by being a priest’Opens in new window ]

The new nuncio succeeds Archbishop Luis Mariano Montemayor (70), who served in Ireland from February 2023 until July this year, when he retired. 

In his three years, Archbishop Montemayor, originally from Argentina and another Vatican career diplomat, oversaw some of the most radical changes in the structure of the Irish Catholic Church in 900 years, with a significant reduction in the number of dioceses.

In 1111, at the Synod of Ráth Breasail, Ireland’s current diocesan structure was set up.

Some “downsizing” had taken place before Archbishop Montemayor’s arrival in 2023. In 2021 Clonfert was joined with Galway. But on his watch this process was sped up, with Achonry joining Elphin in 2025 and, earlier this year, Killala with Tuam. It meant six west of Ireland Catholic dioceses were reduced to three. 

Last July, Ossory diocese – mainly Kilkenny – was similarly joined under one bishop, with Ferns diocese, mainly Wexford.

[ ‘My proposal was to stop Confirmation’: Ireland’s ageing priests under pressure as numbers dropOpens in new window ]

When it came to the appointment and transfer of bishops, Archbishop Montemayor was similarly active. He appointed Fr Paul Connell Bishop of Ardagh and Clonmacnoise in 2023 and Fr Donal Roche as auxiliary bishop of Dublin in 2024. 

In 2024 he oversaw the transfer of then Bishop of Raphoe (Donegal) Alan McGuckian SJ to Down and Connor diocese, mainly Belfast and Antrim. Also that year, then bishop of Achonry Paul Dempsey became an auxiliary bishop of Dublin. 

In 2025 Bishop of Elphin Kevin Doran was named also Bishop of Achonry, while last February, Archbishop of Tuam Francis Duffy was named Bishop of Killala.

Last year too Bishop of Ossory Niall Coll was transferred to Raphoe diocese. Last February, Archbishop of Tuam Francis Duffy was also named Bishop of Killala while last July Auxiliary Bishop of Armagh Michael Router, was appointed Bishop of Derry and Bishop of Ferns Ger Nash was also named Bishop of Ossory. 

It is likely such downsizing will continue under Archbishop Pawlowski.

More immediately, both Bishop of Clogher (mainly Monaghan) Larry Duffy and Bishop of Cloyne (mainly east Cork) William Crean are due to retire later this year, and there has been speculation for some time that Clogher may be joined with its neighbour Kilmore (mainly Cavan) and Cloyne with Cork and Ross diocese.

Further, since 2018 the Catholic Primate and Archbishop of Armagh Eamon Martin has been administrator of the small Co Down diocese of Dromore. It followed the resignation of then Bishop of Dromore John McAreavey in a controversy over his handling of child abuse allegations against the late Fr Malachy Finnegan. That arrangement is expected to be formalised.
news.summary: Polish nuncio succeeds Archbishop Montemayor, who oversaw some of most radical changes in 900 years

pace of reform

The government has cut RTÉ's funding by €20m - and Kevin Bakhurst is not happy about it

The director-general said the decision “is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact on our ability to deliver our five-year strategy”.

4.56pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

RTÉ DIRECTOR GENERAL Kevin Bakhurst has said he “completely rejects the assertion” that the pace of reform within the national broadcaster has been slow, after it was confirmed in Budget 2027 that it would receive €20 million less in funding. 

In 2024, the government committed to providing public funding of €725 million to RTÉ from licence fee receipts and a direct top-up from the Exchequer over three years.

Of this, €260 million was allocated for 2027.

However, media minister Patrick O’Donovan today confirmed that the funding for next year would amount to €240 million. This is made up of €66 million in direct exchequer support, and €174 million in projected licence fee collections. 

Speaking at a post-budget briefing, he said the figure “is less than envisaged by the government in 2024" but reflects “the overall funding available to my department”.

“It is also in the context of progress made by RTÉ in the delivery of their strategy,” O’Donovan said.

“While progress has been made across a number of issues, I am not happy that we have seen sufficient progress in delivering the smaller, more agile organisation that wants to be delivered under the strategy.”

He also said RTÉ will receive an €11 million “uplift” instead of a planned €31 million, adding that “we were simply not in that space to be able to do that”.

Bakhurst says ‘extensive reform delivered’

In a statement this afternoon, Bakhurst said the government’s decision “is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact on our ability to deliver our five-year strategy”.

“RTÉ welcomed and was grateful for the Government’s commitment in 2024 to provide public funding to RTÉ of €725 million over three years, from 2025 – 2027,” he said.

“In fact, the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste said at the time, that predictable multi-annual funding is key to RTÉ being able to deliver a strategy.”

Bakhurst said the decision to cut funding was coming at a “late stage”, when the organisation has “already made important commitments to our audiences, to the independent sector, to other important stakeholders and to RTÉ staff”. 

He said the three-year funding commitment allowed RTÉ to plan ahead and, among other things, deliver independent news and analysis, commit to producing more public service programmes, invest in podcasts and the RTÉ Player, and stabilise its finances. 

“We completely reject the assertion that the pace of reform and transformation within RTÉ has been slow,” he said.

Advertisement

“The Leadership Team and I have delivered extensive reform since I took up the role of Director-General, including implementation of around 90% of the EAC report recommendations.

“We have also already managed to exit almost 100 people from the organisation, despite the late approval of the Voluntary Exit Programme and a short window to enable people to leave.”

Bakhurst said RTÉ board chair Terence O’Rourke was seeking a meeting with O’Donovan about the matter, “particularly given that RTÉ has committed to numerous agreements with its stakeholders based on this written and extensively publicised agreement.

He concluded by saying: “If the three-year multi-annual agreement will no longer be honoured – we now have some important decisions to make.”

‘Not an insignificant amount of money’

When asked about Bakhurst’s statement at the briefing, O’Donovan said public service organisations across a number of sectors have had to demonstrate key efficiencies being delivered over the last 12 months.

Media minister Patrick O'Donovan speaking at a post-budget briefing this afternoon.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

The Fine Gael minister said his department was “a very agency-dependent department” and had “very little scope, to be quite honest, about it in relation to where the resources that we had available to us needed to be assigned”.

He said it was “well-documented” that there were “issues” regarding RTÉ’s voluntary redundancy, something he said “he hopes “would be able to be advanced and ameliorated”.

An internal analysis of the redundancy programme found that substantial work had been put into preparing early exit packages for staff, but only a relatively small number eventually received offers.

O’Donovan said his department would continue to engage with RTÉ on a weekly basis, and noted that €240 million “is not an insignificant amount of money”.

“It’s a quarter of a billion, and there are very few organisations across the state that can point to resource allocation of that order, and it certainly represents an enormous part of the current expenditure amount that is available to me as minister to be able to allocate.”

He concluded by saying he would update the government shortly on the delivery of the RTÉ reform program, “including on progress made and what is yet to be achieved”. 

At the Public Accounts Committee in July, Bakhurst told TDs and senators that RTÉ was “tightening its belt” as it strengthened its financial position and “reversed the trend of reporting deficits” as a result of tighter cost controls supported by its new strategy, and the government’s €725 million multiannual funding commitment.

He said he would “appeal very strongly” for a similar multiannual commitment when it next comes for review.

When asked how much additional state funding RTÉ would be looking for from 2028, Bakhurst said discussions had not started.

He added: “We will need public funding. We will need funding from either the licence fee or a similar source of public funding.”

Woman's case about child sex abuse videos on porn sites adjourned over possible $120m settlement

The woman claims she was drugged and raped by a man when she was a child.

4.52pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

HIGH COURT PROCEEDINGS involving video companies behind Pornhub have been adjourned until March while a proposed $120 million (€105.5 million) settlement of US litigation awaits court approval.

The matter briefly came before Mr Justice Brian Cregan today, when counsel for the woman, identified as Jane Doe to protect her identity, requested an adjournment pending developments in the related US proceedings.

The woman, who lives in the United States, claims that she was drugged and raped by a man in the state of Alabama when she was sixteen years old.

She claims that her abuser recorded what happened and posted the images online.

It is alleged that videos of her abuse were published and distributed on various adult video sharing websites owned by the international group of companies that own, control and manage internet pornography websites including Pornhub.

The woman initially brought US proceedings against companies within the MindGeek group, the business behind Pornhub, which rebranded as Aylo in August 2023.

Those companies are MG Freesites Ltd, MG Freesites II Ltd, MindGeek SARL, Aylo Premium Ltd, MG Social Ltd, Mindgeek USA Incorporated, MG CY Holdings Ltd, Aylo Billing Ltd, Mirmay Ltd, Nutaku Publishing Ltd, Appatomic Ltd and Liquidim Ltd.

Five of those companies – Aylo Billing Ltd, Mirmay Ltd, Nutaku Publishing Ltd, Appatomic Ltd and Liquidum Ltd – are registered in Dublin.

Advertisement

She launched additional proceedings against those companies in Ireland’s High Court last year.

A US judge described the companies as a network that “own or operate several of the most-visited pornographic websites in the world”, including Pornhub, YouPorn, RedTube, Tube8 and WTube.

The settlement proposed in the US case would resolve class actions brought in the states of Alabama and California against the companies involved.

Pollock Cohen, one of the firms representing the plaintiffs, confirmed in August that the “historic” agreement would cover both cases and includes payments and changes to the websites’ practices. It remains subject to court approval.

The Irish proceedings, initiated due to the international structure of the defendant group, sought to preserve assets in Ireland while the US litigation progresses.

Aylo has said that the settlement involves no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement reported by the adult industry publication XBIZ, the company said that only verified creators can publish on its platform and that content uploaded to its websites undergoes technological checks and is reviewed by trained moderators before publication.

The Irish case reflects the international structure of the business and the woman’s efforts to pursue companies and assets across different jurisdictions.

The matter briefly came before the High Court today, when Judge Cregan adjourned the case until March at the request of the woman’s barrister Robert O’Reilly.

Stephen McDermott

news.title: Criteria for Budget 2027's rural pub support scheme to be based on turnover
news.text:
In addition to the €15m fund to support pubs, the budget also allocated €3m for the establishment of the landmark Start Up Ireland initiative, €20m for the launch of the €500m Growth and Sustainability Loan Scheme, €4.5m for Local Enterprise Office, as well as €6.65m for Fáilte Ireland tourism product and destination development in the regions.

In addition, there was a €1bn Ireland’s Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) start-up and scaling investment programme announced for up to 2030. The funding will be in co-operation with Enterprise Ireland to provide a long-term source of capital for Irish scaling companies through equity and debt investments.

Other budget measures announced include an increase in the national minimum wage of 79c, an increase to PRSI thresholds, as well as a cut in the capital gain tax rate from 33% to 31%.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Mr Burke said the rural pubs are a “focal point for much of society to interact” and have been a “key area to combat social isolation”.

However, the number of rural pubs has been steadily shrinking. Rural Ireland has seen 2,200 pubs disappear since 2005. In Cork, there were 1,221 pubs in 2005, but in the two decades since it has fallen to 821.

Mr Burke said he plans to have the scheme ready for applicants by July 1 and he will be looking potentially having a “remit scheme which could most likely track the licences of publicans”.

"If you look at the licenses that are given out, there are a number of tiers or categories based on turnover, which dictate essentially what size the pub is,” he said.

"If you have [a pub] in the second tier, it's about €380,000 turnover,” he said, adding that roughly 70% of rural pubs are captured within that tier.

"I want to ensure that it is getting to our smaller type of publicans that are under pressure, that are facing very significant viability challenges. 

"A scheme will be crafted around that, looking at licensing laws, turnover, and also looking at environmental aid, how we make them more sustainable by encouraging the circular economy and recycling,” he said.

News of the support scheme was welcomed by the Vintners’ Federation of Ireland.

Minimum wage and PRSI

While the minister sold the budget as a pro-enterprise budget, the Small Firms Association (SFA) was critical of it, particularly the increase to the minimum wage which now sets it at €14.94.

To mitigate the rising minimum wage, the Government raised the employer threshold for PRSI from €552 to €600 per week.

However, the SFA had been seeking a temporary rebate on PRSI to help companies absorb the rising costs.

In response to this, Mr Burke said that firms will not be paying as much PRSI as they would have if it had tracked the increases in the minimum wage.

“That will help them a little bit. It's not going the full way but it is an assistance to dealing with the increase in the minimum wage,” he said.
news.summary: The €15m scheme is expected to open for applicants on July 1 next year

news.title: Celia Holman Lee experiences 'major health setback' and is receiving medical care
news.text: Celia Holman Lee has experienced a "major health setback" according to a statement shared on her social media. Taking to Instagram on Wednesday, her family shared a snap of the Irish fashion icon as they revealed she was receiving medical care. They wrote: “It is with heavy hearts that we share that Celia Holman Lee has experienced a major health setback and is currently receiving medical care. "As a result, Celia will be unavailable for public engagements for a period of time. Her family asks that their privacy be respected during this difficult period so that they can focus on her care and recovery. "The family is deeply grateful for the outpouring of love, prayers, and good wishes. Please know, that every message is appreciated and gives them strength. Given the volume of messages, they may not be able to respond individually, and ask for your understanding if they are unable to do so. "An update will be shared at an appropriate time. In the meantime, the family asks that all media respect their wishes.” Celia received an outpouring of kind words and well wishes from friends and followers, as one person commented: "Thoughts & prayers with you Celia & your lovely family." "Celia and family I am so sorry to hear this. I am sending prayers of health and healing to you," another said. A third wrote: "Wishing you strength Celia and sending love & prayers to your family." The news on her health comes just months after Celia opened up about how important is it to her to stay working and keep her mind active. "I work hard," she said. "I keep my mind active. I would say to any woman out there, if you retire... the mind is everything.... I watched one of my brothers. Leonard had very bad Alzheimer's and dementia. He was amazing. My father, Jackie, had it as well." Speaking to Evoke, she confirmed that the fears of not keeping her mind active with work is one of the reasons she has yet to retire. "I'd say it is," she said. "I have to because I know it is in the family. It's not like I'm running around the place. My daughter-in-law runs the agency now but I am at everything. I love it and I love people. "I do honestly feel keep your shoulders back and down, look after your appearance and keep active and you'll keep going." Want to see more of the stories you love from RSVP ? news.summary: A statement has been shared on the social media of the Irish fashion icon as she will be unavailable for public engagements for the time being - her family have asked for privacy
