news.title: Ben Kelliher goal decisive for Sem in O'Sullivan Cup semi
news.text:
St Brendan’s College were pushed all the way by a gusty Mercy Mounthawk side in this Kerry Colleges Senior Football (O’Sullivan Cup) semi-final played at the COE in Currans on a blustery afternoon.

St Brendan's were warm favourites but Mounthawk failed to read the script and powered by Ben Litchfield at midfield and hat-trick hero Mickey Somers on the forty, they were just two points adrift (2-12 to 3-7) with 10 minutes left.

Then St Brendan's College struck for the game-winning goal, when John Henderson, who had been introduced as a substitute, floated in a high ball that invited a classy flick over his head by Ben Kelliher to push the Killarney side five clear. The Sem embellished their margin with late points from Liam O’Brien, Mark O’Carroll and Finan Blackwell.

The opening half had been end to end stuff with 15-year-old Billy Kirby catching the eye for Mounthawk while Harry Murphy was combining well with Conor McGibney and Mikey Somers, under the watchful eye of his brother Ben, home from the AFL.

St Brenda'ns made the better start when Jake Coffey took advantage of a keeper error to finish to the Mounthawk net, while Mark O’Carroll, Cillian O’Donoghue and Jack Culloty added points.

After Rory Bowler opened the scoring for Mounthawk, Paddy Lucid sent Mikey Somers through and the St Senan's youngster buried the ball in the back of Sem net. Somers then levelled the contest with a two-point free but Kerry U-20 player Kelliher replied with an orange flag from play. 

The sides traded points before St Brendan’s struck for a second goal in the 19th minute, when Mark Looney intercepted a pass out of defence. He found Jack Culloty, who set up Kelliher, who finished clinically.

From the kickout, Mikey Somers took a two-point free that dropped under the crossbar to the net, to leave it 2-6 to 2-5 and game on.

Thanks to the foraging of Cian Stack, Jack Hallissey, Zach Cronin and Mark O’Carroll, St Brendan's tagged on three unanswered points from Kelliher, Daniel Cronin and Jack Culloty to retire 2-9 to 2-5 in front.

At the second throw-in, disaster struck Mounthawk, as towering midfielder Litchfield landed awkwardly on his ankle and had to retire.

Mounthawk did get another goal in the 39th minute, in bizarre fashion, when the referee moved a free into the 13 metre line and Mikey Somers, spotting the Sem defence had fallen asleep, fired to an unguarded net.

It was nip and tuck with Mounthawk kicking three bad wides before the St Brendan's captain Ben Kelliher decided the contest with that audacious 54th- minute goal.

 St Brendan's will now face either St Michaels College Listowel or Castleisland CC in a unique final.

 ST BRENDAN’S COLLEGE: J Casey (Spa); D McCarthy (Listry), Z Cronin (Kilcummin), C Clifford (Dr Crokes); C Lynch (Dr Crokes), C Stack (Kilcummin), J Hallissey (Fossa); M O’Carroll (Dr Crokes), J Coffey (Legion); M Looney (Legion), B Kelliher (Dr Crokes), D Cronin (Firies); L O’Brien (Glenflesk), C O’Donoghue (Listry), J Culloty (Legion).

 Subs: J Ahern (Kilcummin) for C Lynch (inj h/t), F Blackwell (Legion) for J Coffey (h/t), J Henderson (Firies) for C O’Donoghue (52), F O’Donnell (Dr Crokes) for L O’Brien (58), J Nash (Dr Crokes) for C Clifford (58).

 MERCY MOUNTHAWK: S Sargent (John Mitchels); C Nolan (Churchill), K O’Shea (Firies), E Crowley (Churchill); R Bowler (John Mitchels), C McGibney (Churchill), D Hobbert (Austin Stacks); B Litchfield (Austin Stacks), P Lucid (Austin Stacks); B Kirby (Austin Stacks), M Somers (St Senans), H Murphy (Austin Stacks); J Diggin (Austin Stacks), L O’Carroll (Churchill), R Onyekwere (Kerins O’Rahillys).

 Subs: J O’Dowd (Austin Stacks) for B Litchfield (inj 31), B Conway (John Mitchels) for J Diggin (43), M Carmody (Austin Stacks) for R Onyekwere (43).

 Referee: C O Dhúbhda (An Ghaeltacht).
news.summary: A classy goal by the the Kerry U20 star saw off a brave Mercy Mounthawk challenge

news.title: Cork City students champion country values in competition final
news.text:
The team, comprising Emma Dilworth, Meabh O’Donovan and Mary-Clare O’Connell, all come from farming backgrounds, with Ms O’Donovan and O’Connell hailing from dairy farms and Ms Dilworth coming from an organic beef farm. 

The team reached the final of this cycle of the competition with their project titled: ‘How organic farm practices can produce sustainable Certified Irish Angus beef’.

Discussing their initial interest in the competition, Ms O’Connell said: “We all come from farming backgrounds, but we have a huge interest in farming… We never ever thought it would take us here and we're so happy we entered.” 

The team’s project looked into researching organic farming practices and whether they could be incorporated into conventional farming systems, reducing emissions on farms, increasing biodiversity on farms through multispecies swards, and what effects it may have, the importance of beef in a diet and highlighting women in the agricultural industry.

Once reaching the final, the team were gifted their five cattle at the National Ploughing Championships last year. Housed on Ms O’Connell’s home farm, the cattle have become local celebrities dubbed “the Famous Five” by those who know them. The team were also lucky enough to secure a Dairygold sponsorship for their cattle meal.

Discussing how eye-opening and vital receiving the cattle were, the team said being able to apply knowledge collected at events or from speakers and researchers and to determine whether it could apply to their own cattle or help with improving their knowledge was invaluable.

“We had to think like the farmers,” Ms O’Donovan explained. “We can go to different events, and we can see and understand it, and that’s why having the cattle is so important,” Ms O‘Connell added.

The team, ever the advocates for their research, hosted a naming competition in their school, allowing the teachers to supply one name, the junior cycle supplied two and the senior cycle provided the remaining two. The cattle were subsequently christened: Bull McCabe, Rebel, Killeagh, Ferdinand and Cnoc.

The St Angela’s team all pitched in helping with the feed and upkeep of the Famous Five. The cattle were weighed every 100 days to monitor progress and were scheduled to go to the factory in August.

“It will be really sad to see them go… it was a great hands-on experience,” Ms Dilworth admitted.

Despite educating classmates on the realities from farm to fork, the team explained they were relieved the cattle were going to slaughter in August before school resumed so they could break the news gently to their fellow classmates.

“It’s a part of farming, and we will have to show them that part too,” Ms O’Connell said.

Through their advocacy and tireless work promoting and exposing their city-dwelling peers to a life of agriculture, the team have also boosted interest for St Angela's students to do agricultural science as a subject, with the school subsequently offering it on the curriculum for the first time last year instead of an after-school extra.

Alongside their teachers, Ms O’Donovan and Mr Barry-Murphy, a big supporter of the team's work was their principal and beef farmer, Mr Curran, who has provided a listening ear to the girls over any snags they came across with their project.

The team focused on multispecies swards, red clover, animal health and the environment as the main pillars of their research.

The cattle were monitored: they had faecal samples taken, and the results were then used to determine whether the animals were dosed for coccidiosis.

With their sponsorship from Grasstech and help from FBA Labs, the girls were able to compare organic multi-species sward growing on Ms Dilworth’s farm to conventional perennial-rye grass on Ms O’Connell’s farm, with the multi-species performing similarly to the conventional fertilised grass.

At FBA Labs, the team tested and compared silage samples between conventional silage and organic red clover silage. Through their trials, they found on conventional silage their cattle were putting on 0.4kg/day, but on organic red clover silage they were putting on double at 0.8kg/day.

With their trials, the girls also visually observed more pollinators and biodiversity with the multi-species swards when compared to conventional.

The team contacted local organic farmers, and under the guidance of Kay O’Sullivan, who farms an organic beef suckler and sheep farm out in Mourneabbey in Cork, she was able to offer insight into organics and educate them on soil testing.

Reaching out to other influential women in agriculture, the team spoke with Katherine O’Leary from the Irish Farmers Journal, who offered advice to the team, who described Ms O’Leary as a “trailblazer” and “mentor” in helping to navigate their project. 

The team also met with Aileen Sheehan, a local teacher and farmer who won FBD Young Farmer of the Year in 2025 as the first woman to win the award, with the team crediting her as a “great inspiration” for them.

While the research focused on biodiversity, animal health, grass growth and nutrition, the students said the biggest lesson they learned was that organic and conventional farming are not as far apart as many people believe.

Throughout the project, the team worked to challenge misconceptions among both farmers and consumers, arguing sustainability does not have to come at the expense of productivity.

For the St Angela's team, it was never about encouraging every farmer to convert to a fully organic system. Instead, they hoped to show small, practical changes could make a meaningful difference on farms of all types.

Their central message is one they hope farmers, consumers and policymakers alike take on board.

 Organic farming is not a million miles away. It’s tangible, it’s achievable, it’s important, it’s sustainable, and it’s economical.

Looking back on nearly three years of research, farm visits, presentations and caring for their “Famous Five” cattle, the students believe the future of Irish farming will involve adopting sustainable practices that work alongside existing systems rather than replacing them entirely.

It is a conclusion backed by the team's research as part of the competition and one they hope will encourage more farmers to see sustainability not as a challenge to their businesses, but as an opportunity to strengthen them for the future.
news.summary: Kicking off our five-part series, we take a look at the team from St Angela's College located in Cork City who are finalists of the Certified Irish Angus Schools Competition

Raised in Turner's Cross and built on the road - the faces and places that made Ireland's Megan Connolly

The 42 sits down with Luke and Michael Connolly to discuss the rise of Megan in professional football.

4.47pm, 7 Oct 2026

Share options

Sinead Farrell

IT’S COMING TO the end of a Munster senior cup final in Cork, and the manager of one of the teams is facing a selection dilemma.

Michael Connolly, who established the women’s section of College Corinthians AFC, is already down to his sub keeper in a 2-2 battle. They’re up against fierce rivals, and defending champions, Wilton United. 

His replacement keeper is pulling off the saves and keeping them in the fight as the game enters extra time. But with neither side looking likely to nab a winner, she comes to Connolly with a crisis of confidence.

“I’m not going in goals for the penalties,” she says.

“Not a bother,” Michael replies with reassurance. “I’ve a plan.”

Megan Connolly pictured in the goalkeeper jersey celebrating with her Corinthians team.Luke Connolly

Luke Connolly

Connolly’s daughter Megan is also a player on the Corinthians team. In truth, he built this team for her when he saw she had a flair for the sport. He canvassed schools. He put up flyers. The whole family helped put the work in to assemble a team. All in the hope that Megan could take her passion further when there were no other opportunities around the Douglas area.

Megan normally plays up front and has provided both of her side’s goals in this game in Charleville. Megan is also a Chelsea fan. Moreover, she’s a hardcore Petr Čech worshipper. She even has a pair of gloves that are similar to the ones he plays with. And now she’s going to get her chance to emulate her idol.

Michael has faith, despite her lack of match experience between the sticks. He knows that she’s good at reading what direction a shooter will aim for.

Megan uses those instincts to save all three of Wilton’s penalties as Corinthians are crowned the new champions. But when it comes to naming the Player of the Match, Megan Connolly is not selected for the award.

Walking out from the pitch, Michael runs into the official who is responsible for this decision. 

“Look, Megan has a load of them, I’d say,” he says, offering his apologies.

“That’s not the point,” comes Michael’s reply.

“The point is that she scored two goals, she saved the penalties, and she was deserving of it. That’s it.”

Michael is recalling Megan’s recent graduation as he sits down to tea with his son, Luke. His son has just moved into a new house in Innishannon, so they’re sipping from disposable cups for the moment. Thankfully, he’s not straying too far from home where he played football for Nemo Rangers and Cork. His playing days are over, but he’s still involved with the Nemo seniors as a coach.

There are some odd jobs left to be done to help Luke settle in with his family. His young son, Shea, has just come home from crèche. Life is blissfully busy.

But they can spare some time to talk about Megan, the youngest of the three siblings. Luke is the eldest, and they have another sister, Nicole.

Megan’s graduation was in London where she picked up a diploma in Global Football Business Management. Australian legend Tim Cahill was also receiving a qualification that day along with former Chelsea star César Azpilicueta.

Megan was especially happy to see him there.

Megan was a big Chelsea and Petr Čech fan growing up.Luke Connolly.

Luke Connolly.

But for Michael and his wife, Freda, the biggest shock was seeing their youngest speak on stage for 10 minutes about her course.

“She never told us that she was being interviewed on stage. To be honest, you can never tell with Megan.”

A new person stood before them compared to the girl they raised in Cork. She’s done a lot of growing up since moving to Florida State University in 2015 on a four-year scholarship as a teenager.

The next four years were spent at Brighton & Hove Albion in the Women’s Super League [WSL], before a brief stint at Bristol City. She’s now into her third year as a Serie A player with Lazio.

All that moving around has altered her accent slightly. Luke is waiting for an Italian flavour to show up in her “mid-Atlantic” twang, but Michael assuredly says that there’s still some Cork in there.

Megan Connolly [right] in action for Lazio.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

“She rings me and goes, ‘Hello, Boyyyyy.’ She’d be mocking me then.”

Freda has remarked in the past how Megan went to Florida as a shy girl, and came home a confident woman. Luke agrees with that observation.

“The Megan that left wouldn’t be the same Megan that captained a WSL team. She’s become more of a leader.”

And as she prepares to turn 30 next year, with 70 Ireland caps banked, she’s looking to the future and the life that awaits after playing professional football.

“She’s looked at what would keep her interested in soccer,” Michael explains. “Coaching is one thing, but then there’s other backroom things that she’d like to get into. From being in the States when she was 18 to now where she’s 29. So over that 11 years, she’s been in and out of the Irish team, and she’s had different experiences.”

The machine wouldn’t accept Michael’s match ticket, and he couldn’t understand why. It was a rainy night in June, and he was trying to get into the Premium Level of Páirc Uí Chaoimh to watch Megan play for Ireland in their World Cup qualifier against the Netherlands. 

Luke had no trouble getting through, and was sinking into some pints with his work colleagues before kick-off. It was a breeze for Nicole and her family too.

But their father was having some technical difficulties. The machine kept popping his ticket back out to him. A friendly steward stepped in to provide assistance, and kindly pointed out that he was in the wrong section of the stadium.

“I was down in the front with the rain,” Michael laughs. “There were a few girls there who work with Freda and they always support Megan. And they were like, ‘Where’s everyone else?’ And I was pointing up to where they were.”

But missing out on the Premium Level luxuries proved to be no loss in the end for Michael. Ireland kept their automatic World Cup qualification hopes alive that night with a dramatic 3-2 victory. Amber Barrett provided the match-winner in the 90th minute, and Michael had the best view in the house.

Advertisement

Michael Connolly was sitting right in front of the celebrations after Amber Barrett's winner against the Netherlands.Ben Brady / INPHO

Ben Brady / INPHO / INPHO

“I was right in front of where Amber celebrated the third goal,” he continued.

“It was great because I got down to Megan for a hug. I wouldn’t have got that, so it worked out well.”

The Ireland women’s team have enjoyed some famous results at Páirc Uí Chaoimh in recent years. It’s quickly becoming their favourite venue. Along with that massive result against the Dutch, you can also add a 1-0 win over Slovenia from the 2025 Nations League to the list.

It all started in 2024, with a 3-1 result against France to mark their first win of their Euro 2025 qualification campaign. It was also Ireland’s first senior women’s home international outside of Dublin since June 2012.

Megan came on in the last few minutes, and sent in a corner for Anna Patten to score Ireland’s third goal of the game. But for the Connollys, there were some challenging emotions to work through during that game.

“She did some of the media before the game but she almost didn’t feature,” Luke begins. “She came on, took a corner, and they got the third goal. That put a positive spin on what would have been a fairly disastrous trip to Cork for us. She just wasn’t getting in under Eileen (Gleeson). But that’s our hit.

“There was huge support there. There were 300 girls down there who wanted to run out onto the pitch after the game. There’s that part of it as well.

“That’s what you sometimes don’t appreciate. From canvassing the schools to winning in Cork in front of girls. Maybe we don’t appreciate that side of it enough.”

Megan Connolly in action at Páirc Uí Chaoimh.Ben Brady / INPHO

Ben Brady / INPHO / INPHO

The Connollys have followed Megan’s Ireland career closely, even when they couldn’t watch her play. In the days before TV coverage, they only had an FAI stream to rely on that didn’t have any live actual footage of the game.

“We remember watching the bar like a Football Manager game,” Luke explains. “If we were attacking, it would go green. We’d just keep watching the bar and if they missed a chance, we’d be like, ‘Oh, fuck sake.’ So, it’s nice to actually watch games instead of making up scenarios in our head.”

They feel all the bad moments with Megan, as much as the good ones. On the night Ireland secured World Cup qualification in 2022, Megan was at home with her family. They were all together for Amber Barrett’s famous winning goal against Scotland at Hampden Park.

A surreal memory. They knew Megan should be playing, but was unavailable due to a serious injury. Two fractured ribs and a grade three laceration of the kidney forced her to watch the drama unfold on TV.

Luke was still playing for Nemo Rangers in those days, and missed the first half of the game due to training. Someone kept him informed of the updates before he could get home to watch the second half.

In 2021, during another World Cup qualifier against Sweden, Luke used a different method to stay informed.

“We watched the first half, and then I had training. We were getting ready for a [championship] semi-final, and I had the phone in my sock.” 

Of course, the Connollys all flew out to Australia too for the tournament itself. A historic occasion for Irish football and a career highlight for Megan. The first group game against the host nation, Australia, was almost overwhelming for Luke.

“We were definitely emotional when they were walking out because it’s kind of like a ‘She did it’ moment.”

It’s about a week into Megan Connolly’s transfer to Lazio, and she wants to come home. This is her third club as a professional footballer, but it’s not her first experience with homesickness.

She was struck down with a bout of it during her final years at Florida State as her role in the team gradually changed from influential leader to impact player.

Now she’s showing symptoms again as she tries to adjust to life in Italy. She’s used to certain training methods from her time with Brighton and Bristol in the Women’s Super League.

But it’s different in Lazio. They use old-school training methods. It’s an all-male coaching staff too.

The heat doesn’t make it any easier. It’s 40 degrees outside and Megan’s accommodation doesn’t have any air conditioning.

Megan Connolly was captain of Brighton during her time there.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Megan’s mother, Freda, sobbed for weeks when her youngest left the house to go to Florida for four years. But in these moments of doubt, she’s the one that says what her daughter needs to hear.

“You’ve signed a contract. You have to honour it.”

It gets easier for Megan as the weeks go by. She checks herself into a hotel for a month to catch up on some sleep in an air-conditioned room. Within a month, she’s in a beautiful apartment. She then makes her first start at centre-back against Roma. The perfect tonic for a bad case of homesickness. 

“When you’re playing well, stuff like that tends to fade a bit,” Luke explains. “She’s at the point now where they’ve had girls come over, and she can see if they’ll last because it is such a culture shock.

“In Brighton, the training facilities are top class. Lazio have improved and have their own facilities. But if the men’s team have to go out on the pitch, they’ll (the women’s team) be demoted to the (other pitch). Because it’s so hot in Italy this month, they actually train on astroturf.

“So, there’s still a bit of an old-school approach there. And in pre-season, they’re running. There’s no footballs.”

The Connolly home lies in the shadow of two great stadiums in Cork. Turner’s Cross is their address, not far from the home ground of Cork City. It was a regular haunt for the Connollys when the children were young.

The home games they attended in 2005 were particularly memorable as Cork City edged out Derry City to win the Premier Division. Their title race went to the final day when Damien Richardson’s side earned a 2-0 win over the Candystripes at a packed-out Turner’s Cross to secure a first Premier Division title since 1993.

Páirc Uí Chaoimh, the headquarters of Cork GAA, is the other major sporting venue within reach of the Connolly household. Visits to Páirc Uí Chaoimh would come in later years for the Connollys. Luke’s career with the Cork footballers, combined with county final appearances for Nemo Rangers, has given them plenty of days out.

That could have been Megan’s life too. She also played for Nemo Rangers and represented Cork up to the U16 grade before she was prompted to make a decision. An All-Ireland final against Galway was clashing with a match for Ireland, and the message relayed to her father was clear.

Megan played centre for for Nemo Rangers. She's pictured second from the left on the bottom row here.

“If she doesn’t come to Dublin, she can play Gaelic for the rest of her life.”

“And I said to her, ‘You’ve got to do one or the other.’”

Michael is certain that a future in a Cork jersey was there for her. Centre-forward was her best position, and she was a dominant force in that sport too.

“I remember when she was 14, 15, they brought out a rule in Cork of one hop, one solo, and you had to get rid of the ball then. Because certain girls would just run through the whole place.

“So I said to Megan, ‘Just throw it on the floor and go with it and dribble through.’

“We played a club in Cork and the manager was running onto the pitch shouting, ‘She can’t do that!’”

Soccer won her heart and brought her down a different road. But she would eventually find herself at the gates of Páirc Uí Chaoimh too.

When they were young, the back garden was the preferred venue for the Connolly kids. Matches. Kicking drills. Basically, anything that involved ball work would keep them out on the grass for hours.

“There’s plants that can speak for the amount of games we had at home,” Luke recalls. “The remnants of tomato trees. Glass houses that didn’t last too long.” 

Nicole would normally retire after a match that was up to five goals. That left Luke and Megan to play on. The new target would be best of 50. Last one left standing. Their battles could go on until nightfall.

At that point, Michael would be pleading with them to come inside.

A young Megan Connolly in her Corinthians gear.Luke Connolly.

Luke Connolly.

“I would be saying to Luke, ‘Just leave her win.’ And then at about six o’clock, Megan would come in with the chest out. ’27-26. I just won.’”

But those victories weren’t built on any appeals for leniency. Luke could see that she was getting stronger with every game, and could do little to stop her.

“There’s four years between us, but it wasn’t too long where I was like, ‘I’m not letting her fucking win.’”

The garden is also where both Megan and Luke became dead-ball specialists. Luke could kick frees off the ground in Gaelic football, while Megan learned to become proficient at swinging in corners as well as hooking frees around a wall of defenders.

A famous example is from the U19 European Championships in 2014. Ireland, who were appearing at the competition for the first time, were 1-1 with Sweden in a group game when Connolly stood over a free with 10 minutes to go. With the aid of the crossbar, she knocked it into the top corner to send Ireland into the semi-finals.

FAI TV / YouTube

(Skip to 1:05 for Connolly’s match-winning free)

Her corners are a staple for Ireland. Both arms raised before applying the whip is the typical routine. Her delivery in the 89th minute of Ireland’s win over France in 2024 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh is an important one to note. Connolly left her mark on the pitch that’s close to home, using the tricks her father taught her.

“Frees and corners were a family thing,” Luke says. “The reason he taught us was basically, ‘If you’re having a bad game, give them a reason not to take you off.’ I don’t think it really happened with Megan, but if there ever was a day when you were having a bad game, you could say, ‘Yeah, but we need her for the corners.’ 

“It’s a key part of her Irish career.”

Megan was always a quiet player on the field. Hardly a word, according to Michael. And not very expressive either. She never broke into wild or excessive celebrations after a goal. Never goaded an opponent when she was dominating a game.

That was an important quality when she was such a formidable presence on the field. Her gamesmanship earned her a lot of respect as she progressed from Corinthians to Florida State. Her international career started by making an U15 squad. In 2014, she was on that Ireland U19 side at the European Championships.

It was packed with future greats of women’s sport. Sarah Rowe, a current star of the AFLW, was involved as was Cork camogie All-Ireland winner Amy O’Connor. Katie McCabe and Chloe Mustaki were there too, and still share an Ireland dressing room with Megan.

Luke had a different personality on the field. His father laughs in agreement, and follows it up with a story to illustrate the difference between his two children.

Luke Connolly captained Nemo Rangers to Cork senior glory in 2022.Lorraine O’Sullivan / INPHO

Lorraine O’Sullivan / INPHO / INPHO

The scene is the 2020 Cork premier senior football final – played in 2021 due to Covid – between Nemo Rangers and their rivals Castlehaven. Luke has just scored his second goal to help seal a 3-7 to 0-13 victory. He raises his arms to the crowd in celebration before dropping a finger to his lips, shushing the Castlehaven supporters.

The Connolly men take up the story.

“His mother was saying, ‘What’s he doing?’ And I says, ‘He’s not doing what he’s supposed to be doing.’ He ran across jeering them.”

Luke laughs as he interjects.

“I don’t think that’s accurate now. They were calling me names.” 

Another visit to Páirc Uí Chaoimh awaits for Ireland. And the Connollys. As the World Cup qualification journey continues against Kazakhstan, the venue where they have a 3-0 record was the only place that could host such a crucial fixture. The first leg of the play-off is coming up this Friday in Astana Arena before Carla Ward’s side return to the banks of the Lee on Tuesday, 13 October.

Another homecoming of sorts for Megan and her lifelong friend, Denise O’Sullivan. An image of the Cork comrades in their Ireland shirts is immortalised in a traffic box mural in the city. A fitting dedication to their legacy. 

Come On You Girls In Green! 

Our new traffic box mural at South Gate Bridge in @corkcitycentre dedicated to Cork's Megan Connolly and Denise O'Sullivan who will be bringing home the @FIFAWomensWorl3 Cup later this summer for @FAIWomen https://t.co/RR9LoZBA8J— People's Republic of Cork (@cork) May 26, 2023

“She’s always had Megan’s back,” Luke adds. “If Megan’s not playing, she’d be saying, ‘You should be playing, girl.’”

The Connollys will also be in Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Saturday, 10 October in their Nemo Rangers colours for a senior football semi-final against Carrigaline. Luke is part of the backroom team these days. He stopped playing in 2023 with five senior county medals and two Munster crowns to his name. They’ve lost the last three county finals, but he’s hoping for a different ending this year.

“I have a jersey for Shea. We have a family photo from last year which is the first time that the three generations were there. It would be nice to win one as a coach.”

Lots to look forward to in the next few weeks just down the road from where it all started in Turner’s Cross.

“You still think it’s going to disappear in the morning. If anything happened, she’s had such a career. She’s been through Florida State, Brighton, Bristol, World Cup, Lazio.

“When we were canvassing in school, you’d be saying, ‘Remember now, this is all for you.’”

news.title: ‘Lean review’ of DAFM TB programme to continue in 2027
news.text:
A 'lean review' of the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine's bovine tuberculosis (TB) programme is set to continue next year.

As part of Budget 2027, government departments have been asked to deliver efficiencies and reforms. 

Among the measures highlighted by DAFM was the continuation of its lean review of the bovine TB programme across all Regional Veterinary Offices (RVO).

DAFM said this will help to identify "increased efficiencies in the operation of the programme".

"This will continue across all areas of the programme throughout 2027 to enforce the building of a Lean culture across the BTB programme," the department added.

Under Budget 2027, DAFM has been allocated €142.4 million for the TB programme for next year.

This is around €15 million less than the allocation for the programme for this year (2026), which was €157 million.

The department is expecting to carry out some 10.7 million bovine TB tests on cattle next year.

It has also been confirmed that the existing valuation ceilings will increase by €500 for all reactor animals valued in 2026.

Among the other efficiencies highlighted by DAFM was the strategic deployment of artifical intelligence (AI) "to drive business value and innovation". 

The department plans to continue developing AI pathfinder projects which could "deliver administration efficiencies to our staff and better serve our customers".

This may include reducing the time to write documents and process applications. 

The department said it will ensure staff have "appropriate training and skills to use AI responsibly and effectively".

DAFM also said it reuses and extends existing technology wherever possible to "maximise value, accelerate delivery, and achieve both time and cost efficiencies". 

It said that spatial analysis capabilities originally developed for forestry schemes have been repurposed to support work on appropriate assessments under the nitrates derogation.

Food controls

In July 2024, the government announced the phased transfer of the official food controls undertaken by local authority veterinary services from the Department of Health (DoH) to DAFM. 

This includes the permanent transfer of funding and the transfer of relevant staff from local authorities to DAFM effective from January 1, 2027.

The department said that it will be more efficient both from an operational and financial perspective to absorb the functions into DAFM’s laboratory complex in Co Kildare.

The department also confirmed that it will carry out a "critical review" of the EU School Fruit and Vegetables and School MilkSchemes ahead of changes to the relevant EU regulations in 2028. 

These schemes are currently cofinanced by EU and national exchequer funding.

The objective of the review will be to simplify and better align these schemes with the Hot School Meals Scheme.

news.title: Tesco looking for new sites for Express chain of stores
news.text:
Tesco confirmed the opening to the Irish Examiner, saying the outlet will open at the end of November and employ 15 people. "As our third Express store opening this year, it will bring the total number of Tesco Express stores across Ireland to 62," a spokesperson said.

Tesco, currently Ireland's second-largest supermarket chain after Dunnes Stores, already operates a full supermarket in Ballincollig. 

It opened another outlet on Cork's South Main Street in 2024, but the company said it is seeking other locations suitable to open further stores.

"We have ambitious plans to continue growing our convenience store network and are actively looking for suitable sites nationwide. 

"We are particularly interested in units of 3,000 sq ft and above, located on busy roads, high streets, or within established retail locations. Both leasehold and freehold opportunities will be considered," the company said.

Tesco has a 24% market share of Ireland's grocery sector. The British chain is led by Cork-born chief executive Ken Murphy.

Publishing results in June, the company said sales in Ireland had grown 5.56% to £838m (€966m), boosted by strong growth in food sales and online shopping.

In July, it was reported that the company was considering the sale of its operations in Central Europe in order to focus on the UK and Ireland.

Discount retailer EuroGiant closed its outlet at Ballincollig's Eastside Centre earlier this year, having opened at the site. The location was previously occupied by supermarket chain Iceland before its exit from the Irish market.
news.summary: British supermarket giant to open new Ballincollig outlet in November

news.title: Ornua PPI indicative milk price up 2c/L
news.text:
The Ornua Purchase Price Index (PPI) has increased for September, resulting in an indicative milk price increase of 2c/L.

The PPI for September is 135.8, an increase of the previous month's index of 130.4.

Ornua said this implies an indicative return of 38.2c/L, including 4.5% VAT, for milk at 3.6% fat and 3.3% protein.

This is an increase on the return for August of 36.2c/L, and is net of Ornua's costs to market.

The price is derived from deducting estimated processing costs for Ornua's member processors. This cost stood at 10c/L for September.

The estimated processing cost is based on Ornua’s estimate of the average cost of processing the Ornua "basket of products", which is not representative of any of Ornua's individual member processors.

The estimated processing cost does not include any allowance for member processor margin, and is based on external indices of variable costs (most importantly energy).

The estimated processing cost can increase or decrease every quarter of the year, depending on movements in those external indices.

Ornua said the latest PPI and indicative milk price return "reflect stronger market returns for the month of September".

However, Ornua also said that the PPI does not directly align with milk production and payments, for "reasons of seasonality".

In other dairy market news, the Global Dairy Trade (GDT) index has increased following the latest trading event held this week.

The index has increased by 1.2% to 1,177 as a result of the auction which took place yesterday (Tuesday, October 6).

The result reverses the impact of a 1.1% fall in the index after the last trading event in mid September.

This week's event saw a total of 41,692t of dairy commodities traded with an average winning price of $3,928/t.

The results show a mixed picture when it comes to movement in the average prices for each of the product sub-indices.

The index for skim milk powder (SMP) rose by 4.3% to an average price of $3,847/t.

Whole milk powder (WMP) was up 1.2% to an average of $3,605/t, while butter milk powder rose by 0.7% to $4,123/t.

However, there was a 6.9% fall in the average price of lactose to $1,677/t.

Cheddar was back 3.7% to $3,925/t and mozzarella decreased by 3.9% to $3,833/t.

There was a slight fall (-0.3%) for butter to leave an average price of $4,740/t, while anhydrous milk fat was down by 1.1% to $5,683/t.

news.title: Number of children requiring special education placements is 'evolving all the time', says minister
news.text:
The department’s budget for 2027 includes funding for 1,352 special education teachers and 2,339 special needs assistants (SNAs) under a €3.8bn allocation to special education.

Separately, the Department of Education figures put the number of children receiving support for special educational needs now at 250,000, growing from 70,000 a decade ago. 

 To receive a special educational placement, either in a special class or special school, parents must register through the Parents Notify portal, run by the National Council for Special Education (NCSE). This year, the deadline to apply for 2027 was brought forward to the end of September.

Announcing the move over the summer, Ms Naughton said it was necessary to give her “the opportunity to feed into the budgetary process to meet the needs of the most vulnerable children in our society”. 

On Wednesday, neither Ms Naughton or Mr Moynihan would provide the figure their department put forward during budget negotiations.

Ms Naughton said: "As part of our budget negotiations, it was really important that we can, number one, forward plan, and having the portal in place is a really critical part of that." 

The numbers for 2027 are coming in “the whole time”, she said.

“We are confident that we have the budget for September in 2027 in relation to the demand for special education.” She added: “These figures are evolving all the time.” 

Bringing the portal deadline back gave the department greater insight around forward planning, said Mr Moynihan.

The October deadline last year was not a “cliff edge” deadline because numbers kept coming in, Mr. Moynihan added. “And we are still accepting numbers after September 1 [this year].” 

He added: “It is wrong to give a number because that would give an impression to families ‘well, that’s the number now, that’s all they are doing’.” 

He urged families who need access to special education for 2027 to continue to use the Parents Notify portal.

“We have sight on what we need to do but those numbers will change right up to next year because students within schools, parents will want to try mainstream schools, maybe it doesn’t work out. We are engaging. The NCSE, ourselves, and the department are meeting on a weekly basis to review and to ensure we’ve sight on where the challenges are.

"But that number will change, and if I give you a number today, that number would not be accurate in two weeks time, or even two days time.” 

 Jess Casey is Education Correspondent.
news.summary: The Department of Education figures put the number of children receiving support for special educational needs now at 250,000, growing from 70,000 a decade ago
news.author: Irishexaminer.com,Jess Casey

news.title: Patients and consultants take case for stem cell transplant unit in Cork to Leinster House
news.text:
The unit closed temporarily almost 20 years ago. Now transplant patients in Munster hospitals are transferred to Galway or St James hospital in Dublin for the procedure.

Musician Mags McCarthy started the campaign, motivated by watching her own father travel to Dublin from Cork for care.

“We’re doing a presentation to get everybody on board, and hopefully prioritise a transplant centre for Cork.

“That would help all patients as there is no stem cell transplantation in the south of Ireland now,” she said before the meeting.

Former patient Denis O’Donovan travelled from Blarney to support the campaign following his experiences in 2021.

“I had to get treated in St James so it meant commuting up and down to Dublin which is so inconvenient,” he said.

“We had to get up at 5.30am to get the 7am train to get up to get my bloods done at 9.30am.” 

He only lives about 20 minutes from Cork University Hospital, he added.

Another former patient Noel Casey made three trips to Galway, including once by ambulance back to Cork. 

“Your immune system is gone so you’re very isolated. It was covid time so if you got covid you were a goner. Galway were very good to us, but it’s just the travelling.” 

Medical experts attending included Vitaliy Mykytiv, clinical director of diagnosis and therapeutics at CUH.

Also present was president of the European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation professor Ibrahim Yakoub-Agha.

The ratio between transplant centres and population numbers in Ireland is “really below the European range”, he said.

He described how two hours is the maximum travel time recommended between patients’ homes and transplant centres.

“Even two hours is a really long time because if you go to see a specialist that is four hours travelling for very tired patients,” he said.

“When we calculate in Ireland you have only one allogeneic stem cell transplant centre in Dublin. So for patients from the south of Ireland the distance is something like three hours. It’s a red flag because it’s a very long distance.” 

Prof. Yakoub-Agha also said medical students at University College Cork should be exposed to the most advanced treatments available.

The meeting was arranged by Fine Gael senator Eileen Lynch.

“There’s over 2,400 people here in Ireland diagnosed with a blood cancer, but currently you can only have a stem cell transplant in Galway and Dublin while you can get pre-care and aftercare in CUH,” she said.

She called for investment through the capital budget for health in the unit.
news.summary: At the moment, transplant patients in Munster hospitals are transferred to Galway or St James hospital in Dublin for the procedure
news.author: Fine Gael,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: Mary McAleese integration  replacement unveiled on Friday
news.text:
Meetings have been called for as early as Thursday evening and the Irish Examiner understands the individual is a man.

“We met as a group on Monday,” said GAA director general Tom Ryan, replying to a question from Fianna Fáil TD for Wexford-Wicklow Malcolm Byrne. “We agreed unanimously on a nominee for that position and that person has agreed to take up that role.

“There’s a small process to be undertaken in each of the three organisations. Each organisation over the course of the next, I want to say, 24 hours will be meeting to formally ratify, appoint that person. We’ll be making that announcement very shortly.” 

Asked by Fine Gael TD Wexford-Wicklow Brian Brennan why he felt McAleese stepped down as SGI chairperson, GAA president Jarlath Burns suggested she did not accept the first deadline of 2027 would not be achieved.

“I think she resigned because she was very adamant that we would reach every deadline that we had, and once she realised we were going to miss the first deadline, I think she decided then that she wanted to walk away from the process, which was very disappointing for us and we regret that deeply.

“But we are still very much committed to integration. We really do want to make it happen and it’s up to us – we will make it happen – but we will make it happen in a way that our numbers are comfortable with and will vote for.” 

There was a reluctance on the part of the Gaelic bodies to provide new timelines in the wake of last month’s confirmation that next year’s deadline will not be met.

LGFA chief executive Lyn Savage said it was “a brave decision” to postpone the deadline of 2027, insisting “we needed to get it right”. She rejected the suggestion it was a failure.

In a response to a question from Sinn Féin TD for Dublin South-Central Aengus Ó Snodaigh about a date for full integration, GAA director general Tom Ryan was happy to say it would take “years”.

Labour TD for Tipperary North and joint-committee chairperson Alan Kelly said the Gaelic bodies would be invited to meet the deputies and senators again in December where he said he and his colleagues "will need to know" the revised timeplan.

In a press release last month, The Camogie Association president Brian Molloy said January 2028 as “the new “delivery date for the GAA to become the single NGB (national governing body) for all Gaelic Games”.

Burns said there had been disquiet among some in the LGFA and The Camogie Association about the structure proposed structure of vice-presidents working under one president. “That was taken by some people to be the GAA are getting the presidency and the poor LGFA and The Camogie Association are only getting the vice-presidents.” 

He admitted he and Molloy had different opinions on how the integration process should proceed. “I think we’re better going incrementally. Brian and I discuss this all the time. Brian feels we should start off with structures and then do the rest at a second Congress.

“I think incrementally is better, start off with structures, and even if we say ‘these are the structures we’re aspirationally going to have’ then all of the county implementation committees can do some meaningful work.

“We have actually found it very hard to get those (committees) into action because they’re saying to us, ‘What are we getting ready for?’”

Burns outlined some of the work the GAA already does for the Camogie Association including a €500,000 annual grant, ticketing, GDPR, vetting, safeguarding, broadcasting, advertising and commercial. “We do all of that together,” he said.

Burns added that they last week outlined the costs of integration to Minister for Sport Patrick O’Donovan and his department officials but he was not prepared to announce them for fear of them being perceived as “prohibitive” to integration. “If I do (reveal the figures), it will come across as the GAA throwing out costs and being prohibitive and not supportive of the process.” 

Burns did reveal they have provided a plan to the Government by which to fund to meet the requirements of integration. He later insisted GAA units should not be charging ladies football and camogie teams for use of their grounds.

The GAA wholeheartedly rejected suggestions of misogyny after McAleese’s claim that some within the organisation are “not entirely happy about the idea of including women in decision-making at the top level of Gaelic sports”.
news.summary: There was a reluctance on the part of the Gaelic bodies to provide new timelines for integration
news.author: Fine Gael Td,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: ‘He never lost his accent’: How missing Cork native built a happy life as a gay man in England
news.text:
When Patrick O’Sullivan disappeared without a trace in 1992, his family feared what might have happened to him.

The man from Lombardstown, Co Cork was much loved by his late parents and six siblings, but unfortunately it was a very different time in Ireland and he went missing 34 years ago, his family believes, because of his sexuality.

They knew he was gay, but it “wasn’t condoned or even spoken about”, his brother Jerry said.

Patrick ‘Patsy’ O’Sullivan disappeared without a trace just after he visited his family home on Easter Monday in 1992.

He never contacted his family again. 

They received a call from gardaí in August this year, who told them that Patsy went on to have a life “full of joy” in the UK, marrying his partner and retraining as an auxiliary nurse. 

The chef, who was 35 years old at the time, was due to return from his job in Kerry for a christening.

His older brother Jerry said it wasn’t easy for Patsy to grow up gay in the Ireland of the 1970s and 1980s. 

“I was afraid something had happened to him back then (when he went missing) because of his sexuality. Because I remember what happened to me for being a brother of him. I can’t imagine what he went through himself.

“In the 80s and early 1990s that (being gay) wasn’t condoned or even spoken about. It was different times. The church was different. The older people were a very different generation than what they are now.” 

Jerry said Patsy was much loved but circumstances were very difficult. 

“I came up with the old generation. My father would have been very strict. They (his parents) knew (Patsy was gay) but it was never spoken about. My mother didn’t have an issue with it (Patsy being gay) but my father would have. But him being gay was never spoken about.”

[ ‘A closure for us’: Cork family learns brother missing since 1992 died in UK two years agoOpens in new window ]

Patsy went to the UK in 1992 with “nothing” and experienced hard times, before receiving help from a nun called Bridget Anne. 

Life improved for him and in 1994 he met his lifelong partner. Jerry had a heartening hour-long phone call with a niece of Patsy’s partner in the UK on Tuesday.

“It gave me so much solace to what kind of life he had and the enjoyment he had in his life. He had been with his partner since 1994 and he changed his name (to Aldridge) in 1995.” 

He and his partner were married by a priest who knew them very well and Patsy changed his surname in 1995 to take the name of his partner. 

“I can’t think as to what he had to go through as he had to start a life all over again and leave six siblings and his parents behind him. And to never turn back and speak to anyone again. That must have been horrendous for him. 

“I can only imagine what he went through. I can take a lot of comfort from what I am after being told today.”

Jerry was told that Patsy never forgot his Irish roots.

“He never lost his Cork accent and always carried a green, white and gold flag. He always drank from an Irish mug. He drank about 15 cups of tea a day which we do to this present moment. It is a big thing in our family. He was a very proud Irishman and never lost any part of that.”

He went on to train as an auxiliary nurse and Jerry said he was always “on the caring side as a person”. 

His partner died in 2022 and his niece calls Patsy her uncle. 

The O’Sullivan family never gave up looking for Patsy. Jerry and his brother Eugene made an appeal for information as recently as two years ago on RTÉ’s Crimecall. 

Heartbreakingly, it has emerged that Patsy was living just over an hour away from a brother who died in the UK last year. 

“I used to go over to my brother in the UK eight or ten times a year. I was very close to my eldest brother. And Patsy was only an hour up the road. That is a killer.”

Patsy died of sepsis two years ago and his ashes were spread alongside the ashes of his late partner in a place that meant a lot to them in London. 

Jerry plans to put a memory box together for Patsy. He also intends to put his name on a headstone in order to give him the closure that he deserves in his native country. 

The case was investigated by gardaí when Patsy went missing. Jerry says that in recent years Garda PJ Roche and his team left no stone unturned in order to find out what happened to him. 

“Since 2015 checks were done with DNA, Interpol, Canada, Australia, America, New Zealand, England, Scotland and Wales. Everything came back a blank even down to the John Does who were dead and buried and had no name. It was looking bleak.”

He was astonished when he found out what had happened to him. He plans to travel there next month to speak to people who knew him. 

“I am going to meet as many people and get as many stories as I can. I believe Patsy started looking very like our brother Eugene (as he got older).”

He cherishes his memories of his wonderful brother and adds he hopes that people who go missing realise that they can always go home. 

[ Behind the mystery that first set off fears of Iranian threats at a UK military baseOpens in new window ]
news.summary: Patsy O’Sullivan disappeared without trace on Easter Monday from Lombardstown, Co Cork in 1992
news.author: Olivia Kelleher

news.title: Leinster hurling revolution promises more jeopardy and a new route to the top
news.text: The proposed new format for the Leinster Senior Hurling Championship has something for everyone. After years of stagnation, the radical shake-up promises greater jeopardy for the province’s big guns while giving emerging counties a clearer route towards the top table. And former GAA president Nickey Brennan , who chaired the reform committee, believes they have finally found the balance between protecting the leading counties and giving the likes of Kildare, Antrim, Carlow, Laois and Westmeath a genuine pathway forward. The biggest change is that the Leinster Championship will effectively be split into two groups from 2028. The teams who finish first to fourth in next year’s championship will be placed in Group A, while the sides finishing fifth and sixth will be joined by the 2027 Joe McDonagh Cup finalists in Group B. But being in Group B will not mean the end of Leinster ambitions. Far from it. Five new knockout games will be introduced, creating a much greater element of jeopardy and giving the second-tier counties a chance to bridge the gap to the Liam McCarthy Cup. At present, Leinster has 31 games but only one knockout fixture — the final. Under the new structure there will be 30 games, but six of them will be knockout matches. The teams finishing third and fourth in Group A will enter the quarter-finals against the teams finishing first and second in Group B. The four quarter-finalists will then be involved in an open draw to determine the semi-final pairings. The two teams who finish first and second in Group A will enter at the semi-final stage, where they will face the quarter-final winners. The Leinster final will then be played alongside a third-place play-off between the beaten semi-finalists, with the winner of that game claiming the third Leinster place in the All-Ireland quarter-finals. And Brennan believes the new format will end the dreaded “yo-yo” effect which has seen counties bounce between the Joe McDonagh Cup and the Liam McCarthy Championship. “The feedback we got from all the teams in Leinster was that this yo-yoing effect is not helping us at all,” said Brennan. “We need to get some sort of certainty. “By coming up with this formula, it does give teams certainty. If you're in Group B, it's very much up to yourself now to work your way up through Group B. “At a minimum, finish sixth in Group B, which means you're in the Leinster knockout quarter-final and you're up against perhaps big hitters. “I can tell you from engaging with them that the likes of Antrim are bursting to get into Group B. “They now see a target for how they get to the final of the Joe McDonagh Cup in 2027 and get into Group B the following year. So it's very much within their own control.” The new system will also crank up the pressure on the established counties. The top four will still have the advantage of avoiding the quarter-finals if they finish first or second in Group A — but there will be no margin for error for those who finish third or fourth. “The jeopardy level has changed,” said Brennan. “The two Group A teams who don't get to a semi-final are gone if they lose their quarter-final. That's them gone — their season is over. “So the composition of the four teams in Group A could change from one year to the next. “And the same at Group B, depending on who's there. If you're not in A, you'll end up in B. “So there's a fair lot of possibilities here with this. But the ball is very much in every county's court. “You'd want to be getting first or second in Group A and avoiding the quarter-finals. And then your concerns are over.” There is also a workload benefit for the teams who perform best in the group stage. Brennan says there will be breaks built into the schedule, meaning teams finishing in the top two in Group A could have three weekends without a competitive fixture during the campaign. “Obviously, if you get first or second, you're going to avoid the quarter-finals. That's another break of a week. And there'll be a break before the final. “The final and the third-place play-off will be played on the one weekend. “So if you come first or second in the eight-week competition, you have three weekends blank. So the better you perform, the better you're going to give your players an opportunity to have breaks here.” But the biggest winners could be the Tier 2 counties who have been caught in the Leinster-Joe McDonagh merry-go-round. Kildare’s struggles this year highlighted the gap between the two levels, despite their ability to compete with the province’s strongest sides for long periods. Under the new system, there is now a defined route forward. “The Tier 2 counties are excited about this because it now gives them some certainty about a pathway forward,” said Brennan. “In the past, it was all about, if we come sixth, we're gone anyway. You know, now you can come sixth. “Whoever comes sixth next year in Leinster is actually going to be in Group B as the second team in Group B. And at least they're starting off 2028 in that position. “Now, what they have to then try and do is win their matches to stay first or second in order to contest the quarter-finals of the Leinster Championship. “So there's lots of possibilities here.” Click here to sign up to our sport newsletter, bringing you the top stories and biggest headlines from Ireland and beyond
news.summary: Radical new format will give Tier 2 counties a clearer pathway while putting the province’s big guns under pressure

news.text: Former Derry hurler Brendan ‘Benny’ Ward has died at the age of 52. Ward was a key member of the Derry side that won back-to-back Ulster titles in 2000 and 2001. news.title: Next Monday set as date for major meeting about malting
news.text:
A major meeting of malting barley growers will take place next Monday, (October 12) to discuss urgent issues affecting the sector.

The Irish Farmers' Association (IFA) will host the meeting at the Dolmen Hotel, Carlow, and Boortmalt representatives have also been invited to attend.

“We have already asked Boortmalt to waive the €10/t drying charge on 2026 crops," Murphy told Agriland.

“But, as yet, we have not received a reply from the company on this matter.

“It’s important that Boortmalt representatives attend the Carlow event.”

Malting meeting

The IFA had been looking for a formal meeting with Boortmalt, but this was declined until late last week when Boortmalt said they would only meet on condition that those representing IFA sign a legal non-disclosure agreement (NDA).

"This would mean that we could not report back to our members on the meeting. This is not acceptable," Murphy continued.

“We feel it is absolutely imperative that Boortmalt meets to discuss the lack of a malting premium and the so-called €10/t parity charge in place for Harvest 2026.

“We would encourage all malting barley growers to be in Carlow on Monday night.”

The meeting will get underway at the Dolmen Hotel, Carlow at 8:00p.m next Monday.

news.title: Horse suffers fatal injury after head-on collision with outrider after making winning debut
news.text: A racehorse has died following a devastating head-on collision with an outrider just moments after securing victory on her debut. Two year old Stringin Me On was competing for the first time in a maiden special weight at Assiniboia Downs in Winnipeg, Canada on Monday night. Breaking sharply from the gates, she dominated throughout under jockey Rachaad Knights, surging clear of her three opponents in the home straight to triumph by five lengths. Just four of the five starters finished the five-and-a-half-furlong contest after Onemoresteptoheaven struck the rail early on and unseated its rider. Tragedy struck after Knights had crossed the line and was returning Stringin Me On towards the winners' circle. While trotting back, they were unable to avoid an outrider who had caught Onemoresteptoheaven and collided directly with Stringin Me On, reports the Mirror . Both riders were thrown into the air while the horses crashed to the ground. Simultaneously, stewards launched an inquiry into the race following multiple objections from jockeys regarding interference. Veterinary staff rushed to treat the fallen horses but sadly were unable to save Stringin Me On. A statement from the racecourse confirmed: "A very unfortunate situation occurred at ASD on Monday night when a loose horse was gathered by the outrider and his horse and then they collided with another horse after the race had concluded. "We can advise that the initial loose horse and the horse belonging to the outrider were unharmed, however, the single horse returning after the race suffered injuries and did not survive. "The outrider and jockey Rachaad Knights were both okay and uninjured and the jockey rode during Tuesday's live races." In a further setback for Stringin Me On's owners, Dark Cloud Racing, and trainer Judy Hunter, the unfortunate filly was later stripped of her placing after stewards accepted an objection regarding early interference from the rider of Ringit, who had finished in last position. news.summary: Stringin Me On won on her debut by five lengths at Assiniboia Downs in Winnipeg, Canada, but suffered a fatal injury after a post-race collision with an outrider on Monday night

news.title: Murphy hat-trick powers Midleton CBS to Dean Ryan win
news.text:
While a 14-point margin at the end was rough justice on the hosts at the Mon Field, there was no arguing that the visitors were deserving of victory, earning the right to garnish the scoreline with late goals.

In windy and intermittently wet conditions, it was an attritional battle. In Murphy and Conor Ronayne, Midleton displayed more of a cutting edge and looked likelier winners at half-time, when they led by 0-8 to 0-5 having played into the worst of the elements.

While Gaelcholáiste Mhuire’s main attacking threat, Séamus Ó Donnabháin, pointed within seconds of the restart, it was as close as they would come for the remainder – Midleton produced a strong riposte with points from Ronayne and Murphy (two).

Aided by the strength of a half-back line where Roan Kelleher impressed, Midleton could have moved further clear in the third quarter but their shooting let them down. At the other end, they had reason to be thankful to goalkeeper Will Stokes – a county minor winner with Midleton on Monday night – for a fine save to deny Ryan Ó Corráin at a time when a goal would brought ‘the AG’ to within a point.

Midleton were not without their own goal chances though: Tomás Ó Sé was unlucky to send a low shot wide after a good run on 51 but they didn’t have too long to wait as Murphy pounced on the break when an Eoghan O’Donovan clearance broke and slotted home for a 1-11 to 0-7 advantage.

The attacker almost added another immediately after that, firing across the face of the goal, but after Gaelcholáiste Mhuire centre-back Mixie Gale landed a big free for what would be their last score, Midleton went into overdrive.

A great catch from sub Ben Aherne was the catalyse for an Ó Sé point before Murphy got his second goal following a counter-attack.

Sub Bill Leahy made it 2-13 to 0-8 and deep injury time Murphy got his hat-trick goal.

Goal chances had been rare in the first half, where Midleton moved into an early 0-4 to 0-1 lead as they moved the ball well only for two Cillian Mac Eocháin frees and an Ó Donnabháin point to bring the home side level.

Murphy, set up by James Doyle, had Midleton back in front before a free from goalkeeper Stokes had them 0-6 to 0-4 in front. They would lead thereafter.

news.title: Dean Ryan Cup: Kyle Murphy fires a hat-trick as Midleton CBS beat Gaelcholáiste Mhuire
news.text:
Midleton CBS 3-13

 Gaelcholáiste Mhuire An Mhainistir Thuaidh 0-8

Kyle Murphy finished with 3-4 as a good finish by Midleton CBS eased them clear of Gaelcholáiste Mhuire in the opening round of the TUS Munster PPS Dean Ryan Cup (U17AHC) on Wednesday afternoon.

While a 14-point margin at the end was rough justice on the hosts at the Mon Field, there was no arguing that the visitors were deserving of victory, earning the right to garnish the scoreline with late goals.

In windy and intermittently wet conditions, it was an attritional battle. In Murphy and Conor Ronayne, Midleton displayed more of a cutting edge and looked likelier winners at half-time, when they led by 0-8 to 0-5 having played into the worst of the elements.

While Gaelcholáiste Mhuire’s main attacking threat, Séamus Ó Donnabháin, pointed within seconds of the restart, it was as close as they would come for the remainder – Midleton produced a strong riposte with points from Ronayne and Murphy (two).

Aided by the strength of a half-back line where Roan Kelleher impressed, Midleton could have moved further clear in the third quarter but their shooting let them down. At the other end, they had reason to be thankful to goalkeeper Will Stokes – a county minor winner with Midleton on Monday night – for a fine save to deny Ryan Ó Corráin at a time when a goal would brought ‘the AG’ to within a point.

Midleton were not without their own goal chances though: Tomás Ó Sé was unlucky to send a low shot wide after a good run on 51 but they didn’t have too long to wait as Murphy pounced on the break when an Eoghan O’Donovan clearance broke and slotted home for a 1-11 to 0-7 advantage.

The attacker almost added another immediately after that, firing across the face of the goal, but after Gaelcholáiste Mhuire centre-back Mixie Gale landed a big free for what would be their last score, Midleton went into overdrive.

A great catch from sub Ben Aherne was the catalyse for an Ó Sé point before Murphy got his second goal following a counter-attack.

Sub Bill Leahy made it 2-13 to 0-8 and deep injury time Murphy got his hat-trick goal.

Goal chances had been rare in the first half, where Midleton moved into an early 0-4 to 0-1 lead as they moved the ball well only for two Cillian Mac Eocháin frees and an Ó Donnabháin point to bring the home side level.

Murphy, set up by James Doyle, had Midleton back in front before a free from goalkeeper Stokes had them 0-6 to 0-4 in front. They would lead thereafter.

 Scorers for Midleton CBS: K Murphy 3-4, C Ronayne 0-3 (0-1 65), W Stokes (0-1f), J Doyle, T Ó Sé, D Collins, W Collins, B Leahy 0-1 each.

 Gaelcholáiste Mhuire An Mhainistir Thuaidh: S Ó Donnabháin 0-3, C Mac Eocháoin (0-2f), R Ó Corráin 0-2, M Gale 0-1.

 MIDLETON CBS: W Stokes (Midleton); F Barrett (Carrigtwohill), L O’Riordan (Dungourney), C Cashman (Aghada); R Kelleher (Dungourney), E O’Donovan (Midleton), P Aherne (Cloyne); J Doyle (Lisgoold), C Coughlan (Cloyne); T Ó Sé (Lisgoold), C Ronayne (Dungourney), D Collins (Cloyne); W Collins (Castlemartyr), T O’Dowd (Midleton), K Murphy (Lisgoold).

 Subs: J Hayes (Dungourney) for W Collins (51), B Aherne (Erin’s Own) for O’Dowd (54), L O’Dwyer (Lisgoold) for Barrett, B Leahy (Dungourney) for D Collins (both 60),

news.title: Full list of social welfare payments set for €520 increase from January
news.text: Budget 2027 was recently announced as the government revealed a slate of measures set to come into effect. An increase to core social welfare rates have become a staple of budget measures, and this year was no different. Over a million people will see their payments increase from January by €10 a week, or €520 a year. They have confirmed the full list of payments in line for the increase. The full list of payments increased were: State Pension (Contributory) State Pension (Non-Contributory) Bereaved Partner's (Contributory) Pension Bereaved Partner's (Non-Contributory) Pension Jobseeker's Benefit Jobseeker's Allowance One-Parent Family Payment Maternity Benefit Adoptive Benefit Paternity Benefit Parent’s Benefit Health and Safety Benefit Farm Assist Deserted Wife's Benefit Deserted Wife's Allowance Supplementary Welfare Allowance Illness Benefit Invalidity Pension Disability Allowance Blind Pension Injury Benefit Disablement Benefit Death Benefit Scheme Carer's Benefit Carer's Allowance Guardian’s payment As well as the €10 core increase, the Child Support Payment weekly rate will increase by: €6, from €58 to €64, for children under 12 €6, from €78 to €84, for children aged 12 and over Fuel Allowance will increase by €5 from €38 to €43 per week. The Living Alone Increase will increase by €3 from €22 to €25 per week. The Living on a Specified Island Allowance will increase by €5 from €20 to €25 per week. A cost of disability payment of €500 will be paid to people getting a long-term disability payment. The lump sum will be paid in 2027. It is for people on long-term disability payments and will benefit 240 thousand people. A Christmas bonus of 100% will also be paid to people getting a qualifying social welfare payment the week starting 7 December 2026. Get the full rundown on Tuesday's budget announcement here . news.title: Roy Keane tears into 'sloppy' England and Arsenal star
news.text: Roy Keane believes Eberechi Eze displays too many careless moments in his performances for Arsenal and England. The former Manchester United skipper has called on him to rise to the competitive demands at both club and international level. Eze, 28, featured in England's starting XI for their Nations League fixture against Czechia and completed the entire 90 minutes of their 3-0 victory. This marks only the second occasion he has avoided being either brought on or taken off across his 25 international appearances. Both instances occurred under Thomas Tuchel, the previous being in the friendly defeat to Senegal last June. Additionally, all bar one of his six starts have taken place since the ex-Chelsea manager assumed control 18 months ago. Prior to Tuesday's match at Wembley Stadium, the player's brief appearance after coming on for Anthony Gordon in the 70th minute of their 7-0 thrashing of Croatia attracted disapproval. Keane told ITV: "I was disappointed with him the other night when he came on. "Obviously, England are attacking and doing really well, so when you get opportunities, you've got to take them. I thought he was really sloppy with some of his play, so it's a big opportunity for him tonight.", reports the Mirror . Keane went on to stress the significance of the fixture for Eze: "It's a big test for him tonight. We know how good he is at coming and getting the ball. "But we didn't see that running power off the ball [against Croatia]. I'm not sure whether he really wants to do it or is unaware he's not doing it, but I think it's a big night for him." 'When you look at the attacking players and the challenges, and I'm including Arsenal, sometimes in his play he can just be a bit sloppy. He needs to bring his A-game. Discussing mentality more broadly, before returning his attention to Eze, the former footballer said: "I just worry sometimes players are going: 'Oh, it's not my time, or he's better than me'.... "Embrace that challenge that the other players have brought to the England squad and at Arsenal. He seems just to shy away from it, embrace that and bring your A-game. "As I said, I've watched him far too many times, and there are just too many sloppy moments. Keane's ITV colleague Ian Wright defended the player, stating: "He's got a playing style where if you're sloppy and you're playing with that languid kind of style, then it can look worse than it is.. "I'm not saying he should change his style. But he just needs to tighten everything up a bit because he's an amazing player." news.title: Southampton boss Tonda Eckert given suspended six-week ban and fine over Spygate
news.text:
Eckert accepted full responsibility and was charged by the FA with three breaches of Rule E3.1 in relation to “misconduct”, which hung over Southampton and their manager heading into the new campaign.

The German coach attended an FA hearing at the start of the international break and is able to continue his role against rivals Portsmouth this Sunday and beyond.

A statement from the governing body read: “Tonda Eckert subsequently admitted the charges, and an independent Regulatory Commission imposed a six-week suspension from all football and football related activity, which is suspended until the end of the 2027/28 season, a £28,000 fine and a reprimand following a hearing.

“The suspended sanction will come into effect in the event he is found to have committed a breach of Rules or Regulations by requesting, authorising, taking, or using information from any observation of the training of another club, in whatever guise that observation may take.” The punishment is likely to draw strong opinions from across the game, with Southampton saying in a statement “this now brings a conclusion to a regrettable period of our history”.

The club, who sit 13th in the Championship, say “measures have been put in place to ensure that such errors in judgement never happen again at our club” and they are “excited to move forward together towards a bright future”.

Southampton owner Dragan Solak said: “I’m pleased that the independent panel has come to a decision and that we have an outcome.

“We have already suffered enough, and we appreciate the panel’s recognition of that.

“We are confident the manager has learned from this matter, and a suspended sentence allows him to continue in his role.

“I firmly believe that Tonda is one of Europe’s most exciting young coaches, and with this distraction removed, I am confident he can lead the team to a successful season. I’d like to thank our fans for standing by us and showing the team so much support during a time when we have needed them more than ever.

“The FA process has been a positive experience. Tonda has been given the opportunity to be open and honest with the panel, and the panel has been able to see that he is simply a good person who made poor decisions.

“The same cannot be said for the EFL process, and the way they have subsequently treated us is not something we will forget.

“However, now is the time to look forward to what I believe will be a great future for our club.” The English Football League declined to comment.
news.summary: Saints were kicked out of the Championship play-off final and docked four points this term having admitted three breaches of EFL regulations after being caught snooping on semi-final opponents Middlesbrough and two other teams.

news.title: Simon Harris responds to scathing comments by RTÉ's Oliver Callan who labelled him a 'college dropout'
news.text: Simon Harris has responded to scathing comments made by RTÉ’s Oliver Callan, who said the Tánaiste is a "college drop out" who is as "unpopular as Donald Trump". The satirist is known for impersonating politicians and taking them down a peg, and often gets away with it. However, people were quick to brand a recent column the RTÉ broadcaster wrote for the Irish Independent as classist. The piece was widely shared on social media with the eye-catching headline: "That’s right, our €600bn economy is in the grip of a college dropout who likes TikTok and Coldplay." In the piece written before the budget, Mr Callan wrote: "Next week, a college dropout will deliver the budget for our €600bn economy. "Don’t be too alarmed – Simon Harris isn’t actually making all the key decisions. There are serious people for that sort of thing." Mr Callan was questioning the Tánaiste’s credentials, after he took over the finance portfolio last November following his colleague Paschal Donohoe’s departure. But even sharp-tongued Ivan Yates said the broadcaster was talking "total shite" in the column, brandishing it as "absolute snobbery" and "nonsense". Speaking on the State of Affairs podcast, the former Fine Gael minister said: "You can say Simon Harris lacks substance, he tries to be all things to all people. There’s a million things, but to attack being a dropout from college as being unsuitable to be minister for finance….it’s absolute snobbery." Mr Yates himself, a broadcaster and businessman, didn’t complete his Leaving Cert, instead attending agricultural college and running the family farm at 16 years old when his father was diagnosed with cancer. The Tánaiste dropped out of a journalism degree at the DIT to focus on autism activism and politics. At 22 he gained a seat in Wicklow County Council, and became a TD in the Dáil two years later. Mr Callan also studied journalism, completing his degree from DCU in the early 2000s before working in various newsrooms and entering the comedy scene. On Tuesday, Mr Harris delivered his first budget as finance minister, a package the opposition have criticised for giving money to people who already have it. Just four days before this his wife Caoimhe gave birth to a baby girl, the couple's third child. With a budget and baby all in one week, the Tánaiste wasn’t too keen on lashing back at his RTÉ critic. Asked what his thoughts were on the column and the "college dropout" comment, the Finance Minister told us: "I haven't really thought about it. I've had a pretty busy week. But, yeah, Oliver… Oliver is…. we live in a free country." Subscribe to our newsletter for the latest news from the Irish Mirror direct to your inbox: Sign up here.
